World.title: Why public servants have less than a month to update pension records
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Public servants given until August 14 to update pension records [File]

Government has directed all public servants to update their records with the Public Service Superannuation Fund (PSSF) by August 14, 2026, in the latest step towards modernising pension administration.

In a circular signed by Principal Secretary for Public Service and Human Capital Development Dr Jane Imbunya, all PSSF members are expected to update their personal information and beneficiary details through the PSSF Member Self-Service Portal or the PSSF Mobile Application.

The circular was addressed to Ministries, State Departments, Constitutional Commissions, Independent Offices, County Public Service Boards and County Governments.

The exercise is expected to streamline pension administration and accelerate the processing of retirement benefits supported by a new Pension Administration System (PAS), a digital platform developed by PSSF to deliver faster, more transparent and more efficient pension services.

The registration exercise targets 529,635 members drawn from across the public service, including 332,950 teachers under the Teachers Service Commission (TSC), 120,084 officers in the disciplined services, 60,322 employees in Ministries, Departments, Constitutional Commissions and Agencies (MDCAs), and 16,279 county government employees.

PSSF Chief Executive Jonah Aiyabei said updating member records is critical to the success of the pension reforms and the delivery of efficient retirement services.

“By updating their records, public servants will enable quicker processing of retirement benefits, reduce administrative delays, improve data integrity, allow members to access pension services seamlessly through digital channels and ensure that the right benefits reach the right beneficiaries at the right time,” he said.

Under the new system, members can access their pension statements in real time, monitor contributions, view projected retirement benefits, update beneficiary nominations and personal details and initiate and track pension claims remotely.

The platform also features a Sponsor Portal that enables employer institutions to submit payroll information, contribution schedules and member data electronically, significantly improving efficiency and accountability in pension administration.

Dr Aiyabei said the Pension Administration System marks a significant milestone in the government’s efforts to digitise pension administration and restore dignity to retirees through faster, more accessible and transparent services.

“It will provide our members with real-time access to their pension information, enable seamless engagement with the Fund and support a fully digital, paperless pension administration process. Ultimately, our goal is to restore dignity in old age by ensuring every public servant receives timely and efficient pension services,” he said.

World.title: Inside Kenya's Ebola defences as seven Americans enter quarantine
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A doctor provides care to a patient with Ebola virus disease at the Rwampara Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC) in Bunia, Ituri, July 13, 2026. [AFP]

Seven American humanitarian workers are spending 21 days under medical observation in Kenya not because they are ill, but because they could become ill.

A Reuters report published today confirms they are seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART) staff from the Christian humanitarian organisation Samaritan's Purse . Franklin Graham, the organisation's President and CEO, confirmed this, saying:

“Samaritan's Purse has seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team staff members there. None of them have any symptoms, but they are being quarantined by the Kenyan government for 21 days."

The aid workers, all returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where they were involved in responding to the world's largest recorded outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, have no symptoms and have not tested positive for the virus.

Yet under new US public health rules, they cannot travel home immediately. Instead, they are completing a precautionary quarantine on Kenyan soil.

Their arrival has reignited debate over Kenya's role in regional outbreak preparedness and raised a question that extends far beyond the fate of the seven Americans:

If Ebola crossed Kenya's borders tomorrow, is the country ready?

The answer, infectious disease experts say, lies not in panic but in years of quiet preparation that most Kenyans have never seen.

That preparedness became evident during a recent visit by The Standard to Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH), where access to one of the hospital's high-security isolation areas was restricted.

Hospital officials informed the reporting team that patients with Mpox were being managed in the unit and, for safety reasons, journalists were not allowed to enter or film inside.

The brief encounter offered a glimpse into the strict infection prevention measures that underpin Kenya's readiness for dangerous infectious diseases.

According to an infectious disease physician at the Kenyatta National Hospital and head of the isolation ward, preparedness is far more than having an isolation room.

"One thing we should never do as Kenyans is panic," he says. "Panic only makes the situation worse. Instead, we should ask ourselves one question: Are we prepared?"

His answer is unequivocal. "As a government and as health institutions, we are in preparedness mode."

Dr Nyukuri explains that preparedness begins long before the first patient arrives at a hospital.

It means evaluating whether enough trained personnel are available, whether laboratories have the necessary testing reagents, whether protective equipment is adequate, and whether health workers understand every step required to safely manage a suspected Ebola patient.

"Here at Kenyatta National Hospital, we have conducted extensive training for healthcare workers," he says. "We have carried out readiness assessments, simulated patient scenarios and practised every stage of care from the moment a suspected patient arrives, through admission, isolation and treatment."

The simulations, he explains, are designed to ensure that no decision is being made for the first time during a real emergency. "When we eventually encounter a suspected case, it should not be something new to us." Dr Duncan Nyukuri, an Infectious Diseases specialist, during an interview with The Standard on July 16, 2026 at Kenyatta National Hospital. [Benard Orwongo, Standard]

Preparedness also extends beyond hospitals. Health surveillance teams remain stationed at airports and land border crossings, screening travellers arriving from affected regions while rapid response teams stand ready to investigate suspected infections.

"So far, Kenya has done a good job," Dr Nyukuri says. "We have not recorded a confirmed case despite the increasing numbers in the DRC. We pray that remains the case. But if we receive one patient, we are prepared."

How Ebola jumps from animals to people

Although Ebola is often associated with outbreaks, the virus begins its journey quietly in nature.

Dr Nyukuri explains that fruit bats are believed to be the natural reservoir of the virus. "They carry the virus without becoming sick themselves," he says.

Problems arise when increasing human activity brings people into closer contact with wildlife.

Mining, logging, hunting, charcoal burning, expanding settlements and encroachment into forests all increase the likelihood of viruses crossing from animals into humans.

"We call these zoonotic diseases," Dr Nyukuri explains. "Once the virus infects a human being, it can then spread from person to person through contact with infected body fluids, leading to outbreaks within families and communities."

You see, Ebola is a family; many people speak about Ebola as though it were a single virus.

In reality, scientists recognise five different species.

The best known is the Zaire strain, responsible for the devastating West African epidemic between 2014 and 2016.

"It is highly infectious and highly deadly," says Dr Nyukuri. "But because we have studied it extensively, we now have licensed vaccines and effective treatment options."

The Sudan strain, which has repeatedly caused outbreaks in Uganda, is the second most significant.

The current emergency, however, involves the Bundibugyo strain, first identified in Uganda's Bundibugyo District.

"This is the third recorded outbreak caused by Bundibugyo," Dr Nyukuri explains. "We have not studied it nearly as much as the Zaire strain."

There is currently no licensed vaccine specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola.

Instead, researchers are evaluating experimental vaccines while clinical trials in eastern DRC are testing promising treatments, including the monoclonal antibody MBP134 and the antiviral drug remdesivir.

"That is why this outbreak concerns many of us," he says. "We still have limited tools compared to what exists for the Zaire strain."

While Kenya has not recorded a confirmed case linked to the current outbreak, neighbouring countries remain on high alert.

Uganda on Thursday declared its last Ebola patient and has begun the mandatory 42-day countdown required before the country can officially be declared Ebola-free.

In contrast, eastern DRC continues battling sustained transmission, placing enormous pressure on treatment centres and frontline health workers.

It is against that backdrop that Kenya has found itself playing an increasingly important role in regional preparedness.

Their presence has nevertheless fuelled public debate over Kenya's preparedness infrastructure and the country's place in global health security.

Earlier this week, two American humanitarian workers who contracted Ebola while working in eastern DRC were medically evacuated to Germany for specialised treatment after receiving initial care in Bunia. Their evacuation underscores an important distinction: Kenya is currently serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed but healthy personnel, while confirmed Ebola patients requiring advanced clinical care have been transferred to Germany.

For Dr Nyukuri, the conversation should remain grounded in science rather than fear.

Preparedness, he says, is not measured only by isolation wards or specialised equipment, but by the ability of an entire health system to detect threats early, respond quickly and protect both patients and healthcare workers.

"My prayer is that Kenya never records a case," he says. "But preparedness means planning for the day you hope never comes."

As seven healthy humanitarian workers quietly complete their quarantine in Kenya, that preparation is no longer an abstract exercise.

It is being tested in real time. The development has also drawn attention to the contrasting roles played by East African countries during the current outbreak.

Uganda, widely regarded as one of Africa's most experienced countries in responding to Ebola, recently brought its own outbreak under control and has now entered the 42-day countdown required to be declared Ebola-free. Over the years, the country has built a reputation for rapidly detecting cases, tracing contacts and isolating patients, earning praise from the World Health Organization for repeatedly containing outbreaks before they spread widely.

Yet despite that experience, Uganda did not become a destination for foreign humanitarian workers requiring precautionary quarantine or post-exposure observation.

Instead, that role has fallen to Kenya, where seven American aid workers are now completing a mandatory 21-day quarantine after working in Ebola-affected areas of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The contrast raises broader questions about how countries are selected to support international outbreak responses. While Uganda has demonstrated its capacity to treat Ebola patients within its own borders, Kenya's involvement appears to reflect a different function—serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed personnel rather than a treatment centre for confirmed cases.

Health experts caution against interpreting the distinction as a measure of either country's clinical capability. Instead, they say such decisions are often influenced by a combination of bilateral agreements, operational logistics, evacuation arrangements and the specific objectives of international public health partners.

World.title: MPs push for urgent resolution of higher education funding crisis
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

HELB Chief Executive Officer Geoffrey Monari before the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Education on July 16, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

The National Assembly Departmental Committee on Education has called for urgent and coordinated action to address persistent funding challenges affecting Kenya's higher education sector.

The MPs proposed a joint engagement involving Parliament, the National Treasury and the Ministry of Education to streamline implementation of the Higher Education Funding Model.

The committee, chaired by Vice Chairperson Eve Obara, made the recommendation after holding separate meetings with officials from the State Department for Higher Education, the Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) and the Universities Fund during a review of the 2025/2026 Budget Implementation Status.

Appearing before the committee, Higher Education Principal Secretary Dr. Beatrice Inyangala said the Higher Education Funding Model is operational but continues to face implementation challenges due to inadequate alignment between the funding framework and budget allocations.

"The funding model is functional. However, the main challenge lies in budget alignment," Dr. Inyangala told Members.

The funding model was introduced to allocate financial support to university students based on their level of need, while ensuring sustainable financing for public universities.

However, implementation has generated debate over affordability, funding adequacy and delays in disbursement of resources to institutions.

MPs observed that the mismatch between policy and budgetary allocations has undermined effective financing of universities and agreed that a joint meeting involving the National Treasury, the Ministry of Education and Parliament would help harmonise the funding framework.

The committee also sought explanations over the growing stock of pending bills owed by public universities.

Dr. Inyangala informed Members that most of the outstanding obligations were inherited over several years, with universities continuing efforts to clear the debts despite increasing interest charges.

According to the State Department for Higher Education, public universities had accumulated pending bills amounting to Sh100.3 billion as of January 2026.

The ministry said institutions are prioritising settlement of pending obligations, suspending stalled development projects and exploring alternative revenue streams to prevent further accumulation of debt.

During a separate session, Members questioned HELB officials on how the board allocates student loans when available funding cannot meet demand from all eligible applicants.

Led by Chief Executive Officer Geoffrey Monari, HELB officials were asked to explain the criteria used in determining beneficiaries during periods of constrained resources.

Legislators emphasised that the allocation process should be fair, transparent and predictable to protect deserving students from being unfairly excluded.

World.title: High court suspends President Ruto's executive order placing IPOA under Interior Ministry
World.content:
The High Court has temporarily suspended the implementation of president William Ruto's Executive Order No. 2 of 2023 that placed the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) under the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, pending the hearing and determination of a constitutional petition challenging the directive.



Justice David Mburu of the High Court in Milimani law court issued the conservatory orders in a case filed by Jonathan Obwogi under Maalim and associates advocates against the Attorney General, the Cabinet Secretary for Interior and National Administration, and the Independent Policing Oversight Authority.



The court ruled that the contested section of the Executive Order would remain suspended until the constitutional petition is fully heard and determined.



The decision does not amount to a final declaration on the legality of the Executive Order. Instead, the court restored the legal position that existed before the order was issued to safeguard the constitutional issues raised in the petition from further prejudice.



Under Section 4 of the IPOA Act, the authority is required to operate independently and is not subject to the direction or control of any person, office or institution in the performance of its functions. The law further requires all government agencies to assist and protect IPOA's independence, prohibits interference with its decision making and operations, and obligates Parliament to ensure it receives adequate funding.



The conservatory orders mean that the Ministry of Interior cannot, for now, supervise, administer, direct or exercise authority over IPOA based on Executive Order No. 2 of 2023.



The court's decision, however, does not affect IPOA's day-to-day operations. The authority will continue carrying out its statutory mandate, including investigating complaints against police officers, probing deaths and serious injuries arising from police action, and undertaking all responsibilities assigned to it under the IPOA Act.



In the petition, the applicant also sought to compel IPOA's Chairperson, or another authorised officer, to disclose through an affidavit whether the authority had implemented the Executive Order, the extent to which it had operated under the Ministry of Interior, and any operational changes that may have resulted. The petitioner argued that such information would help establish whether the authority's statutory independence had been compromised.



The High Court observed that the question of whether Executive Order No. 2 of 2023 is constitutional will only be determined after hearing submissions from all parties.



The matter is scheduled for a mention on September 21, 2026, when the court is expected to issue further directions.

World.title: Huthi blockade threat raises risk of dual energy chokepoint crisis, Kpler says
World.content:
A threat by the Iranian backed Houthis to blockade Saudi-linked shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has raised the prospect of the Middle East’s two key energy chokepoints coming under pressure at the same time, shipping analytics firm Kpler warned Tuesday.

A “simultaneous and prolonged disruption of Bab el-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz could affect maritime routes carrying approximately one-quarter of global oil supply,” the firm said in a written analysis.

The firm said Bab el-Mandeb – which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean – remains open, but traffic is already running far below pre-crisis levels while conditions in Hormuz have “deteriorated sharply.”

According to Kpler, crossings through Bab el-Mandeb averaged about 41 vessels a day between July 15 and July 20, “43% below the 2023 peak of 72/day.”

Saudi crude loadings through the strait fell 34% in two weeks, dropping from 29.58 million barrels in the week of June 29 to 19.50 million barrels in the week of July 13, the analysis said.

Kpler said the Houthi threat is especially significant because Saudi Arabia has increasingly used the Red Sea route as a fallback for exports after disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.

Kpler examined several possible scenarios, ranging from limited self-diversion by cautious operators to a full blockade. Under “selective targeting,” it said, “compliant commercial traffic could fall 40–50% within weeks, pushing crossings toward 20–25/day.” Under a full blockade, Bab el-Mandeb “could follow Hormuz and fall below 15 vessels/day within days,” the analysis said.

In a separate note published Tuesday, Kpler said two tankers carrying Saudi crude reversed course in the Red Sea after the Houthi declaration.

World.title: How a YouTube video accidentally proved the existence of Libya’s ‘desert ghosts’
World.content:
It’s not every day that a YouTube video triggers a major wildlife discovery, yet that’s exactly what Mohammed Almuntasir unknowingly did when he hit upload in 2017.

Clocking in at just 18 seconds, the clip showed a fun-sized feline curling up under the shade of a desert shrub in the photographer’s native Libya. Almost a decade later, it was confirmed as the first documented evidence that the North African country was home to the sand cat, a wild felid that is as elusive as it is adorable.

A longtime field photographer of plants and animals across the North African country, it was not that Almuntasir had not realized what he was looking at. He had seen sand cats in Libya previously, but their nocturnal nature had foiled his attempts to capture footage.

“As soon as I saw the animal, I knew it was a sand cat because I had seen the species before at night,” Almuntasir told CNN via email.

“However, I had never been able to photograph it because I did not have a camera suitable for night photography, or camera traps.”

Almuntasir was initially oblivious to the scientific significance of his footage. Courtesy Mohammed Almuntasir

Almuntasir assumed the diminutive desert cats — which typically grow to a maximum of 22.5 inches (57 centimeters) and 7.5 pounds (3.5 kilograms) — had already been documented in his homeland.

Yet despite some scattered reports dating back to the mid-20th century, the sand cat (Felis margarita) had never been officially verified as native to Libya, Firas Hayder, an expert on North African small carnivores, told CNN; instead, it was primarily associated with Sahara regions across other North African countries like Morocco, as well as Southwest and Central Asia.

Hence Hayder’s shock when he contacted Almuntasir a few weeks after the video was posted, and the photographer nonchalantly confirmed that — true to the YouTube video’s title — “sand cat in Libya” had indeed been filmed in the Al-Hamada Al-Hamra region of the Libyan Desert, close to the Tunisian border.

“I told him, ‘No!’” laughed Hayder, a wildlife ecologist and North Africa regional coordinator for the African Small Carnivore Research Initiatives, a nonprofit headquartered at South Africa’s Sol Plaatje University.

“’For you, it is normal, but for us not.’ He was surprised. He told me, ‘Are you sure?’ And I said, ‘Yes, this is the first record.’”

Ghost hunting

From there, the duo joined forces on an eight-year effort to collate documented sightings of sand cats — as well as Saharan striped polecats — in Libya, culminating in “Rediscovering desert ghosts,” a research paper published in the Journal of Arid Environments in February this year.

A collaboration of seven researchers, the study saw Hayder quarterback the operation remotely, teaching Almuntasir how to record GPS coordinates of where the sand cats were sighted. The photographer worked closely with local guides to track and observe the animals.

Almuntasir quickly realized it would be an “extremely challenging” undertaking. Hunting mostly at night for rodents and reptiles, sand cats are prolific diggers: they are known to stay in burrows during the hottest daylight hours, as well as burying both feces and remains of kills to eat later. With water at a premium, the cats can survive solely on the moisture received by drinking the blood of their prey.

Known to travel huge distances and with sand quickly sweeping away paw prints, the elusiveness of the naturally camouflaged species is a key contributing factor to their under-researched status — kittens were only photographed in the wild for the first time in 2017.

That trio of juvenile felines were spotted hiding in a Moroccan desert shrub by Dr. Grégory Breton, managing director of the French branch of global wild cat conservation organization Panthera, with images of the tiny cats immediately going viral.

Perseverance paid off, though, as Almuntasir personally accounted for 24 of the study’s 36 sand cat observations. Overall, they were logged at 13 locations across the Libyan Sahara, predominantly in the southwest of the country, suggesting the region is a “potential stronghold” for the species.

Yet “major knowledge gaps” remain, the study stressed, and closing them could be essential to ensuring that sand cats do not become true ghosts in Libya and beyond.

While the species is currently listed as “least concern” by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) — meaning it doesn’t qualify for an at-risk category — researchers have previously pushed for the authority to reconsider the assessment, which was made in 2014.

Sand cats could be more endangered than previously suspected due to “their home range, the limited resources and fragile ecosystem,” Breton, who coauthored a study of Moroccan sand cats published in 2023, told CNN at the time, adding that there had been cases of the species being captured for the illegal pet trade.

Like several other small carnivore species in the region, sand cats are under threat. Courtesy Mohammed Almuntasir

Hayder echoes Breton’s conservation concerns, particularly around environmental factors. Acutely sensitive to increases in temperature, small carnivores like the sand cat can act as a “sentinel” for climate change.

“If you want to check if a habitat is in good (condition), you have to study the small carnivores,” said Hayder, who theorizes that climate change could have already contributed to a drop in sand cat populations.

Observations in Libya supported more of Breton’s fears. During his field work, Almuntasir reported seeing sand cats sold at local markets, often as pets, while Hayder said he had spoken to hunters who killed them for meat.

For Hayder, it is a painfully familiar tale that spurs him to want to increase awareness and understanding of small carnivores — from caracal to fennec foxes — across North Africa.

The ecologist believes a lack of public knowledge around the various species is fueling human-carnivore conflict, an area of research he has previously explored in relation to negative social media perceptions of the Egyptian weasel.

“For me, it is like a challenge,” Hayder said. “I feel that I have to change the mentality.”

World.title: Why a week of protests pushed Zelensky to bring in a younger military chief
World.content:
For a war imposing such radical change on the battlefield, the retention of 60-year-old Oleksandr Syrskyi as Ukraine’s top commander had become an anomaly. That’s not ageism, but a reflection of the recently sacked Ukrainian military chief’s mindset.

In this light, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision Tuesday to replace Syrskyi with 43-year-old Mykhailo Drapatyi – a younger general from a newer generation of military leaders – seems perhaps overdue.

Syrskyi was a creature of the Soviet era, and brought to the first years of the war a dogged, brutal persistence, coupled with flourishes of strategic brilliance. He suited Ukraine’s initial need to match, and occasionally outwit, a larger, bloodier enemy. The defense of Kyiv in 2022, the rapid recapture of Kharkiv region later that year, and the sudden invasion of Kursk – Russia itself – in 2024, all are to his credit.

But his leadership was also marked by tremendous losses in Ukraine’s ranks. And ultimately, the same political infighting and naked ambition that led to his rise would lead to his downfall.

Zelensky listens to Oleksandr Syrskyi as he visits a position of Ukrainian servicemen in the town of Kupiansk on November 30, 2023. Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Reuters

Syrskyi got the job after the 2023 counteroffensive failed, and the-then top commander, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, was moved to London as Ukraine’s ambassador. Many analysts suggest the failure stemmed from Syrskyi convincing Zelensky that a simultaneous push against the eastern city of Bakhmut and the Zaporizhzhia front in the south would split Russia’s defenses. Instead, it split the strength of Kyiv’s much vaunted summer push, which failed.

Syrskyi rose to the top also because Zaluzhnyi had perhaps become too popular, with his face often seen on military café walls; polls showed him wildly more liked than anyone else. And so, failure on the battlefield guaranteed his departure.

Fast forward two years, and a similar situation repeats itself: a clash on strategy flares up and leads Zelensky to – at first – dispense with a rising, popular star, 35-year-old Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. The disrupter-in-chief, he had too openly sparred with Syrskyi about reform, and Zelensky – also too openly – had to admit he’d become the arbiter between the men. You can’t run a war like that, he said, quite correctly. The removal of Fedorov, a pioneer in technology and recruitment, sparked rare protests in Ukraine’s streets.

People protest against Zelensky’s decision to replace Mykhailo Fedorov as defense minister in Kyiv on July 17. Thomas Peter/Reuters

The week of melodrama followed a familiar pattern for Zelensky – reminiscent of a crisis a year ago over the fate of Ukraine’s anti-corruption bureau. Zelensky limited its powers, and then changed his mind, firing his chief of staff over corruption allegations, all because a protest movement had chipped away at his Teflon veneer. Zelensky seems to have learned almost nothing from that episode. And the repeat cycle – of action, protest, reaction – reveals two things about where Ukraine’s war is at now.

First, Ukraine’s military Tuesday underwent a generational shift. Syrskyi’s way of war – large frontal assaults that were costly, if not the only real way to reclaim land – had begun to look dated. Fedorov’s assault on the old ways – instead using robots, drones, automation, data to determine why troops were injured – all made sense in a country desperately short of troops. They put Ukraine at the global forefront of battlefield technology.

This new army was not Fedorov’s idea alone, but he had become its central proponent, and slowly the face of the victories it won: the headlines about robot rescues and assaults, and the relentless toll of Ukraine’s long-range strikes into Russia. The successes were those of Ukraine, but also of Fedorov, who trumpeted his decision to fund drone purchases earlier this year.

Service members of the 422nd Unmanned Systems Regiment prepare a strike drone for a flight in an undisclosed location in southern Ukraine. Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

It is too early to tell if drones and robots truly can replace troops on the frontlines. Ukraine has little choice but to find out, and the time spent learning that lesson has provided Kyiv a useful pause to regroup, and a powerful technological upgrade that Moscow still has to match. War will never be the same again – until, that is, someone learns how to switch off the machines. Even now, some strategists argue, artillery retains a role in halting large-scale Russian advances. Not everything from the past is redundant overnight.

Yet Fedorov’s rise – the egos and jockeying aside – marked a simple shift: the younger Ukrainians who fight the war would be led by generals who are about the same age as them.

The new commander, Drapatyi, fought across the war’s toughest front lines, and video was even recycled on his appointment on Tuesday of him driving an armored personnel carrier through a pro-Russian separatist barricade in 2014. He is no novice, but he is not from Syrskyi’s generation. Eight years separate him and Fedorov, with his hacker mentality; 17 years separate him and Syrskyi, whose appetite for brutal assault units earned him the nickname, “the Butcher.”

Drapatyi gained similar experience to Syrskyi in the war, yet garnered a reputation for wins and reform. He was key to halting Russia’s initial invasion around the city of Kryvyi Rih, and then oversaw its rout from Kherson, but also stopped Russian advances later in Kharkiv region. He was an early champion of the use of drones to create a “kill zone” along the front line and effectively immobilize the Russian advance. His leadership of the land forces also saw a radical structural and leadership rethink.

Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi attends a meeting with Zelensky in Kyiv on Monday. Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Reuters

Ukraine’s challenges do not vanish with this injection of relative youth to the top ranks. The country still lacks manpower, cash, and critical infrastructure to endure the next winter. But they have brought in new talent and retained a focus on new ideas and technology that had turned both the narrative of the war, and its dynamics, in their favor. In that sense,the past few days have been a small victory. Yet the episode provides another, less edifying lesson for Ukrainians.

The takeaway is that, politically, Zelensky dislikes the narrative slipping from his hands, almost as much as he dislikes parallel personalities garnering popularity. In hindsight, the entire incident was avoidable; Zelensky could have removed Syrskyi a week ago – as had seemed inevitable for months, as talk of his failings echoed around Kyiv. Instead, the public spat between the young Fedorov and older general led Zelensky to stick with the old, loyal guard.

Syrskyi had over the years proven himself the more capable political operator, and perhaps Zelensky feared the disruption in the established command his departure would provoke. Or was he more concerned that the young disruptor might have been seen to force upon him a key personnel change?

Zelensky’s instinct was to ditch the rising, popular star. Then the streets erupted with sizeable – but not massive – protests. And Zelensky began the slow, purposeful task of reversing course, with a series of public meetings with top military commanders – a sounding board, and auditions for a post that Syrskyi had clearly already lost.

It is unlikely Zelensky sought this protracted route to an outcome he could have expedited last week. Yet still, the spectacle of the enlightened president, listening to both the people, particularly the younger generation, and his military commanders, remains.

Ukraine’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov attends a meeting at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Belgium, on February 12. Tom Nicholson/Reuters

It is unclear what “prominent” role Fedorov has been offered in the government, or if he will accept it. That has become less the point: Zelensky has shown his Western allies and voters that he listens and can make disruptive change permanent. It is only really through changing the landscape of the fight that Kyiv can injure Moscow.

But one curiosity remains: Zelensky once said he would sit on the beach and drink a beer when the war ends. Indeed, it is hard to imagine why he would still want the country’s top job after the true, “just” peace he seeks takes hold. There is, in wartime Ukraine, no real mechanism to replace him, as valid elections are almost impossible. To that degree, he is invulnerable. Yet still he remains acutely obsessed with his popularity, to the extent that possible rivals, Zalyuzhnyi and Fedorov, are removed, despite their talents – and notably after they both clashed with Syrskyi.

Zelensky has been the consummate showman and salesman for Ukraine’s war effort in the international arena. But these glimpses of frailty at home betray a Bankova presidential headquarters where bad decisions – against corruption and Fedorov – are made quickly, and then slowly unpicked after popular pressure.

It is democracy in action, yes, but begs the question: How many other poor calls have gone unchallenged over the past four years?

World.title: Trump approves deal with Saudi Arabia that could allow kingdom to enrich nuclear fuel, official says
World.content:
President Donald Trump has approved a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia that could lead to the kingdom enriching its own fuel for civilian reactors, according to a US official.

The deal would last 30 years and could be announced as soon as Wednesday, according to the official, who added the agreement would involve American companies providing technology and expertise in developing the Saudi program.

The Trump administration intends to send the deal to Congress after it is announced.

Any agreement to give Saudi Arabia access to nuclear technology could prove controversial, both domestically and within the wider Middle East region, since the ability to enrich nuclear fuel could, in theory, eventually lead to the creation of nuclear weapons.

The agreement includes limits on what inspections might be carried out on the Saudi program, according to the US official, which may draw skepticism from lawmakers.

Israel, a country that is widely believed to have undeclared nuclear weapons, has long been wary of Saudi Arabia accessing nuclear technology.

Iran, Saudi Arabia’s main rival in the region, has a stockpile of enriched uranium and has vowed to cling to its nuclear program even after months of US bombardment, claiming the program is for civilian purposes.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has pledged to seek a nuclear weapon if Iran were ever to produce one.

Uranium enrichment and plutonium reprocessing are the two main pathways to create the core materials necessary to build nuclear weapons. Most countries with civilian nuclear reactors that require enriched uranium don’t produce it domestically — they instead purchase the material from vendors like the US or Russia and receive it in sealed shipments under strict international supervision.

The US has been eying a Saudi civilian nuclear agreement for years. Under the Biden administration, such an arrangement was viewed as part of a broader normalization pact between Saudi Arabia and Israel. But those efforts faltered after the October 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks. The Trump administration picked up the nuclear discussions last year.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

World.title: Turkish President praises Spain’s humanitarian stance on Palestine
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan praised Spain’s humanitarian stance on the Palestinian issue, adding that it was one greatly appreciated by football fans worldwide.

According to a statement issued by the Turkish Presidency, Erdogan congratulated Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Spain’s World Cup victory during a phone call.

He expressed his deep appreciation for the joy of the Palestinians in Gaza who watched the match amidst the rubble following Spain’s triumph.

During the call, on Tuesday, the two leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional and international issues.

Erdogan expressed his gratitude for Sánchez’s attendance at the NATO summit in Ankara on July 7-8.

Erdogan added that he would be pleased to welcome Sánchez back to Turkey in early 2027 for the Turkey-Spain Intergovernmental Summit, which is expected to witness the signing of new agreements and the strengthening of bilateral cooperation in several sectors.

World.title: Egypt condemns any threats targeting Saudi Arabia’s security
World.content:
Egypt strongly condemned any threats targeting the security of Saudi Arabia, which undermines the security and stability of the region and threatens the safety of maritime navigation, international trade, and vital waterways.

In a statement issued by the Foreign Ministry, Egypt affirmed that these threats constitute a flagrant violation of international law, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and relevant Security Council resolutions.

Egypt stressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and all the Gulf Cooperation Council states, and its support for all measures they take to preserve their security, stability, sovereignty, and territorial integrity.

It emphasized the importance of prioritizing political and diplomatic solutions and respecting the rules of international law, in order to maintaining peace within the region.

World.title: Has Egypt’s government shut down loan apps?
World.content:
An informed source at the Financial Regulatory Authority denied social media speculations on Egypt’s government closing the branches of a large number of non-banking financial companies and institutions.

In a statement to the Middle East News Agency, the source explained that the decision circulating on social media dates back to October 2025, and only involved the cancellation of microfinance licenses for a number of Category C NGOs and institutions.

The source emphasized that the names mentioned on those anonymous social media accounts have no connection whatsoever to the previous decision.

He urged citizens to carefully verify information and consult the proper official channels before sharing information on social media.

World.title: Prosecution closes investigations into unofficial AI-generated Messi and Salah GEM video
World.content:
The Haram Prosecution Office on Tuesday has moved to close investigations into the creation of an AI-generated Lionel Messi and Mohamed Salah video at the Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM), and to dismiss any suspicion of a crime against the video’s author, graphic designer Abdel-Rahman Khaled.

The case dates back to a report filed by the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities denying any connection to the video, which had been widely circulated on social media platforms – to much confusion.

This led to the arrest of the designer at his residence in Cairo.

Khaled faced accusations of publishing unauthorized visual content infringing on intellectual property rights.

The prosecution’s decision to close the case came after technical examinations and investigations revealed “the absence of criminal intent on the part of the accused, and that the video did not cause any material or moral harm to official bodies or public figures.”

The decision indicated that the work was simply an example of a hobbyist showcasing digital skills without any financial gain.

World.title: Government, THP-Z launch additional food security project in Sinda
World.content:
The Hunger Project – Zambia has partnered with the government to launch an additional food security project in Sinda District of Eastern Province, called Food Second Project, valued at K5.8 Million.

The move compliments the Epicenter initiative being implemented in Ching’ombe and Kamwaza Wards in Sinda.

The two-year Australian Donor Funded Food Second Project, targets to empower 530 farmers with agricultural inputs and support.

Sinda District Commissioner, David Tembo, who officiated at the launch ‎has acknowledged the massive support The Hunger Project – Zambia (THP-Z) has demonstrated in the district towards improving the livelihoods of the locals.

Mr Tembo noted that THP-Z’s Water First Project while implementing an Epicenter, has complimented government’s efforts in curbing the water crisis in rural Sinda.

The project has seen 16 water schemes being constructed across Ching’ombe and Kamwaza Wards.

The District Commissioner said the Food Second Project will not only benefit the 530 farmer households that have been targeted, but the entire district as it stands to gain economically, with a strengthened household food security.

Mr Tembo, who boasted of Sinda’s many successes in various sectors such as agriculture and education, has assured THP-Z and its donors that the project will be successful.

“I want to express my gratitude to the various cooperating partners who have been complimenting government efforts in various sectors. My office further pledges the government’s full support towards the implementation of projects in the district,” he indicated.

And The Hunger Project – Zambia Country Director, Samuel Mutambo, also stated that the Food Second Project is aiming at strengthening food security not only in the two wards but the entire district.

‎Mr Mutambo noted that with hands put together, ensuring the project’s success to achieve greatness is the goal.

“The project intends to help communities become food secure as it aims at supplying targeted farmers with hybrid maize, beans and ground nuts seeds with fertilisers and other agricultural requirements and tools for production,” he disclosed.

He also revealed that, working with the Department of Agriculture, the farmers will be trained in climate smart agricultural practices as they are currently limited with what they can produce due to climate change effects.

“I am optimistic that once the project is running, malnutrition and poverty will drop to the lowest numbers, if not curbed,” he said.

He reiterated that his organisation remains committed to‎ complimenting government’s efforts of ensuring better livelihoods for the marginalised population.

World.title: Dept. of Health in Nakonde targets all under-fives for polio vaccination
World.content:
The Department of Health Services in Nakonde District of Muchinga Province is optimistic that no child under the age of five will be left behind in the third round of the national polio vaccination campaign.

Nakonde District Health Promotions Officer, Getrude Chipampe, says health teams will move across communities to administer oral polio vaccine to an estimated 70,109 children.

Speaking in an interview with the media today, Ms Chipampe said the campaign is aimed at protecting children from the poliovirus, which can cause irreversible damage if contracted.

“Health officers will be going round giving children below the age of five years polio vaccine to prevent the polio virus,” she said.

She explained that the department will use both door-to-door visits and fixed teams stationed at schools, markets and other public places to reach every eligible child.

The Nakonde District Health Promotions Officer appealed to parents and guardians, particularly mothers, to keep children at home during the campaign period.

Ms Chipampe also addressed concerns from some religious groups that have previously resisted vaccination, urging them to reconsider for the sake of child health.

She further clarified misconceptions about multiple doses, stating that receiving the vaccine during the campaign will not replace routine immunisation.

“Those children that need to get the routine polio vaccination at 9 months will still be required to do so when it is time despite being administered during this campaign.

“Some people would say the concentration of the medicine would be too much in the body but that is not the case, it only strengthens the immune system and makes it hard for the virus to penetrate,” she explained.

Ms Chipampe indicated that the district performed well in the first two rounds despite challenges with one religious community that initially refused the vaccine but later cooperated after intervention by health promotion officers and UNICEF.

She stated that the department has been consistently engaging those that refuse and expressed hope that they will not face similar challenges during the third round.

According to district records, in round one, the target was 55,730 children and 66,440 were vaccinated while in round two the target was 66,440 and 70,109 children were reached.

The campaign commenced yesterday, Tuesday July 21, and will run up to tomorrow, Thursday, July 24, 2026.

World.title: Truck parking bay commissioned in Kasenengwa
World.content:
Government has commissioned a truck parking bay valued at over K2.1 Million in Kasenengwa District of Eastern Province.

The project which is located near the recently commissioned fuel depot, aims at boosting the local authority’s revenue collection base among other benefits.

Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development Permanent Secretary for Technical Services, Nicholas Phiri, says the move has been necessitated through the Zambia Devolution Support Programme.

Mr Phiri explained that the project is aimed at uplifting the livelihoods of people in rural areas.

“This project aims at uplifting rural communities like Kasenengwa, by presenting them with equal opportunities,” he said.

And Kasenengwa District Commissioner, Rachael Phiri, said the move will help to provide a secure parking space for drivers among other benefits.

Ms Phiri further pledged the government’s commitment to enhancing the safety of truck drivers as well as the vehicles.

“We are deeply grateful for your leadership and the support evidenced by such projects like the parking bay,” she said.

And, Kasenengwa Town Council Secretary, Lynda Mapara, represented by Director Human Resource, Fredrick Peneshi, observed that the move will boost revenue collection for the local authority.

Meanwhile, Headman Kapachika called on the local authority not to relent in developing rural areas.

“As traditional leaders, we are encouraged to avail land for such development. We know our people are the main beneficiaries,” he said.

World.title: President Hichilema assures completion of Lusaka-Ndola Dual Carriageway
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has assured the completion of the Lusaka-Ndola Dual Carriageway.

President Hichilema says the road which is nearing completion, will improve connectivity, facilitate trade and contribute to the country’s economic development.

He said the USD650 million project is being implemented through a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) at no cost to the government, compared to the proposal under the previous administration which would have cost more than one billion United States dollars.

President Hichilema was speaking today during a drive through inspection of the Lusaka-Ndola Dual Carriageway to appreciate the works done so far on the project.

“We are going to ensure that this Great North Dual Carriageway is complete. We made sure the road is being constructed at a more reasonable price as opposed to the initial cost under the former government,” President Hichilema said.

Addressing the residents of 10 miles area, President Hichilema urged Zambians to vote for the UPND in next month’s general elections to ensure that the project and other ongoing development programmes are completed.

“I am urging you to vote for continuation of development in the country,” he said.

The Head of State advised citizens not to return to what he described as the days of political violence and economic instability under the previous administration.

He further reminded citizens of the importance of the Free Education Policy and the school feeding programme, saying the initiatives have expanded access to education and provided support to learners.

President Hichilema said there would be no justification for changing the current leadership if the opposition supports many of the policies being implemented by the New Dawn Administration.

And President Hichilema directed that four volunteer nurses who were part of the gathered residents along the roadside be recruited into the public service next month.

The President later continued with his drive-through inspection of the Lusaka-Ndola Dual Carriageway.

World.title: Patson Daka starts life in Germany
World.content:
Chipolopolo striker Patson Daka has begun life in Germany after signing a one-year contract with Bundesliga side Hamburg SV.

He was officially unveiled by the club on Wednesday.

Daka, 27, was club-less since the expiry of his contract at English side Leicester City at the end of the 2025/2026 season.

He was part of the Wednesday training after joining his new teammates.

Daka told the club media: “I’m very happy to be here and can’t wait to get started. I’m a passionate and energetic player whose job is to score goals. I believe I can help the team by doing exactly that.”

He spent five years at Leicester City but suffered demotion twice to from the Premier League to League One with the Foxes.

“I’ve watched a few HSV matches. It’s an exciting team, and I’m delighted to now be part of it. The club’s management gave me a very warm welcome and made me feel from the very beginning that this is a family environment.”

“The overall package made perfect sense to me, so I didn’t have to think for long. The many positive conversations made the decision an easy one,” Daka added.

He appeared cheerful during training.

World.title: Govt. calls for scalable models to accelerate food systems transformation
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to building productive, resilient and nutrition sensitive agri-food systems with the recent launch of the National Food and Nutrition Security Policy, its Implementation Plan and the National Stunting Reduction Strategy.

Office of the Vice President Permanent Secretary Administration, Lilian Kapusana, says the three instruments provide a comprehensive framework to address Zambia’s food security and nutrition challenges during the Food Systems Technical Dialogue on Scalable Success Models and the Convergence Initiative.

Ms Kapusana who was represented by Director Planning and Information, Yengwe Kakusa was speaking during the food system technical dialogue on the scalable success model and convergence initiative in Zambia.

She stated that the Policy provides strategic direction for strengthening multi-sectoral action, while the implementation plan translates policy into clear actions and responsibilities.

Ms Kapusana indicated that the stunting Reduction Strategy, targets one of Zambia’s most persistent development challenges by improving child nutrition and safeguarding the future health and productivity of children.

“These policy frameworks reaffirm Government’s commitment to ensuring that every Zambian has access to sufficient, safe, affordable and nutritious food,” Ms Kapusana said.

She noted that the Office of the Vice President is mandated to coordinate Zambia’s Food Systems Transformation Agenda and Nutrition Security, and has strengthened multi-sectoral collaboration as it works with the National Food and Nutrition Commission, National Food Systems Convener and cooperating partners.

Ms Kapusana said the dialogue is timely as it provides an opportunity to assess progress, identify challenges and agree on practical actions to accelerate transformation.

She highlighted climate change, prolonged droughts and floods, land degradation, rising food prices and changing consumption patterns as key threats, but also as opportunities to transform how Zambia produces, processes, distributes and consumes food.

Ms Kapusana has called for increased investment in climate-smart agriculture, diversified food production, resilient value chains, improved market access, reduction of food loss and waste, and sustainable fisheries and livestock systems, while ensuring healthy diets and protecting natural resources.

“Let us focus on interventions that have demonstrated results and explore how they can be expanded through stronger coordination, increased investment and effective partnerships,” she urged participants.

She encouraged delegates to develop actionable, evidence based recommendations to guide the next phase of Zambia’s Food Systems Transformation, stressing that transforming food systems is a shared national responsibility requiring coordinated action by Government, cooperating partners, civil society, academia, the private sector and farmer organisations.

And Food Systems Regional Advisor for Africa at the UN Food Systems Coordination Hub, Martin Bwalya, noted that food insecurity, malnutrition, climate change, biodiversity loss and youth unemployment are deeply interconnected and require integrated responses.

“Food systems transformation is one of the strongest accelerators of the 2030 Agenda and of key national economic growth and development goals,”Mr Bwalya said.

Mr Bwalya said the Hub was established after the 2021 UN Food Systems Summit to support countries in translating national pathways into action through demand driven technical assistance, coordination and access to financing.

Meanwhile, United Nations Resident Coordinator, Beatrice Mutali, represented by Food and Agriculture Organsation Representative, George Chomba, said food systems must become more resilient and nutrition sensitive to meet the needs of present and future generations.

She noted that millions still face hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition, while climate change, environmental degradation and economic pressure continue to strain systems.

“The United Nations recognises that no single institution can transform food systems without partnership,” she said.

Ms Mutali reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to supporting Zambia in strengthening food security, improving nutrition, promoting climate-friendly practices, enhancing resilience, supporting sustainable natural resource management, strengthening social protection and improving livelihoods.

She also acknowledged the support received from the Government and the European Union, stressing that partnership with government, European partners, research institutions, civil society, farmer organisations and the private sector is central to delivering results.

World.title: Govt. renews call for safer facility-based childbirths
World.content:
Lusaka District Commissioner, Rosa Kayuni has reiterated government’s call on expectant mothers to utilise health facilities in the district to prevent maternal mortality.

Ms Kayuni said government has built maternity annexes in the district to ensure that no woman dies during or after giving birth.

She was speaking during the launch of the polio round 3 vaccinations in Lusaka’s Mandevu Township.

“The new dawn government considers health as a strategic investment, as can be seen in the consistent recruitment of healthcare workers from 2022 to date, construction of maternity annexes, health posts, and health centres and hospitals,” she said.

Ms Kayuni added that the provision of adequate medicines and medical supplies in the health facilities is also a testament of government’s commitment to providing quality health services to the citizenry in the district and the country at large.

The District Commissioner said Lusaka District remains at high risk of importation and transmission of polio virus due to increased population movements.

She called for concerted efforts from all the stakeholders to help ensure that all eligible children are vaccinated against polio.

She also called on communities to be vigilant and get information about measles prevention.

Ms Kayuni said measles remains a significant public health threat in the district.

“I am appealing to stakeholders, the local authority and other sectors to come on board to help mitigate the spread of measles in the district,” she said.

Speaking earlier, Mandevu Subdistrict Public Health Specialist, Dr Chota Chishimba said the launched polio campaign is a critical step in protecting children, safeguarding families and moving communities closer to a polio free future.

“Let us adhere to the vaccination protocol of reaching every child, follow safety and cold-chain procedures, maintain accurate records, and engage communities. Together we can close immunity gaps and prevent any resurgence of disease,” she said.

Representing the District Director for health services, Astridah Maseka, Acting Public Health Specialist, Dr Kelvin Sinkala echoed the need for support from all stakeholders if the vaccination exercise is to be successful.

The vaccination exercise which commenced on 21st July, 2026, ending on the 24th July, 2026 is being undertaken under the theme: “Polio is preventable, get your child vaccinated.”

World.title: Over 70,000 learners benefit from TIEEZ programme
World.content:
More than 70,000 learners in 170 government primary and secondary schools across Northern, Southern and Eastern provinces have benefited from education interventions under the Targeted Improvement for Equitable Education in Zambia (TIEEZ) programme.

Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Technical Services Kelvin Mambwe, disclosed that over 7,000 learners, 56 percent of them girls, are now enrolled in the Promoting Equality in African Schools (PEAS) school network.

Speaking during the Empowerment and Development for Girls’ Education (EDGE) Programme in Lusaka, Dr Mambwe said the achievements demonstrate the impact of partnerships in strengthening Zambia’s education system and expanding access to quality education.

He said lasting improvements in education begin in the classroom but must extend across the entire education system.

Dr Mambwe said the collaboration between the Ministry of Education, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) and PEAS has strengthened school leadership, improved teaching practices, promoted safeguarding and created better learning environments, particularly for girls and other vulnerable learners.

He explained that between 2021 and 2026, four new PEAS secondary schools were established in Chinsali, Ndola, Chirundu and Sinda, while existing schools were expanded from 30 to 108 classrooms.

Dr Mambwe said the investments have improved access to safe learning spaces, expanded boarding facilities and created opportunities for many young people who would otherwise have been unable to continue their education.

He further noted that the programme has strengthened pre-service teacher preparation by expanding practical training from two to five colleges of education, benefiting hundreds of student teachers before they enter the teaching profession.

Dr Mambwe added that approaches developed through the EDGE programme, including school leadership, school improvement planning, safeguarding, teacher coaching and improved teaching practices, are now informing broader reforms across the country’s education system.

He urged education stakeholders and cooperating partners to continue aligning their efforts with government priorities to build a stronger, more inclusive and sustainable education system that delivers quality learning outcomes for future generations.

PEAS Zambia Country Director, Beatrice Likando said school improvement plans, stronger teacher support and enhanced safeguarding measures have significantly improved the quality of education in Zambia’s schools over the past five years.

Ms Likando said the programme has demonstrated that sustainable improvements in education are achieved when government, cooperating partners and implementing organisations work together towards a common goal.

Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), Human Development Team Leader, Nicola Oldham commended government and stakeholders for the milestones recorded in the EDGE Programme.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - July 22, 2026
World.content:
Ghana Opposition Slams 20-Year Illegal Mining Sentence

Ghana's opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) has condemned the conviction of its Ashanti regional chairman, Bernard Antwi Boasiako, popularly known as "Chairman Wontumi", after he was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment with hard labour for illegal mining offences. Boasiako has been convicted of granting mineral rights without approval and facilitating unlicensed mining through his company, Akonta Mining. He is the first senior Ghanaian politician to be convicted since the government's crackdown on illegal mining began in 2017. The NPP has said the verdict is politically motivated and it will appeal. Environmental campaigners have hailed the conviction as a major step in holding powerful people accountable for illegal mining, which has caused widespread environmental damage across Ghana.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigerian Officers Arrested Over Alleged Extortion of Anti-Graft Chief

Four Nigerian police officers are facing disciplinary action after allegedly setting up an illegal checkpoint in Abuja to extort money from motorists, including the head of the country's anti-corruption agency. Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission chairman Musa Aliyu alleged that the officers stopped him and forced him to withdraw $38 from an ATM after threatening to take him to court over a supposed traffic offence. Following Aliyu's complaint, police launched an operation that led to the officers' arrest. The Commissioner of Police, Ahmed Sanusi, said that the alleged abuse of power will not be tolerated, and officers who commit criminal acts will have no place in the police service.

Senegal Backs Macky Sall's UN Chief Bid

President of Senegal, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, has endorsed former President Macky Sall's bid to become the next secretary-general of the United Nations. It is a major turnaround in the relations between the two leaders. The endorsement follows a meeting between Faye and Sall and comes despite years of political tensions after Sall's controversial presidency and the 2024 election that brought Faye to power. Faye has instructed his government to rally support for Sall's bid as "Senegal's candidacy in the service of Africa." The decision has drawn criticism from opposition figures, civil society groups and victims' families, who argue Sall's record of alleged political repression makes him unsuitable for the UN's top post.

DR Congo Battles Fastest-Growing Ebola Outbreak

The Democratic Republic of the Congo is battling its fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, with 2,423 confirmed cases, 967 deaths and 469 recoveries reported as of 19 July. The outbreak, driven by the Bundibugyo virus variant, has spread across five eastern provinces, with Ituri accounting for more than 90% of infections and 80% of deaths. The World Health Organization (WHO) warned that ongoing insecurity, population displacement and the absence of an approved vaccine or treatment are hampering efforts to contain the disease. In some areas, including Kisangani, rapid response actions have helped stop further spread. Early detection, contact tracing and community engagement remain central to the response.

144 Migrants Dead or Missing Off Mauritania Coast

The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) has said that at least 144 migrants are dead or missing after a series of maritime tragedies off the coast of Mauritania. Many of the migrants, including refugees, had spent 25 days stranded at sea after departing from The Gambia headed for Spain's Canary Islands. Rescue efforts culminated in an operation on 18 July where teams found 38 survivors and 143 dead or missing. Among the survivors that day were two children who lost their entire families at sea. UNHCR said the tragedy highlights the urgent need for safer legal migration pathways. It urged countries to consider "meaningful and quicker access to legal pathways through higher resettlement quotas, increased labour opportunities and education pathways as alternatives to the dangerous sea crossings."

Close 

Africa Now World's Hunger Hotspot, UN Warns

A new United Nations report has found that global hunger declined for the third consecutive year in 2025. But Africa has become the epicentre of the world's food crisis and the continent now has the largest number of hungry people worldwide. The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report estimates that 645 million people globally went hungry last year. Two-thirds of Africans could not afford a healthy diet and more than half suffered moderate or severe food insecurity. The global number of hungry people decreased by almost 14 million compared with 2024 and by 43 million since 2022. The UN warned that progress remains fragile and far too slow to achieve the Sustainable Development Goal of ending hunger by 2030. The UN warned that conflict, climate shocks and declining humanitarian funding continue to threaten progress. The group urged governments to invest in resilient food systems and make nutritious diets more affordable.

World.title: South Africa: Power Utility Eskom Says Koeberg Remains Safe - South African News Briefs - July 22, 2026
World.content:
Eskom Reassures Public After Koeberg Radiation Incidents

Eskom has assured the public that there is no danger to people or the environment following three radiological contamination incidents at Koeberg Nuclear Power Station's Unit 2 during maintenance between June 30 and July 7, reports EWN. The utility said the low levels of radioactive contamination were contained within the reactor building and that no radioactive material was released outside the facility. Eskom's Chief Nuclear Officer, Velaphi Ntuli, said the incidents were safely managed under strict protocols and do not affect the National Nuclear Regulator's decision to extend the operating life of Unit 2 by 20 years.

UK Murder Suspect Returns to Johannesburg Court



British-Zimbabwean national Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma is set to appear in the Johannesburg Magistrate's Court after his case was postponed for legal status verification and address checks, reports SABC News. The 45-year-old was arrested in Johannesburg on July 10 after police found him in possession of an unlicensed 9mm firearm. He is also wanted in the United Kingdom in connection with the alleged murders of his wife and two daughters. South African authorities are processing a provisional extradition request while he first faces the local firearm charge.

Matlala Trial Continues as Witness Resumes Testimony

The trial of alleged criminal kingpin Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala and his four co-accused continues in the High Court in Johannesburg, reports SABC News. The first State witness is expected to resume cross-examination. The accused face 25 charges linked to three alleged attempted assassinations between 2022 and 2024, including those of taxi boss Joe "Ferrari" Sibanyoni, Tebogo Thobejane and DJ Vettys. Security officer Bethwell Cele testified that gunmen armed with AK-47 rifles opened fire on Sibanyoni and his entourage at a golf estate before also shooting at him during the attack.
