This year's White House Correspondents' Dinner is the first time Trump has attended the annual event as president after previously skipping it throughout his first term. He previously attended the dinner as a private citizen in 2011.

World.title: Sports media rushes to cast Ryan Clark as victim while portraying ESPN as the villain
World.content:
Within hours of Ryan Clark’s dismissal, many of the biggest names in sports media had already reached the same conclusion: Clark was the victim and ESPN was the villain.

Stephen A. Smith said he confronted ESPN executives over the decision and called Clark "arguably the best NFL analyst in America." Emmanuel Acho accused the network of handling the situation in a "cowardly" and "wildly disrespectful" manner.

RYAN CLARK BECAME A HEADACHE FOR ESPN

Sarah Spain described Clark as "another incredibly smart, thoughtful, nuanced talent let go," while Pro Football Talk’s Mike Florio declared that Clark took "the high road" after "ESPN took the low road."

Jemele Hill went even further.

Hill suggested Clark had "a hater," perhaps multiple haters, inside ESPN. She attacked OutKick as a "disgusting" right-wing "rag" and theorized that someone within the network intentionally leaked Clark’s dismissal to OutKick in order to create a conservative media narrative against him. She offered no evidence for that claim.

But the fact that Clark’s dismissal leaked so widely and so quickly raises a question that his defenders have mostly avoided: How many enemies had he made inside ESPN?

Much of the criticism centered on the fact that Clark was informed during a live edition of NFL Live. The assumption was that ESPN knowingly allowed a longtime employee to begin the show before abruptly firing him during a break.

I don’t think that’s what happened.

I think ESPN planned to inform Clark later and simply failed to anticipate that news of his dismissal would leak first. Once OutKick contacted the network with a confirmed story, ESPN realized it had lost control of the timeline and had to tell Clark before he learned about it publicly.

That’s not cruelty. It’s poor planning.

My colleague Bobby Burack and I developed separate lines of reporting that the network was preparing to part ways with Clark. Four sources confirmed the information. Despite concerns that alerting ESPN could jeopardize the story, I contacted the network’s communications department at 4 p.m. and asked ESPN to confirm or deny the report before our publication deadline.

ESPN asked us to wait until 5:45 p.m. while it was "trying to chase this down." We declined but told the network we would add anything it provided before that time. It's reasonable that ESPN wanted more time to inform Clark before the news became public.

At 4:49 p.m., ESPN unexpectedly told us we could "stick to" our original timeline. Fourteen minutes later, Andrew Marchand published a brief report in The Athletic. OutKick’s more detailed story followed one minute after that.

The most logical explanation is that ESPN believed it still had time to manage Clark’s exit quietly. Once OutKick informed the network that four sources had already confirmed the decision, executives were forced to accelerate a conversation they apparently had not planned to have during NFL Live.

ESPN’s mistake was not deciding to embarrass Clark on live television. It was failing to anticipate that the information would leak before the network was ready to tell him.

That raises a more uncomfortable question than the ones Clark’s defenders have been asking: Why were so many people inside or around ESPN willing to talk about his dismissal?

Hill may be correct that Clark had "haters" inside the company.

What she never seriously considered, or chose to ignore, is how he might have acquired them.

How Ryan Clark made enemies inside ESPN

I worked at ESPN for years and spent time in rooms with Clark. He appeared on several shows I produced. The thing I remember most clearly is how uncomfortable he could make those rooms.

Clark often carried himself as though he were the smartest person present, and he made sure everyone knew it. That dynamic was especially difficult for producers and other employees beneath him in ESPN’s hierarchy. There was little room to challenge him or offer feedback that amounted to anything other than telling him he was great.

I distinctly remember one NFL season when talent, producers and other ESPN employees gathered on Sunday afternoons to watch the games in a large conference room. There were usually 25 or 30 people there. The mood was light. Chris Berman often sat near the front and cracked jokes throughout the afternoon.

Clark joined the group one Sunday and sat in the back with his arms folded. Several times, someone offered an opinion about a game and Clark scoffed. Eventually, most people stopped talking. I left and watched the games from a control room because he had completely ruined the experience for me.

How dare anyone offer an opinion when the world’s greatest NFL analyst was available to explain what everyone else was apparently too stupid to understand?

That was one afternoon years ago. It does not prove why ESPN fired Clark, nor does it mean every person who worked with him had the same experience.

It does, however, make the speed of the leak less surprising to me.

People rarely risk their relationships with a company to leak sensitive personnel news about a universally beloved colleague.

Clark's defenders largely presented his dismissal as though it happened in a vacuum.

It didn't.

Clark was forced to apologize after making inaccurate claims on ESPN about the investigation into former LSU receiver Kyren Lacy’s role in a fatal crash. He presented claims from Lacy’s attorney as established fact and accused law enforcement of wrongdoing before Louisiana State Police released additional evidence that contradicted key parts of the story Clark told viewers.

He later acknowledged that he had failed to provide complete and accurate information.

Clark also admitted on ESPN that he had argued in favor of Bryce Young over C.J. Stroud despite privately believing Stroud was the superior quarterback. His explanation was that Young needed someone to support him publicly.

That’s a remarkable admission from an analyst whose job is supposed to be giving viewers his honest evaluation.

ESPN'S RYAN CLARK WANTS TO BE AN NFL GM, LIES ABOUT C.J. STROUD & BRYCE YOUNG TO PROVE HE CAN DO IT

Then there was Clark’s public feud with Robert Griffin III, during which he suggested Griffin was not qualified to discuss Black women because he is married to a White woman. The dispute became deeply personal and reportedly frustrated people inside ESPN. This led to another Clark apology.

Then there was Clark’s on-air confrontation with Peter Schrager that became another viral controversy. Clark later apologized (again), but the exchange likely contributed to concerns among network executives.

Plus, Clark’s difficult relationship with ESPN management was hardly limited to interpersonal friction.

His 2024 contract negotiations became a public spectacle. Clark allowed his deal to expire, posted videos about his status and openly applied pressure to the network while seeking a substantial raise. ESPN eventually brought him back on a deal reportedly worth around $2 million per year, but the process was contentious.

ESPN executives do not enjoy being publicly cornered during contract negotiations, particularly by employees using their own platforms to rally outside pressure against the company.

My belief is that Clark’s 2024 extension was always going to be his final contract with ESPN. The network may have decided that keeping him temporarily was preferable to another public fight at the time, while also concluding it had no desire to negotiate with him again.

That would help explain why ESPN was willing to move on despite his high salary and recent extension. The decision may not have been prompted by one argument, one apology or one uncomfortable television segment. It may have been the culmination of a relationship that had already run its course.

Essentially, Clark’s tenure had become more complicated than his defenders acknowledged.

Spain praised him as "thoughtful" and "nuanced" without mentioning the multiple inaccurate claims that forced him to apologize on national television. Hill assumed the existence of internal enemies proved something nefarious without examining Clark’s own role in creating friction. Smith emphasized Clark’s talent, which was never really in dispute.

Acho offered perhaps the most exaggerated defense, claiming Clark helped build NFL Live into the "juggernaut it is today."

Acho pointed to the show’s Sports Emmy victories as evidence. But awards demonstrate that people within the television industry and the Hollywood elites like a program. They do not necessarily demonstrate that the public at large enjoys a show.

The available audience data show that NFL Live drew larger audiences before Clark became one of the faces of the program than it has in recent years. ESPN reported that the show averaged 688,000 viewers during a comparable early-season period in 2013 and 624,000 in 2012. It averaged roughly 486,000 in 2015, 492,000 in 2016, 449,000 in 2021 and 440,000 in 2025.

That doesn't mean Clark hurt NFL Live. It does make the claim that he "built" a show that debuted in 1998 into a modern ratings juggernaut impossible to support.

The argument becomes even more amusing when compared with Acho’s commentary about Caitlin Clark. He has argued that the WNBA would be better off without her, even though she has driven enormous gains in television audiences, attendance and general interest.

By Acho’s standard, Caitlin Clark has a much stronger claim to having "built" the modern WNBA than Ryan Clark does to having built NFL Live.

Apparently, the meaning of the word depends on which Clark is receiving the credit.

By the time ESPN reached this week’s layoffs, Clark was an expensive employee who had publicly pressured the company during his previous contract negotiation, accumulated enemies inside the building and repeatedly created controversies outside it.

ESPN TO PART WAYS WITH CAM NEWTON AS PART OF TALENT LAYOFFS THAT ALSO INCLUDED RYAN CLARK

The sports media narrative was that ESPN betrayed Ryan Clark.

OutKick's reporting suggested something different.

ESPN didn’t lose control of the story because OutKick uncovered some closely guarded secret. It lost control because too many people already knew.

And too many people were willing to talk.

That doesn’t happen by accident.

World.title: William Shatner and daughter Melanie reveal they battled Stage 4 cancer at the same time
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

William Shatner and his 61-year-old daughter revealed this week that the two of them battled cancer at the same time several years ago.

Melanie Shatner Gretsch first discovered her cancer four years ago when she woke up in the middle of the night and felt a little lump on her breast she thought might be a bug bite.

She told People magazine she decided to have it checked out despite a mammogram not finding anything just five months earlier.

DAVE COULIER REVEALS 45-POUND WEIGHT LOSS, GRUELING SIDE EFFECTS FROM CANCER FIGHTS

Although the technician didn’t find anything during a scan the next day, "something pushed me back and said, ‘No, have her recheck it.’ She put the wand exactly where I put my finger and under her breath said, ‘Now, I would have missed that.’"

She was diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer that had spread to lymph nodes in her chest.

Shatner said his daughter was "very conscious of the importance of her life for herself and for her family. I was devastated."

Gretsch is a mother to two daughters she shares with husband Joel Gretsch.

Gretsch said her father told her not to worry about the medical costs and to send him the bills.

"Then you made me laugh so hard when I was still going to the doctor a year later," she added. "You said, ‘You’ve got to get well. We’re going to be in the poorhouse.’"

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

For the next 18 months, her life was filled with multiple rounds of chemo, 30 radiation treatments and a double mastectomy.

"Chemo was the most physically draining, and the radiation I found so emotionally draining," she admitted.

Just as she was nearing the end of her treatments, a lump appeared on her dad’s cheek.

He said a family doctor told him it was just a blocked salivary gland that was nothing to worry about, but a doctor friend whose advice he asked while they were horseback riding advised him to get it removed.

CAMERON MATHISON SAYS NOTICING SUBTLE BODY CHANGES ‘SAVED MY LIFE’ AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS

"He placed his hands on my cheeks, and he said with love in his voice, ‘You better get this out,’" Shatner explained.

In June 2023, Shatner was diagnosed with Stage 4 malignant melanoma that had spread to his lungs and brain.

"I remember vividly thinking, ‘I don’t have the strength to take care of myself and lose my father at the same time,’" Gretsch admitted.

Shatner was more upbeat.

"They said, ‘You got cancer. If you came in later, you would have been dead.’ See? That’s my life. I think the universe is taking care of me."

The 95-year-old had the tumor removed and underwent two years of immunotherapy.

CLICK HERE TO 

"He wouldn’t stop his life," his daughter told People magazine. "He kept working and moving forward. Whenever he was home, Joel and I would bring dinner to him and watch movies, just always made sure that he’s not alone."

Shatner added, "We got the perfect doctors for her cancer and my cancer."

The "Star Trek" actor, who was the oldest man in space when he went up in a Blue Origin rocket, has stayed busy with two new books and two records, all expected to come out next year.

"I’m healthier now than I’ve been in years," Shatner said. "The brain is like a muscle. It feeds on activity."

Near the end of 2024, both were declared cancer free.

"It was the third time in my life I had heard him cry," Gretsch admitted of telling him her cancer was gone.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Shatner said the experience has given him a new perspective on life.

"I’m thinking of the miracle of a hummingbird, and of my dog taking a ball and my children," he said. "I’m aware of the magic of it all."

World.title: Fox News Poll: Voters want major change amid economic and political discontent
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Several findings in the latest Fox News Poll show voters are unhappy and want major change, which bodes well for Democrats in November: President Donald Trump’s job approval remains near a record low, more Democrats are motivated to vote, Republicans join Democrats and independents in rating the economy negatively, and 4 in 10 voters want "dramatic" or "revolutionary" change. Plus, more view the GOP as tied to elites than the Democratic Party.

Voters say Democrats can better handle income inequality (+22 points), healthcare (+21), inflation (+10), the economy (+9), and foreign policy (+7). Republicans hold the advantage on crime (+7 points), while government spending (Democrats +3) and national security (R +2) are more evenly divided. On immigration, the GOP had an 8-point edge in April. Now, Democrats are preferred by one point.

FOX NEWS POLL: AN EARLY LOOK AT THE GEORGIA SENATE RACE

More Democrats (68%) say they are extremely motivated to vote in November than Republicans (57%) by an 11-point margin. By a 25-point spread, more MAGA Republicans (66%) are extremely motivated than non-MAGA Republicans (41%).

FOX NEWS POLL: A CLOSE SENATE CONTEST IS BREWING IN IOWA

If the election were today, 53% of voters would back the Democratic candidate in their House district and 46% the Republican. That 7-point edge is just outside the poll’s margin of error. Democrats were up by 5 points in April. Notably, 53% is the highest percentage either party has received on the generic House ballot in Fox News polling since 1996.

When looking only at counties where the 2024 presidential vote was close — Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris within 10 points — the Democratic candidate leads by 59-41%.

"Although these data look promising for the Democrats, some of their support is in less-contested districts, padding their national totals without adding House seats," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson. "The best estimates I’ve seen suggest the GOP could retain the House even if the Democrats win the national vote by 2-3 points, but if Democrats win by 6-7 points, they probably take the House."

The Democratic advantage comes amid weak ratings for Trump and continued economic pessimism. Trump’s job approval stands at 39%, unchanged for the third month in a row and one point above his low of 38% in October 2017. Approval of Trump is a touch lower than former President Barack Obama’s at the same point in his second term (42% in July 2014).

Trump received net-negative ratings for handling immigration (42% approve, 57% disapprove), Iran (34-66%), the economy (33-67%), and inflation (27-73%).

Three-quarters rate the economy negatively, about the same for the past six months.

Another three quarters say inflation has caused them financial hardship, including 34% who say "serious" hardship, up from 26% last year.

Fifty-four percent expect the economy to worsen in the coming year; only Republicans express optimism (71%), while Democrats (75%) and independents (64%) expect it to worsen.

Dissatisfaction extends beyond individual figures to both political parties and the broader economic system.

"Democrats and Republicans have a surprisingly broad array of shared beliefs about politics today," says Shaw. "Both think elected officials answer to the elites, both think the system is rigged, both want to see new blood in office, both feel betrayed by their party, both disapprove of their members in Congress, and both want a mandatory retirement age for Congress."

Some 70% say the Republican Party is closely tied to elite interests, while 55% say the same about the Democratic Party. The 15-point gap reflects more Democrats and independents saying the GOP is tied to elites, yet even Republicans are equally likely to describe both parties as close to elites.

There’s disillusionment in both parties. Many Democrats (48%) and Republicans (41%) say they feel betrayed by their party, and for both it is primarily for selling out to special interests.

Perceptions that the political system favors elites are reshaping views of the economy as well. The number who accept income inequality because "that’s how our economy works" has fallen 16 points compared to 2014 (from 62% to 46%), while the share who want government action has more than doubled (from 13% to 30%).

At the same time, an increasing number, 65%, think the country’s system is rigged in favor of the wealthy (up 9 points compared to 2019).

By 2-to-1, voters say it is more important to elect new people than keep those with experience.

Overall, 19% say they want revolutionary change in the nation’s government, while many others want substantial (38%) or dramatic (23%) change.

Almost twice as many Democrats (52%) as Republicans (28%) want dramatic or revolutionary change.

Nearly 7 in 10 voters disapprove of both Democrats and Republicans in Congress.

Some 32% of Republicans disapprove of their party’s lawmakers, while 39% of Democrats disapprove of theirs. More than 8 in 10 independents disapprove of both.

Fully 85% support a mandatory retirement age for members of Congress, up 20 points since 2002.

Of those in favor of setting a cap, 80% think it should be before age 75, with 61% selecting a cutoff between 65 and 74 — a boundary supported by more than half of every generation.

Poll-pourri

Just 50% of voters have a positive view of capitalism, down from a high of 57% in 2019. For socialism, it’s 30% favorable, up from 27% last year but below the 32% who said the same in 2021. The Democratic Socialists of America are viewed positively by 31%.

By an 11-point margin, more Democrats have a favorable opinion of socialism (52%) than capitalism (41%), while by a 50-point margin, more Republicans have a positive view of capitalism (61%) than socialism (11%).

Forty-five percent of voters have a favorable view of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., That makes him more popular than Vice President JD Vance (41% favorable), Trump (38%), and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., (35%). Each is viewed more unfavorably than favorably. Voters under 30 and those ages 65+ are equally likely to view Sanders positively (48% and 46% respectively). For AOC, more voters 65+ (41%) have a favorable view than young voters (33%), and three times as many of those under 30 say they’ve never heard of her (30% vs. 9%).

Overall, 44% have a favorable view of Israel, down from 58% a decade ago. Positive ratings are lower today among Democrats (by 14 points), Republicans (-12), and independents (-21). Voters ages 65 and over (56%) are twice as likely to view Israel favorably as those under 30 (27%).

CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE

Conducted July 17–20, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,003 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (70) and cellphones (681) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (252). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. The survey includes an oversample of 200 voters aged 18–29, bringing the sample size for that subgroup to 350 (±5). Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling errors, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data.

Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

World.title: Migrant allegedly kills 3 apartment building staffers over parking lot contract dispute
World.content:

An African migrant upset over being unable to cancel his monthly $65 parking garage contract allegedly shot and killed three property managers at his Minnesota apartment building over the dispute, authorities said.

Tsegaab Ademassu Binessu, 30, was charged with three counts of second-degree murder with intent following the alleged slayings Monday of Nansi G. Fuentes Zambrano, 25, Dena M. Silcox, 56, and 43-year-old Adam J. Wilwerding at the St. Paul complex, court documents state.

The rampage began after Binessu, from Ethiopia, called the apartment building staffers to cancel his $65 monthly parking contract because he had sold his car. He was told he could not do so after recently renewing the agreement.

Despite being told the contract could not be canceled, Binessu said he would be going to the management office in person, prosecutors said.

EXCLUSIVE: DHS SEEKS CUSTODY OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER TRUMP DEPORTATION, BIDEN RELEASE

Once there, he allegedly opened fire, killing all three victims. Police later found 21, 9 mm shell casings in the leasing office.

Shortly after the shooting, a man called the police stating that he had been Binessu's roommate since 2018. He said Binessu, who had aspirations of joining the U.S. Navy, called him and confessed to the triple murder, adding that he was walking to the police station.

Binessu worked as a trucker but quit two months ago, the roommate told authorities, and had planned on enlisting in the military. He sold his car the same day as the shooting, police said.

The roommate said he spoke with Binessu, who allegedly said he "argued with apartment management and ended up killing three people."

FAMILY SHATTERED AFTER 3-TIME DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ALLEGEDLY BLEW THROUGH STOP SIGN, ROILING HOUSE RACE

Surveillance footage reviewed by investigators captured Binessu talking with Silcox and Wilwerding.

At some point, Binessu allegedly pulled up his shirt, grabbed his gun from his waistband, pointed the weapon at Wilwerding, who put his hands in front of his body, and shot him three times.

Binessu then fired three more times as Wilwerding fell to the floor, court documents said.

Silcox screamed and covered her ears when Binessu allegedly shot Wilwerding, saying, "No, no — no, no, no."

Binessu is then accused of shooting Silcox five times in rapid succession, according to court documents. As she wheeled her chair away from the desk, Binessu allegedly shot her a sixth time.

Binessu stalked around the office and said, "Motherf------ b----," court documents said. He then moved toward a hallway out of the camera's view, where a woman's screams could be heard followed by four more gunshots.

Prosecutors said Binessu was arrested while driving Fuentes Zambrano's car, which contained what appeared to be newly purchased camping gear, according to the charges. Inside the vehicle, authorities found his U.S. passport, Social Security card, an empty handgun magazine and his gun permit.

During an interview with investigators, Binessu allegedly voiced frustration with the "prolonged immigration process" and not being able to bring his wife and children to the United States for seven years, which he said contributed to his divorce and separation from his children.

"Binessu believes he was treated unfairly because he is Black and an immigrant," the documents said. "Binessu repeatedly said he has lost everything he cared about: his wife, his children, his business, his peace of mind. Binessu said life without his family no longer made sense."

He remains in police custody.

World.title: Spanish soccer players got a bizarre reward for winning the World Cup that'll probably spoil in a week or two
World.content:
The great thing about winning a major tournament like the World Cup isn't just the trophy itself; it's all the other stuff that comes with it.

Prize money, endorsements, the adulation of millions across your nation.

And, in the case of two Spanish soccer players, the win has scored them a metric assload of tomatoes.

SPAIN BEATS ARGENTINA TO WIN 2026 FIFA WORLD CUP BEHIND FERRAN TORRES' EXTRA-TIME GOAL

Midfielders Fabian Ruiz and Gavi both hail from the city of Los Palacios y Villafranca, which has a tradition of rewarding champions with tomatoes.

According to UPI, the province that the city is in, Seville, is known for tomato production, but it doesn't just give out a commemorative tomato on a plaque. Instead, the two champs had to hop on scales at an event at a town hall, because each of them was being rewarded with their weight in tomatoes.

Ruiz left with 187 pounds of the fruit (I know, I think it should be a vegetable too, but you have to trust the science) while Gavi's supply is a little smaller at 151 pounds.

I'm torn on this one. I like the idea of towns, states, cities and provinces rewarding people with their weight in whatever their greatest export is.

This is mainly because under these rules, if I did anything good enough, I'd have a lot of Lebanon bologna (how many pounds is not important, just know that it would be plenty).

But, on the other hand, aren't like 130 pounds of those tomatoes just going to go bad?

WORLD CUP HERO FERRAN TORRES DOUBLES DOWN AFTER CRITICISM, POSTS PICTURE WEARING 'MAKE SPAIN GREAT AGAIN' HAT

And where do you store them? I know it's the thought that counts, but if someone said to you, "Hey, here's 200 pounds of tomatoes, champ," you'd be like, "I guess I can keep some of them in the guest bathroom tub..."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

You have to just give them away. That happened to me with a giant case of Tastykakes that I once happened to receive (long story). Everyone who came by my house for anything left with a box of Butterscotch Krimpets.

Nonetheless, it's a cool tradition, and I think there is going to be a lot of pan con tomate (which is delicious) in Ruiz and Gavi's future.

World.title: Trump attends dignified transfer of 4 service members killed in Iran attacks since the ceasefire ended
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday attended the dignified transfer of the remains of four service members killed in Iranian attacks this month after hostilities ramped up following the collapse of the ceasefire.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The four service members being flown from the Middle East to Dover Air Force Base were 28-year-old Angel S. Rampersad of New York, 30-year-old Michael Emmanuel Swinton of North Carolina, 25-year-old Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii and 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales of Texas.

Dignified transfers are some of the most solemn occasions for presidents, who often attend to pay respects to troops killed in conflicts overseen by them as commander in chief. Trump has attended two prior dignified transfers since the war began in February, but this is his first since he declared on July 8 that the ceasefire was over.

President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth salute as members of a U.S. Army carry team move a transfer case Wednesday. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

The event marked the latest impact of the war, which has garnered criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle who question the administration’s strategy in the monthslong conflict. The hostilities, which were paused after the two sides agreed to a peace plan that quickly fell apart, have thrown the region into chaos, leaving at least 18 Americans dead, costing at least $37.5 billion and inflating the price of oil.

The president and his administration have vigorously defended their handling of the war, arguing it is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Trump told reporters earlier Wednesday: “We’re going to Dover. Some of you are going with us. To honor our heroes, and they are indeed great heroes, actually. They said, and all of them said very strongly, we can’t let, we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon. They won’t have a nuclear weapon. So we’re going to honor them. And it’s one of the hardest things to do, for me, it’s one of the hardest things to do as a president, but has to be done.”

The family members of the fallen service members attended the dignified transfer, where the bodies of their loved ones were moved in American flag-draped transfer cases from a plane into waiting vans.

Uniformed service members marched the transfer cases past officials, including Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt. Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Chris Coons, D-Del., also attended.

Trump and other officials saluted as the remains passed before them, while others placed their hands on their hearts. The president also met privately with the families, the White House confirmed.

From left, Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, Sgt. Angel Rampersad, Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton. DVIDS

Flag-draped transfer cases are loaded into vehicles Wednesday at Dover Air Force Base. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images

Gonzales was killed Friday and Feehan was killed Saturday, the Pentagon said. It also said that Swinton was killed Sunday “during a controlled detonation” of an attack drone.

Rampersad was “believed to have been killed” in Jordan, the Pentagon said, adding that “the incident is under investigation.” The Pentagon has said that she is believed to have been the missing soldier who is presumed dead.

Hegseth faced questions from senators Tuesday about the cost and strategy of the war during a tense hearing on the Pentagon’s budget request.

During one particularly heated exchange, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., called the Trump administration’s efforts “an utter and complete failure” and pressed Hegseth on what the long-term plan is to end the war.

“You have over a trillion dollars,” Peters said. “You’re asking for one and a half trillion dollars. It’s not a question of money. It’s a question of leadership and understanding what it takes to actually win.”

World.title: U.S. signs landmark nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia
World.content:
The U.S. signed a landmark nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Energy announced in a post on X.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

“U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy His Royal Highness (HRH) Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement, commonly known as a 123 agreement, alongside an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement,” the announcement read. “Together, these two agreements lay the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar partnership that advances several priority economic and strategic objectives, including nuclear nonproliferation.”

In the announcement, Wright added: “Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world’s best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States.”

Earlier, a senior administration official told NBC News that President Donald Trump had approved the deal.

The agreement will see the U.S. support the creation of a nuclear power program and see American companies build the program in the kingdom, said the official who was granted anonymity by NBC News so that the person could speak about the deal before its official announcement.

News of the agreement was first reported in The Wall Street Journal.

Congress will be required to vote on the agreement, but would need a veto-proof majority to actually block the deal, which could pave the way for the kingdom to pursue its own uranium enrichment and likely raise fears of nuclear proliferation.

Asked ahead of the announcement about those concerns and reports of an expected deal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that the U.S. would not “reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation.”

The agreement comes as the war against Iran that was launched by the U.S. and Israel in late February goes on. Trump has insisted that Tehran should not be able to develop a nuclear weapon, despite the Islamic Republic consistently denying that it plans to do so.

An agreement to normalize ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia had previously been a U.S. requirement for any deal allowing the kingdom to enrich uranium, but Saudi leaders insisted this would not be possible without meaningful progress toward a Palestinian state.

However, Wright discussed building the country’s commercial nuclear power industry with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, on a visit to the kingdom last year, shortly before Trump traveled there himself in May 2025.

Any deal without appropriate guardrails in place would be “concerning from a proliferation perspective,” according to Darya Dolzikova​, a senior research fellow with the proliferation and nuclear policy program at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank.

“Any country, period, but particularly countries of proliferation concern have to be really, really robust on their nonproliferation provisions,” she added.

And Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously warned that the kingdom would try to obtain a nuclear weapon if Iran was also able to do, Dolzikova​ noted.

Saudi Arabia also signed a mutual defense pact with Pakistan, the only Muslim nuclear nation, in September. Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif then said his nation’s nuclear program would “be made available” to Saudi Arabia if required.

The Middle Eastern kingdom is a member state of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which promotes peaceful nuclear work but also inspects nations to ensure they don’t have clandestine atomic weapon programs. Based in Vienna, the agency reports to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council.

While enrichment does not necessarily lead to a nuclear weapon, it can open the door to it. However, any country wishing to do so would also have to master other technologies including the use of synchronized high explosives.

And there has been focus on whether any deal would include the “gold standard” safeguards that would block the kingdom from enriching uranium and reprocessing spent nuclear fuel, both of which are potential pathways to nuclear weapons.

It also remains to be seen whether the agreement includes the “Additional Protocol” that grants the IAEA greater oversight of a country’s nuclear activities.

Ultimately, “the devil will be in the details,” Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa program at the London-based think tank Chatham House, said. If Saudi Arabia does retain the right to enrich, she said, “it’s the issue of domestic enrichment that will be more concerning and alarming.”

The deal with the U.S. came a day after senior Saudi and United Arab Emirates officials shared similar social media posts ​affirming their close historical ties and “wise leadership,” a move that follows months of tensions owing to a rift ‌between the two Gulf monarchies.

The Gulf nations have been split over ​their support for opposing sides in the war in Yemen that culminated in a Saudi airstrike late last year, on what it said was a shipment of UAE military equipment to the Yemeni faction Abu Dhabi backed.

Their interests have diverged over a number of issues including oil quotas.

But the posts from the Saudi Minister of Media Salman Al-Dosary and Abdulla bin Mohamed Alhamed, Chairman of the UAE National Media Authority, said they should focus on their shared history and heritage.

World.title: Oil surges past $95 as U.S. downplays Iran diplomacy and 2nd key trade route is disrupted
World.content:
The price of oil surged nearly 5% Wednesday as U.S. officials talked down the chance of new peace talks after an 11th straight night of strikes on Iran and with major disruption now facing two of the world’s key supply routes.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

International Brent crude oil rose as much as 4.9% to more than $95 per barrel for the first time in almost six weeks. U.S. crude oil rose as much as nearly 5.1% to nearly $89 per barrel.

Those prices pulled back slightly by the afternoon. U.S. crude closed higher by 2.9%, at $86.83 per barrel while Brent closed up 3.4%, at $94.07 per barrel.

While Brent is widely considered the international oil benchmark, it also influences the retail cost of gas in the U.S.

Those pump prices rose again Wednesday, extending their climb above $4 per gallon. The national average price rose 4 cents overnight to $4.06 per gallon, according to motor club AAA data tracked by NBC News.

Treasury yields spiked, following oil’s latest jump and its likely impact on inflation. As of midmorning trading, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was hovering around 4.65%, its highest since May.

As a result, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage rose to 6.75% Wednesday, matching its highest level of the year.

Since the start of the month, oil prices have gained 25% and are now up more than 50% since the start of the year. That move has largely erased the drop in prices that came after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June.

Rhetoric escalates tensions

President Donald Trump had declared that tentative deal, which was aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, “over” on July 8.

But on Wednesday, Trump ratcheted up the rhetoric once again.

“Any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran,” he posted on social media.

Overnight, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the U.S. remained open to diplomacy with Iran, “but right now they don’t seem to be serious about that.”

Rubio added that the U.S. would continue to try to protect commercial shipping.

But in the last two days, the U.K.’s Maritime Trade Organization has reported multiple attacks on vessels in the area. In at least two of those, said the maritime monitoring group, which is aligned with the British navy, crews were forced to abandon ship.

Those attacks are one reason traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains extremely low.

On Monday, only 13 ships crossed the vital waterway, and on Tuesday that number was only nine, according to an analysis of ship movements by MarineTraffic.

World.title: Trump hypes Mike Collins’ Senate campaign at Georgia rally
World.content:
MARIETTA, Ga. — President Donald Trump came down to Georgia on Wednesday to help boost the campaign of Republican Rep. Mike Collins, a Senate candidate who he said was one of the most “highly respected” members of Congress.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Trump took several shots at Collins’ opponent, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, who he said looks like “Pee-wee Herman.”

“You have to vote for Mike because he is running against Pee-wee Herman,” Trump told a standing-room-only gymnasium crowd at Wheeler High School. “He will bring a lot of action back to your state. ... Vote for Mike.”

Republicans have an uphill climb in the nationally watched race, in part because Ossoff has already raised a massive $77 million this election cycle.

Meanwhile, Republicans in the state endured a messy and expensive Senate GOP primary, which eventually concluded with Collins as the party’s nominee but with comparatively little money in his campaign account after having raised $6.5 million to date.

Collins, a current member of Congress, was not at the event because of key votes in Washington.

Trump opted against endorsing early in the GOP primary, leaving a field that included a handful of well-funded candidates to attack one another as they jockeyed for Trump’s approval.

Trump eventually endorsed Collins just days before the June primary runoff, a last-minute nod as he already appeared poised to win the nomination.

After the brutal fight, Collins emerged with roughly $2 million cash on hand, compared with Ossoff’s $42 million, as of June 30.

Because of Ossoff’s incumbency advantage and huge financial lead, the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the seat “leans Democratic,” but it is very much seen as in play.

Democrats must defend Georgia as they try to play offense in other states and net four seats, which would flip the Senate majority. Democrats are targeting Maine, Texas, Iowa, Alaska, Ohio and other states while defending Democratic-held open seats in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Georgia also has a nationally watched governor’s race, with Trump-endorsed Republican businessman Rick Jackson facing Democratic former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms.

The overall focus of Trump’s event Wednesday was education, specifically the new “Trump Accounts,” which offer tax-advantaged investing for Americans under 18. The federal government will put $1,000 into accounts for babies born from 2025 to 2028.

The speakers leading up to Trump, including state and Trump administration officials, all praised Trump Accounts.

“For too long, many have felt the American dream is slipping into the past — not anymore,” U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we are opening every possible pathway to pursue that dream again.”

Trump said the “money is pouring in” to Trump Accounts and then called Jackson on to the stage. Jackson announced that if he becomes governor, he will push Georgia lawmakers to match the federal government’s initial $1,000 investment contribution for Georgia families taking part.

Jackson then said that if lawmakers do not pass the proposal, he would pay for them himself.

Speakers also touched on the Iran war, which Trump initially said would be a short incursion when it began in February. Now, almost six months in, 18 service members have been killed, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth put the cost of the war at $37.5 billion at a congressional hearing Tuesday.

The Defense Department is asking Congress for $67 billion in supplemental funding for the war effort.

The war has been unpopular, but Trump has maintained support with some of his most fervent MAGA supporters.

“He [Trump] is going to make sure Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” U.S. Treasurer Brandon Beach said, generating applause and cheers.

The military conflict in Iran is coming with large domestic ripple effects, including higher fuel costs. Those are complicating the midterm election for Republicans as the party tries to emphasize efforts Trump and Republicans have made to lower costs, an issue that most public polling finds is top of mind for most voters.

The price of crude oil recently increased to more than $95 per barrel, the highest in almost six weeks. The price of fuel stabilized following news of a ceasefire with Iran in April, but it has ticked up since bombing has resumed.

Much of the Republicans’ midterm economic message will center on passage of Trump’s “big beautiful bill,” his biggest legislative win during his second term in office. Republicans have focused on parts of the bill, including the Trump Accounts, ending things like taxes on tips of hospitality workers and expanding the Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit. Democratic opponents have noted that wealthy Americans will benefit most from passage of the bill.

“They doubled the child tax credit,” Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler said. “And ended taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security. All of that might seem like common sense, and it is, but it is also a fact every single congressional Democrat voted ‘no’ on letting you take home more of what you earn.”

Loeffler, a former senator from Georgia, specifically noted that both of Georgia’s Democratic senators, Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, voted against the bill. Warnock defeated Loeffler in a special election six years ago.

Trump also touted another one of his top issues: election integrity.

He has struggled to persuade Senate Republicans to pass his SAVE America Act, and senators have repeatedly warned that they do not have the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster and move the bill toward passage.

The proposal, which at times has been Trump’s near-singular legislative focus in recent months, would require proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, severely limit voting by mail and require states to purge voter rolls of noncitizens.

Trump used a primetime speech this week to push Senate Republicans to pass the proposal, but it did little to move the needle.

He has, however, maintained his pressure campaign.

“The Senate, what they are doing is just not right,” Trump said. “We are not going to take this any longer.”

World.title: Secret Service warns of high threat levels before White House Correspondents' Dinner
World.content:
Days ahead of the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, Secret Service officials warned nationwide threats have reached an unprecedented level — with agents opening roughly 10,000 protective intelligence cases since January, a nearly 40% increase from the same period last year.

"The numbers are numbers that this agency and certainly I have never seen in my 24-year career," U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran said Wednesday.

Officials who briefed reporters also said the agency has carried out nearly 10 times as many mental health-related interventions involving those making threats to protected individuals or venues, compared to last year. That includes both voluntary and involuntary commitments and efforts by agents and officers to work with relatives and mental-health providers to stabilize people in crisis.

Secret Service officials attributed the uptick to a combination of online threats, lone actors, ideological grievances, foreign threats and cases involving mental-health concerns. Officials say most threats now originate online, rather than through handwritten letters or other traditional forms of communication.

"The environment has become very volatile, and that's just across the board," Curran said. He added, "The threat picture and environment is as large as I've ever seen it."

The agency treats reported threats as potentially credible threats until investigators can determine whether a person has the intent, means and ability to carry out targeted violence, according to the Secret Service officials.

A person doesn't have to make a direct threat to draw the agency's attention. The threat assessment process relies on behavior, rather than a specific demographic profile. Agents look for potential warning signs like obsessive fixation, escalating grievances, stalking, harassment, paranoia, delusions, suicidality, significant behavioral changes and an unusual interest in violence.

Washington Hilton security during first 2026 White House Correspondents' Dinner

Curran defended the security plan used at the Washington Hilton during the White House Correspondents' Dinner, where an armed individual was stopped at a screening checkpoint outside the event.

When pressed by CBS News, he said the magnetometers were approximately 120 yards from the podium and argued that stopping the individual at the checkpoint demonstrated that the security system worked as intended.

"We have to start and end our perimeter somewhere," Curran said. "If it were up to me, I'd love to end it at the bridge, but that's going to inconvenience a lot of people," he added in an apparent reference to the Francis Scott Key Memorial Bridge in Washington, DC.

"We're talking almost 120 yards from magnetometers to the podium," he added. "That's over a football field."

Curran said the Secret Service anticipates that potentially dangerous individuals may reach screening locations, which is why checkpoints and specialized response teams are positioned there.

"We do expect bad people to show up," Curran said. "It's just a reality of where we are."

He added: "We do expect things to happen at the magnetometers, unfortunately, but that's why they are there. And that's where it happened, and that's where it ended. So it did work. The system worked."

Curran said the Secret Service must balance standoff distances and other security requirements against the effects of closing streets, hotels and businesses around an event.

Asked about preparations for Friday's rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, which will be held at the Washington, D.C., Waldorf Astoria, Curran said the agency was not approaching it as a "redo," but as a separate presidential visit requiring a new assessment.

"If the president goes to the same site 100 times, we will send an advance team there 100 times, because things change," Curran said. "The environment changes. The actual footprint will change."

Iran threats

Asked by CBS News about the new Air Force One, Curran declined to discuss specific protective measures connected to threats from Iran or decisions involving presidential transportation, saying the agency would not disclose its operational methods.

"We're never going to get into methods or means and how we do business," Curran said. "I don't want to tip our hand to the enemy."

Secret Service deputy director Matt Quinn said the well-known Iranian threat against President Trump is only part of the intelligence incorporated into the agency's planning.

"I don't think it's any secret that it's been in the media that Iran has publicly said they want to kill President Trump," Quinn said, adding the Iranian threat and additional information the agency cannot disclose are factored into Secret Service protective planning "all the time."

Drones: "The threat's real"

Quinn said the Secret Service is highly concerned about the potential use of drones against protectees and protected sites.

Asked how concerned the agency is about drones, Quinn responded: "Very."

"The threat's real," he said. "We look at Ukraine. We look at just basic intelligence. It's a matter of time before it comes to the United States."

Quinn said the agency is deploying advanced drone detection and mitigation systems at the White House and at other protected locations.

"No one in the federal government or law enforcement is doing more to proactively get after the drone threat than the Secret Service," he said.

Quinn said the White House is currently "very safe" from a drone attack but acknowledged that detection and mitigation technology must continue to evolve as drones become more difficult to identify and disrupt.

"The threat continues to get tougher and tougher," Quinn said, citing fiber-optic-controlled and "dark" drones. "It's a constant chase to keep up with it."

Curran said counter-drone assets travel with the president, and some of the systems have been used on American soil for the first time.

"We will use anything and everything," Curran said. "There's nothing that we aren't willing to do."

Quinn acknowledged that the agency previously failed to provide the appropriate level of counter-drone resources when Trump was a former president.

"At that time, a former president wasn't getting the resources that they potentially should have been getting," Quinn said. "I just own it for the Secret Service. That's not happening anymore."

Operational demands for massive events

Secret Service officials said the agency has conducted nearly 3,000 protective visits during the calendar year, including domestic and international travel by its protectees and protection for visiting foreign heads of state.

Agents recently screened approximately 100,000 attendees, employees and guests at MetLife Stadium for the World Cup championship; secured the July 4th celebration on the National Mall; protected a UFC event at the White House; and handled a presidential appearance at Madison Square Garden during the NBA championship series.

Officials said much of the work occurs before a protectee arrives and includes protective intelligence assessments, counter-surveillance operations, technical security measures, logistics and coordination with federal, state and local partners.

Curran said improving communication with field personnel has been one of his central priorities. Major protective operations now routinely use unified command posts where the Secret Service and partner agencies work together and share information in real time, Curran said.

"We're all talking," Curran said. "We're all in the same room, ensuring that what one person hears, everybody hears."

Advanced threat interdiction: Stopping attackers before they reach the White House

Secret Service officials said the agency has established an "advanced threat interdiction" capability designed to identify and stop potential attackers before they reach the White House, presidential events or other protected locations.

The agency is using technology and its legal authorities to locate both people who make threats and individuals connected to previous cases, and to determine whether they may be traveling toward Washington or another protected site.

They said their aim is to push the agency's security aperture outward and intercept a threat before it reaches the immediate perimeter of a protected location.

Officials said tips from relatives and members of the public remain critical because individuals planning violence may not make a direct threat or otherwise come to the attention of law enforcement.

They said it was a concerned family member's report that was a key factor in uncovering an alleged plot targeting a UFC event at the White House. The family member had noticed concerning behavior, online statements and the accumulation of weapons, officials said.

The agency receives potential threat information through a variety of sources: social-media analysis, federal and local law enforcement, fusion centers, government agencies, relatives and concerned citizens.

World.content:
A federal advisory council filled with Trump appointees is poised to gut a federal review process that assesses the impact of new projects on historical properties before they are approved and remove the requirement for public comment, according to multiple sources.

The Advisory Council for Historic Preservation is voting this week on a measure to slash the role of states, tribes and the public in Section 106 reviews under the National Historic Preservation Act. Twenty of the 24 members of the council are Trump administration appointees. The council does not currently have a chairman, who must be nominated by the president and Senate-confirmed, and one appointee appears to have stepped down in June. Three of the members are ex-officio representatives of national preservation organizations.

Section 106 is a 60-year-old law that says federal agencies "must consider the effects on historic properties of any project they propose to carry out." If a project could affect a historic property, a review process takes place, where the council, relevant parties and the public can weigh in on the project before it moves forward.

The issue is of interest to President Trump, since the president has several construction projects underway in the region. The ballroom addition to the East Wing of the White House is not governed by the rule, since it is on White House grounds. But the president's plans for a triumphal arch to be built near Arlington National Cemetery are currently undergoing a Section 106 review, and the nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation says it's worried the review has been too hurried.

"We are deeply concerned about the limited nature of the consultation, the rushed timeline, the exclusion of many parties (including the National Trust) from the consultation process, and the failure to consider less harmful alternatives," said Rob Nieweg, senior vice president of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, in testimony before the National Capital Planning Commission earlier this month.

Experts warn that the changes, which would take effect after a final rule is passed and would impact future projects, could expand the federal government's power to build or renovate historic sites with less oversight.

The review process currently requires the Advisory Council for Historic Preservation to consult with state preservation officials and Tribal Historic Preservation officers.

Under the proposal, which was reviewed by CBS News, the definition of a historic property would be changed, and the State Historic Preservation Officers' review would be optional, rather than mandatory. Public comment would also no longer be required.

The changes would also limit the ability of Indian tribes or Native Hawaiian organizations to protest projects that may affect their land.

In a letter obtained by CBS News, the National Trust for Historic Preservation said it opposes the moves by the council to change Section 106, arguing it will "eviscerate the preservation of our shared civic and cultural heritage in the United States," and says the group will take legal action to press for the withdrawal of the proposal.

"If implemented, federal agencies will no longer be required to avoid or minimize damage to our nation's historic sites and landscapes, or seek public input on federal projects that would impact historic places," Brent Leggs, CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, said in a statement.

The National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, which sits on the advisory council, said the proposed changes would fundamentally weaken the role of Tribal Nations in the review process and undermine the protection of sacred places.

Ira Matt, the association's executive director of Indigenous Diplomacy and Federal Relations, called the proposal "an affront to Tribal sovereignty."

"Any effort to diminish our voice or disregard the places, traditions, and practices we hold sacred is egregious and represents a violation of the federal government's trust and treaty responsibilities that is neither morally nor ethically defensible," Matt said.

The National Conference of State Historic Preservation Officers also objected to the proposed changes.

"It is baffling that during our semiquincentennial the very agency charged with overseeing Section 106 appears to be trying to relive that history, deliberately mislead its own members about what it is doing, and making it easier to destroy our historic places," Erik Hein, the group's executive director, said in a statement to CBS News.

The White House and Interior Department declined to comment.

World.title: U.S. and Saudi Arabia sign nuclear cooperation deal
World.content:
Washington — The U.S. and Saudi governments have signed a commercial nuclear deal that could allow Saudi Arabia to have a civilian nuclear program on its soil in cooperation with American companies, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Wednesday.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed what the Trump administration calls a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement, along with a safeguard agreement that the Energy Department says will lay the groundwork for a multibillion-dollar partnership to boost Saudi energy capacity. The deal could set the stage for a nuclear program for energy and other civilian purposes, not to build nuclear weapons.

CBS News previously reported the expected signing, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

"These agreements reflect our two nations' shared commitment to strengthening U.S.-Saudi commercial relations, delivering prosperity at home and security to our allies abroad," Wright said in a statement. "Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world's best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States."

The deal would create the potential for uranium enrichment on Saudi soil, though that would be controlled by a contracted corporation and only after a lengthy study is completed, CBS News previously reported. A civilian program is for energy supply for things like AI data centers, and not a military program.

The U.S. will want to see protocols and monitoring. The text of the deal has not yet been released.

The agreement will go to Congress for review, the Energy Department said. A 1954 law requires congressional review of all nuclear cooperation deals with foreign countries.

Westinghouse Electric Company, which builds nuclear reactors, is one of the U.S. companies planning to help develop Saudi Arabia's nuclear sector.

"The U.S. government's announcement to launch a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia is a landmark step that strengthens energy security, expands opportunities for U.S. industry and workers, and drives significant long-term economic growth and investment benefits for both countries," said Westinghouse CEO Dan Sumner.

A Trump administration framework for civil nuclear cooperation had been publicly announced in the fall of 2025. At the time, Wright described it as including bilateral safeguard agreements to bring U.S. nuclear technology to the kingdom. At the time, Wright stipulated that this keeps a "firm commitment to nonproliferation."

The original framework for this agreement was developed under the Biden administration, which a former U.S. official with direct knowledge described as requiring U.S.-only enrichment at a U.S.-controlled facility. It would also have been subject to congressional approval.

Under former President Joe Biden, the deal had been tied to a U.S. push to incentivize Saudi Arabia to follow through on the normalization of relations with the state of Israel. Normalization was also dependent on Israel providing a pathway to a future for self-determination by Palestinians, not necessarily a state of their own, and it offered investments and diplomatic representation. After the deadly terrorist attack by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, and the launch of the war in Gaza, that deal was put on hold.

But fuel-rich Saudi Arabia was still interested in the nuclear energy cooperation, particularly given the high degree of energy supply needed for artificial intelligence. The late Sen. Lindsey Graham had continued to work on this effort through both administrations.

The Trump deal does not appear to be overtly linked to a foreign policy objective, though the administration is at pains to reassure regional allies of the U.S. commitment to their security amid the ongoing Iran war. Saudi Arabia and other regional allies have borne the brunt of Iranian attacks since the war began at the end of February.

The landmark deal signifies the strengthening alliance and trust between the U.S. and the Saudis. But the civilian nuclear deal is likely to irritate Iran, Saudi Arabia's chief rival, which has long insisted on its right as a signatory of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons to maintain a civilian nuclear program.

Saudi Arabia will not be the first Gulf state with a civilian nuclear program. Back in 2009, the Obama administration signed an agreement with the United Arab Emirates that included a pledge for peaceful nuclear energy under nonproliferation controls.

World.title: House GOP advances $95 billion plan to fund Iran war and SAVE America Act
World.content:
Washington — The House adopted a GOP-backed budget blueprint on Wednesday that would provide up to $95 billion in funding for the Iran war, aid to farmers and parts of President Trump's voting regulations bill known as the SAVE America Act.

The House adopted the budget resolution in a 216 to 214 vote, with all Democrats, two Republicans and one independent who caucuses with Republicans voting in opposition.

It's the latest effort by Republicans to enact Mr. Trump's top priorities as the bipartisan appropriations process has broken down. Democrats remain vehemently opposed to continuing the war in Iran as well as strict new voting requirements championed by the president.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, called it the GOP's "best shot" to enact as much of the SAVE America Act into law "as possible."

Wednesday's vote is just the first step in the party-line reconciliation process. The Senate also needs to approve of the resolution, which instructs the committees of jurisdiction to begin crafting the $95 billion reconciliation package. The package will then need to clear both chambers. Republicans chose the reconciliation route — which they've also used to pass tax cuts and immigration enforcement — because it allows them to overcome Democratic resistance in the Senate and approve the funding via a simple majority.

The resolution directs the House Armed Services Committee and the House Intelligence Committee to write legislation that increases spending by up to $60 billion and $13 billion, respectively. The House Agriculture Committee received a $12 billion limit and the House Administration Committee was given a $10 billion cap.

The plan faces major hurdles in the upper chamber, where the SAVE America Act has been stuck for months and lacks even a simple majority of support. It's also unclear whether the voting regulation provisions — such as requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and a photo ID to cast a ballot — will survive the Senate's rules governing the reconciliation process, which prohibit the inclusion of non-budgetary policies. Funding for the Iran war could also run into pushback. A handful of GOP senators have voted in recent months to rein in Mr. Trump on Iran as the war continues without congressional authorization.

The plan also does not include provisions to offset spending increases, which frustrated some conservatives in the House.

"I think the problem is there's no plan to pay for it," GOP Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio said last week ahead of House Republicans' meeting with Vice President JD Vance, who came to the Capitol to rally members behind the plan. "A no-offset plan is dead on arrival."

On Monday, Mr. Trump called on House Republicans to unify behind the budget resolution and "fight" for the SAVE America Act. Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought met with House Republicans on Tuesday morning as the administration worked to get the resolution across the finish line.

World.title: House passes Pentagon funding and limits on stock trades in a last dash before recess
World.content:
House passes Pentagon funding and limits on stock trades in a last dash before recess

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

House Republicans passed $1.1 trillion in funding for the military on Wednesday, in a final flurry of activity before leaving Washington for a more than month-long recess.

The funding, an annual military policy bill called the National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA, passed by a vote of 216 to 212, with six Democrats joining Republicans to support the bill. It now heads to the Senate, where it faces an uncertain path forward.

The bill — typically advanced with broad bipartisan majorities — has become a largely party-line effort this year. Republicans call the bill "a generational investment in America's national defense" that "builds the fighting force of the future by prioritizing innovation, lethality, and readiness."

Sponsor Message

Democrats, even reliable military advocates, disagree.

"The problem with this year's defense authorization bill is that it comes with the inclusion of $1.15 trillion in discretionary spending," Rep. Adam Smith of Washington state, the top Democrat on the House Armed Service Committee, said in a statement. "I cannot and do not support meeting these needs by making massive cuts to critically important domestic programs and slashing taxes."

Republicans in the Senate will need support for the bill from Democrats in order to clear the 60-vote threshold needed to pass most legislation through the chamber. Last week, Senate Democrats blocked a version of the bill from coming up for a vote, demanding concessions that curb President Trump's war effort in Iran.

The NDAA debate comes at a contentious time for the Pentagon. Any progress toward a resolution to the U.S.-Iran war has crumbled as the two sides continue to trade attacks. Meanwhile, the war has already cost taxpayers $37.5 billion, according to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

In recent days, at least four U.S. service members have been killed, bringing the nation's death toll from the conflict to 18. Nearly 500 service members have been injured. The average price for a gallon of gas is back above four dollars a gallon in the United States, according to AAA.

Sponsor Message

A second track for Pentagon funding

Separately on Wednesday, House Republicans advanced a $95 billion budget blueprint. The framework, which still needs to pass the Senate, outlines more than $70 billion for the Iran war, $12 billion in assistance for farmers and money to implement provisions of the SAVE America Act, President Trump's signature election overhaul bill.

The vote was 216 to 214. GOP fiscal hardliners were frustrated that none of the spending called for by the bill would be paid for by spending reductions elsewhere. Other lawmakers were concerned about appropriating more funds for a war effort that seems to be rapidly escalating and remains unpopular with the American public.

Ultimately, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., was able to convince enough members to set aside their concerns in order to advance the framework legislation. They used a parliamentary procedure known as reconciliation, which means the package is not subject to the Senate's typical 60-vote margin and could, in theory, be passed on a party line vote.

The timeline for Senate action on the reconciliation framework is an open question.

On Tuesday, Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he wanted to prioritize negotiations to extend funding for the government beyond the midterm elections. Government funding is currently set to lapse at the end of September. Thune said he would try to negotiate a deal with Democrats, but if he can't reach a deal he would consider revamping the budget framework bill to extend government funding on a strictly party-line basis.

The House passed its own bill to extend government funding through December on Tuesday, but Thune said the plan doesn't include several funding requests sought by the White House.

New limits on trading stocks

By a vote of 232 to 198, the House also advanced a bill that would ban lawmakers from acquiring new individual stocks while in office. They would still be able to retain stocks they already own, reinvest stock dividend payments and sell stocks with disclosure.

The measure, dubbed the Stop Insider Trading Act, has been roundly opposed by non-partisan good government advocacy groups, who said in a letter to Congress that the bill does not ban members of Congress from owning stock or making decisions that would affect the value of the stocks they hold, prevent members from profiting off stock trades or from profiting off ownership or trades of other asset classes.

Sponsor Message

All but 13 Democrats opposed the measures, citing what they describe as major loopholes and concerns about an unrelated voter ID provision that was attached to the package.

World.title: Trump administration signs commercial nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Trump administration signs commercial nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

The Trump administration has signed a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia that would allow American companies to run commercial nuclear power plants on Saudi soil.

The agreement was signed by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Arabia's energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Department of Energy announced on Wednesday. They also signed an accompanying agreement about safeguards. The deal must be reviewed by Congress, which has 90 days to consider it.

The cooperation agreement gives American companies priority access to the Saudi nuclear energy program, meaning they can supply nuclear reactors and fuel, according to an administration memo about the agreement seen by NPR. It's expected to last decades and be worth billions of dollars, the Energy Department said.

Sponsor Message

"These agreements reflect our two nations' shared commitment to strengthening U.S.-Saudi commercial relations, delivering prosperity at home and security to our allies abroad," Wright said in the announcement. "Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world's best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States."

However, the memo seen by NPR said the agreement does not include provisions known as the "gold standard" that would prohibit the kingdom from enriching uranium and reprocessing nuclear fuel, nor does it require Saudi Arabia to adopt terms that would lead to greater oversight from the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The lack of those restrictions will raise concerns over providing the kingdom a pathway to weapons development. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has said that if Iran were to develop a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia would follow suit.

"Congress should approve only if the deal has the same gold-standard safeguards as our deal with the UAE," Rep. Brad Sherman, D-Ca., posted on X on Tuesday evening, before the agreement was announced. "A President waging war to prevent nuclear proliferation in the Middle East should not facilitate proliferation just because U.S. companies stand to make a profit."

Sponsor Message

The memo says the U.S. does not support a Saudi nuclear weapons program, and that the agreement is limited to peaceful cooperation on nuclear energy.

The memo notes that the agreement includes nonproliferation terms under the Atomic Energy Act. It also says that while the agreement provides a legal pathway for cooperation on the nuclear fuel cycle, it does not obligate the U.S. to transfer any fuel cycle capabilities or technologies to Saudi Arabia.

"I think it may make negotiating a reasonable deal with Iran more difficult," said Matthew Bunn, a nuclear proliferation expert at Harvard's Kennedy School of Government in an interview with NPR's All Things Considered.

Bunn said that Iran was less likely to sign an agreement involving intrusive inspections of its nuclear program if Saudi Arabia was also not committing to such agreements.

World.title: What to know about Ukraine's military shakeup
World.content:
What to know about Ukraine's military shakeup

toggle caption Paula Bronstein for NPR

KYIV — After a week of nationwide protests over the direction of Ukraine's military strategy in the ongoing war with Russia, the Ukrainian military has a new armed forces commander, Mykhailo Drapatyi.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy named Drapatyi to replace military chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi, whom he fired late Tuesday.

"There is a difficult task ahead, so we are not making loud promises," Drapatyi wrote in a Facebook post after his appointment was announced. "We are working with responsibility for our decisions and for the people who hold the front line and help Ukraine stand firm."

toggle caption Ukrainian Presidential Press Office/AP

The 43-year-old major general, widely viewed as a reformer, takes the reins at a time of political and military transition in Ukraine. He is also the face of a younger, post-Soviet generation of military leaders in Ukraine who are adapting more quickly to a tech-focused approach to the battlefield.

Sponsor Message

Drapatyi helped develop the use of the "drone line," which involves creating a "kill zone" near the front line filled with drones that attack and surveil. He takes over from the 60-year-old Syrskyi, a mastermind of traditional warfare who came under fire after clashing with the country's tech-savvy former defense minister.

Zelenskyy praised Syrskyi for "delivering results for Ukraine," defending Kyiv early in the Russian full-scale invasion, which began in February 2022, and liberating parts of northeastern Ukraine later that year.

"We have come a long way," Zelenskyy said in a video address . "Ukraine's defense continues, and every warrior must be treated with dignity."

Syrsykyi's dismissal comes after Zelenskyy's latest government reshuffle, which sparked mass protests across the country after he removed the popular, technology-focused defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, on July 15.

toggle caption Anastasia Vlasova/For The Washington Post via Getty Images

One protester in Kyiv, 42-year-old Mila Timchenko, said Syrskyi was experienced and integral to Ukraine's defense early in the war, "but times have changed, the way wars are being fought has changed."
