World.title: Georgia jails opposition TV host for 14 days over Facebook posts
World.content:
Arrests over social media posts in Georgia

On 22 July 2026, the Tbilisi City Court sentenced journalist and Formula TV host Vakho Sanaia to 14 days of administrative detention over posts he published on Facebook. The ruling was handed down by Judge Zviad Tsekvava.

The case against Sanaia was launched over Facebook posts about Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and MP Vladimer Bozhadze. Bozhadze has represented the European Socialists party since 2025, although he entered parliament on the ruling Georgian Dream party list following the 2024 parliamentary elections.

The Hate Speech Department, established within the Ministry of Internal Affairs, referred the case to Tbilisi City Court for legal review.

Following an investigation by the department, Sanaia was fined 6,000 lari on 10 July.

In the post that led to the fine, Sanaia wrote: “I hope no one called [Vladimer Bozhadze] d**k, because the law prohibits calling Lado d**k. I would also like to urge everyone not to call Lado a d**k.”

After being fined, Sanaia published another post of a similar nature on social media: “I wrote a post saying, ‘Don’t call Papuashvili and Bozhadze d**k,’ and I was fined 6,000 lari. Am I missing something? Give them a call.”

On 18 July, Sanaia said the court had contacted him over the post and informed him that a hearing had been scheduled in his case.

Sanaia did not attend the court hearing.

“I’m laughing,” he wrote on social media after news emerged that he had been sentenced to administrative detention.

Brief overview of the department

Administrative cases over opinions expressed in the public sphere are initiated on the basis of reports compiled by the Hate Speech Department, which was established within the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

The new department has been operating since 1 June.

Its mandate is to monitor and identify public statements that violate human dignity, contain insults or elements of hate speech, where they may constitute an administrative offence.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, between the department’s launch and 2 July, it identified 170 alleged offences, 150 of which were referred to court.

Of those 150 cases, rulings had been issued in 33 by that date. Thirty-one people were fined, while two received verbal warnings. Most of those fined were activists. Vakho Sanaia became the first journalist to be fined on the basis of a report compiled by the department.

АArrests over social media posts in Georgia

World.title: Russia destroyed 40,000 Armenian roses shipped via Belarus
World.content:
Russia destroys Armenian roses

Officials from Russia‘s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor in Smolensk Region discovered a shipment of freshly cut roses from Armenia that was being transported via Belarus.

According to the Belarusian outlet Euroradio, the shipment was deemed illegal because Russia has banned the import of nearly all Armenian goods since the spring.

Armenian roses imported via Belarus / 32.fsvps.gov.ru

Moscow says the import ban was imposed in response to what it described as violations of phytosanitary requirements. However, the restrictions were introduced after Armenia declared EU integration as a foreign policy goal, leading officials in Yerevan and the EU to view the move as politically motivated.

Russia has previously imposed similar trade restrictions on Georgia and Moldova to exert economic pressure amid political disagreements.

According to the accompanying documents, the lorry travelling from Belarus’s Minsk Region to Moscow was carrying non-alcoholic carbonated energy drinks. However, an inspection found 39,200 roses instead.

The flowers were being transported without the required phytosanitary certificates or shipping documents.

Rosselkhoznadzor said some of the boxes still bore labels identifying Armenia as the country of origin.

The roses were destroyed, while the carrier was held administratively liable.

Russia suspends flower imports from Iran over suspected re-exports from Armenia

Shortly after the reports emerged that Armenian roses transported via Belarus had been destroyed, Russia’s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor suspended the certification of flowers for export to Russia from Iran, also over suspicions that they had been re-exported from Armenia.

The agency said flower shipments from Iran in 2026 had significantly exceeded the volume recorded during the same period last year.

Rosselkhoznadzor also said that although Iran was listed as the exporting country, the appearance of the flowers and their packaging were identical to products previously supplied from Armenia.

Background

Since early spring 2026, Russia has gradually introduced restrictions on Armenian products.

Initially, the measures targeted Jermuk mineral water, followed by a range of alcoholic beverages.

On 30 May, Russia banned imports from Armenia of tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, herbs and strawberries.

This was followed by a temporary ban imposed by the Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (Rosselkhoznadzor) on the import of flowers and ornamental plants from Armenia.

Rosselkhoznadzor has also reported problems with imports of certain livestock products, as well as fish and fish products.

Armenia also received a letter from Russia warning of the possible termination of an agreement on supplies of natural gas, petroleum products and rough diamonds.

The restrictions imposed by Russia are significant for Armenia, as the Russian market has been the main destination for Armenian agricultural exports for decades.

The Armenian authorities are currently working, with active support from the European Union, to rapidly open alternative export markets for Armenian products.

World.title: Armenia begins recruiting and training border guards for Azerbaijan border
World.content:
Armenia launches border guard recruitment

The Armenian government plans to gradually transfer responsibility for guarding the entire Armenia-Azerbaijan border from the Defense Ministry to the Border Guard Troops of the National Security Service (NSS).

To make that possible, the agency needs additional personnel. The government therefore plans to expand the NSS by introducing the “I Have the Honor“ programme, which the Defense Ministry already runs successfully.

Under the programme, university students sign a contract to undergo military training while completing their studies. After graduation, they perform their military service at the location and under the conditions specified in the contract.

Under the new proposal, participants will first serve as conscripts in the rank of private in Defense Ministry units. They will then transfer to the NSS as commissioned officers.

“The new mechanism will help strengthen the National Security Service, particularly the Border Guard Troops, by recruiting personnel with higher education,” the explanatory note to the draft says.

Under an intergovernmental agreement signed in 1992, the Russian Federal Security Service’s Border Guard Service has been responsible for guarding Armenia’s borders with Turkey and Iran. In recent years, however, Armenia has steadily moved to place the protection of its borders entirely under its own control. In 2024, Russian border guards withdrew from Zvartnots International Airport and from border areas along the frontier with Azerbaijan. On January 1, 2025, Russian border guards also left the border crossing on the Armenia-Iran frontier. Then, on March 1, Armenia’s National Security Service assumed sole responsibility for guarding the Margara border crossing with Turkey. Since the beginning of 2026, only Armenian border guards have been serving at the Akhurik border crossing on the Armenia-Turkey border.

Deferring military service during university in exchange for serving as an officer

The “I Have the Honor” programme allows students to defer compulsory military service while at university. In return, they commit to serving later as commissioned officers.

“Students attend university free of charge, with the state covering tuition fees in full at the rate set by the university for the relevant programme.”

After graduating from university and completing the required military training, participants receive the rank of lieutenant and begin contract service.

Officers receive their assignments through a lottery system.

Those trained as platoon commanders serve for two years and three months.

Those trained for military medical service serve for four years after graduation, followed by one year of clinical residency.

What other changes does the draft propose?

The legislative package also includes amendments to several laws governing military service, the National Security Service’s Border Guard Troops, and the country’s national security agencies.

In particular, the draft would clearly define the circumstances in which NSS officers may use firearms, special equipment and physical force.

Before using force, officers would have to issue a warning and allow enough time for a person to comply with a lawful order, unless any delay posed an immediate danger. The draft also requires officers to use force proportionately to the level of resistance or threat. They would also have to provide first aid to anyone injured.

If parliament passes the legislative package, border guards will also be able to use video and audio recording devices while carrying out their duties.

The draft would also raise the retirement age for senior NSS officers from 52 to 55.

Armenia launches border guard recruitment

World.title: Georgia’s Asian pivot: What does Tbilisi seek in Central Asia?
World.content:
Georgia’s Asian pivot

A section of Georgia’s Baku–Tbilisi–Kars highway. Photo: Reuters

Since the start of summer 2026, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has met the leaders of all five Central Asian states.

Tbilisi has signed strategic partnership agreements with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The Georgian prime minister has also made his first official visits to Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. In July, Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov paid his first official visit to Tbilisi.

The Georgian government says the renewed engagement is aimed at strengthening the country’s role as a regional transit hub. For the Central Asian states, new trade routes are becoming increasingly important alongside those through Russia and China.

Georgia is offering them access from the Caspian Sea to the Black Sea and onwards to Europe.

The growing ties with Central Asia come against the backdrop of an almost complete freeze in relations between Tbilisi and the West. The European Union has significantly scaled back political contacts with the Georgian government and suspended part of its direct assistance.

According to official EU statements, the measures are a response to what Brussels describes as democratic backsliding in Georgia.

Georgia’s EU accession process has effectively been put on hold until the government changes its political course. The EU’s 2026 report states that no political dialogue took place between the EU and Georgia during the reporting period.

Against this backdrop, the Georgian government describes its foreign policy as multi-vector.

Central Asia has become one of the main pillars of that policy. The key question, however, is what lies behind this shift: an effort to expand Georgia’s economic opportunities, or a political response to deteriorating relations with the West?

Economic data present a mixed picture. Exports to Central Asia have increased, but most of the growth is not driven by goods produced in Georgia. Re-exported vehicles account for the bulk of exports to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

Moreover, Central Asia’s interest in Georgia is largely based on access to Western markets. If Tbilisi moves away from the European political and economic space, its value as a transit hub could also diminish.

Kyrgyzstan: Exports driven almost entirely by vehicle re-exports

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze visited Kyrgyzstan on 11 June 2026. According to the Georgian government, it was the first official meeting between the two countries at the highest level.

Kobakhidze held talks with President Sadyr Japarov. Bishkek also hosted the second meeting of the Georgian-Kyrgyz Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.

The two sides signed a series of agreements covering aviation, veterinary services, education, sport, legal cooperation and the management of state property. They also signed an agreement on the advance exchange of customs information.

Trade was the main economic focus of the talks. However, Georgia’s exports to the region remain heavily dependent on re-exports.

According to Georgia’s statistics office, Geostat, the country exported goods worth $355.2m to Kyrgyzstan between January and May 2026, while imports amounted to just $1.2m. In 2025, exports reached almost $1.5bn.

Data for the first four months of 2026 show that passenger cars accounted for 95.5% of exports. Other goods made up only a small share and included alcoholic drinks, soft drinks, lorries and medicines.

In practice, however, Kyrgyzstan is only nominally one of Georgia’s largest export markets. Georgia does not manufacture the cars it exports. Instead, it acts as an intermediary, purchasing, servicing and re-exporting the vehicles.

Direct investment from Kyrgyzstan also remains limited. It totalled $374,000 in 2025, down from $656,000 in 2024.

The most significant long-term project is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which will connect the Chinese city of Kashgar with Andijan in Uzbekistan via Kyrgyzstan.

Tbilisi expects the railway to bring additional freight to the Middle Corridor. The cargo would then travel through other Central Asian states, across the Caspian Sea, and onwards via Azerbaijan and Georgia.

According to Mariam Kvrivishvili, a significant increase in cargo volumes is expected from around 2031. However, different completion dates have been cited for the railway project, while the onward route across the Caspian Sea has yet to be finalised.

Georgia and Kyrgyzstan are also considering launching direct flights. In 2025, Georgia received 21,542 visitors from Kyrgyzstan. The figure remained virtually unchanged in the first quarter of 2026.

Tajikistan: Relations beginning to take institutional shape

Kobakhidze visited Tajikistan on 19-20 June in what was the first official visit by a senior Georgian official.

The prime minister held talks with President Emomali Rahmon and Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda. During the visit, the two sides signed 11 agreements. Previously, only three bilateral agreements had been in force.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon.

Tbilisi and Dushanbe established an intergovernmental commission on economic cooperation. Agreements were also signed in the fields of air transport, tourism and agriculture.

The two sides identified a broad range of potential areas for cooperation, including trade, investment, transport, energy and mining. Pharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence and digitalisation were also mentioned.

However, no specific projects in these sectors have yet been announced.

Trade with Tajikistan has also been boosted by vehicle re-exports. In 2025, Georgian exports totalled $179.6m, while imports did not reach even $1m. Between January and May 2026, exports fell to $47m.

In 2025, Georgia exported 7,592 passenger cars to Tajikistan worth $162.3m. They accounted for about 90% of total exports.

Other exports included medicines, soft drinks, mineral water and heavy machinery, but their combined share remained small compared with cars.

Direct investment from Tajikistan in Georgia is virtually non-existent. Tourist flows are also limited. In 2025, Georgia recorded 4,704 visits from Tajikistan, fewer than in 2024.

The two sides also plan to launch direct flights between Tbilisi and Dushanbe. However, no date has yet been announced for the start of services.

Tajikistan is a landlocked country with no direct access to the Middle Corridor. Its cargo must pass through other Central Asian states before reaching the Caspian Sea. As a result, linking Tajikistan to Georgia’s transit route requires coordination among several countries.

Kazakhstan: Georgia’s most viable economic and energy partner

Irakli Kobakhidze visited Kazakhstan on 29 June, where he met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov.

The main political outcome of the visit was a joint statement on strategic partnership. Tokayev also awarded Kobakhidze the first-class Order of Friendship.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The economic talks covered the Middle Corridor, energy, the port of Anaklia and tourism.

Of the five Central Asian states, Kazakhstan has the most extensive economic ties with Georgia. However, passenger cars also dominate Georgian exports to the country.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Kazakhstan reached $910m. Between January and May 2026, they fell to $218.2m, while imports over the same period amounted to $34.5m.

The main reason for the decline was a drop in vehicle re-exports. In the first five months of 2026, car exports amounted to $163.8m.

Georgia also exports mineral water, soft drinks, poultry meat and frozen fish to Kazakhstan. In return, it imports oil, petroleum products, wheat, cotton and metal ores.

Oil transit is another important area of cooperation. According to Tokayev, Kazakhstan plans to increase oil shipments through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline.

Transporting Kazakh oil through the pipeline reduces the country’s dependence on Russian routes, while generating additional transit revenue for Georgia.

According to a BP report, 49m barrels of oil were transported through the pipeline in the first quarter of 2026, equivalent to about six million tonnes.

The port of Anaklia is also important for Kazakhstan. According to Georgia’s Economy Ministry, the port project was one of the main topics discussed during the meetings in Astana.

Kazakhstan is Central Asia’s wealthiest country in terms of natural resources. It has reserves of oil, uranium, copper, tungsten and other important minerals. Western interest in the country is therefore linked not only to transport routes.

In November 2025, Kazakhstan signed a $1.1bn agreement with a US company to develop a tungsten deposit. The deal illustrates the scale of Western economic interest in Central Asia.

Uzbekistan: Strategic partnership and interest in Georgian ports

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev visited Georgia in July 2026. He and Irakli Kobakhidze signed a declaration on strategic partnership.

The two sides also signed agreements covering the economy, finance, customs, education and healthcare. The documents also addressed agriculture, culture and information technology.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev

Following the visit, Uzbekistan’s investment and transport ministers toured the ports of Anaklia and Poti. They also visited the Poti Free Industrial Zone.

Uzbekistan views Georgia as an important partner and transit hub in the South Caucasus. Its main interest lies in trade routes and access to Black Sea ports.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Uzbekistan totalled $220.2m, while imports reached $89.4m. Between January and May 2026, exports amounted to $64.3m and imports to $25.9m.

Investment remains far more limited. Uzbek direct investment in Georgia totalled just $220,000 in 2025. In the first quarter of 2026, it stood at $276,000.

Over the past six years, Georgia has received about $19m in investment from Uzbekistan. Uzbek businesspeople have mainly shown interest in trade, property and the hotel sector.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is also important for Uzbekistan. The project will provide the country with a direct rail link to China. The route could also be extended towards the Caspian Sea and Georgia.

The visits to Georgian ports were a practical sign of this interest. However, no specific Uzbek investments in the ports of Anaklia or Poti have yet been announced.

Turkmenistan: Gas, oil and access to Black Sea

Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov arrived in Georgia on 17 July, where he held talks with President Mikheil Kavelashvili and Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

The main topics of the talks were the Middle Corridor, TRACECA, port infrastructure and energy cooperation. The two sides also signed agreements covering education, industry and healthcare.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

The Turkmen president spoke of the joint use of ports on the Caspian and Black seas.

“Serious negotiations are already under way on the use of port infrastructure. This involves using ports on the Caspian and Black seas on a mutually beneficial basis,” Berdimuhamedov said.

He did not name any specific ports or provide details on the scale of investment or the project’s timeline.

In 2025, Georgian exports to Turkmenistan totalled $63.6m, while imports exceeded $39m. Between January and May 2026, bilateral trade fell to about $38.6m.

Georgia mainly imports oil and petroleum products from Turkmenistan, while exporting passenger cars and meat.

Energy expert Murman Margvelashvili sees short-term potential for refining Turkmen oil in Georgia, particularly at the new oil refinery in Kulevi.

A more long-term project is the Trans-Caspian gas pipeline. It would carry Turkmen gas across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, before continuing through Georgia and Turkey.

“A more strategic and long-term direction could be a project that has been under discussion for many years: the Trans-Caspian gas pipeline,” Margvelashvili said.

Turkmenistan has some of the world’s largest natural gas reserves. However, the Trans-Caspian pipeline has been discussed for several decades and there is currently no firm timetable for its implementation.

Middle Corridor: shared strategic interest for Georgia and Central Asia

One issue featured consistently in Georgia’s talks with all five Central Asian states: the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, better known as the Middle Corridor.

What is the Middle Corridor? The Middle Corridor, officially known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), is an international trade route linking China and Central Asia with Europe while bypassing Russia. The route runs through China, Kazakhstan, across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, through Georgia and onwards across the Black Sea to Europe. Why is it important? nterest in the Middle Corridor has grown since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as European and Asian businesses have sought alternatives to transport routes passing through Russia. The corridor offers several advantages: — it reduces dependence on Russian transit routes; — provides an alternative to the Northern Corridor; — can be faster than maritime shipping in some cases; — and connects Central Asian economies with European markets. Georgia’s role Georgia is one of the key countries along the Middle Corridor: — it provides the rail and road links connecting Azerbaijan with the Black Sea; — it is home to the ports of Poti and Batumi; — the planned deep-water port at Anaklia is widely seen as central to expanding the corridor’s capacity. Its main advantage is that it would be able to accommodate large container ships, something Georgia’s existing ports cannot fully support.

The Middle Corridor has gained strategic importance since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Central Asian countries are seeking alternatives to transporting goods through Russia, while Western governments and businesses are increasingly interested in supply chains that are less dependent on both Russia and China.

However, the Middle Corridor still faces a number of challenges:

Limited capacity at ports on the Caspian and Black seas;

Customs procedures that differ from one country to another;

A lack of coordinated tariff policies;

Delays at the junctions between maritime and rail transport;

High transportation costs;

Insufficient infrastructure.

As a result, political declarations alone will not be enough to make the corridor competitive. It will require ports, railways, a digital customs system and a coordinated tariff policy.

Anaklia: A project that could benefit Central Asia

The Georgian government has described the deep-water port of Anaklia as the key infrastructure project of the Middle Corridor.

According to the Ministry of Economy, the first phase of construction is scheduled for completion in 2029. The port will have an annual capacity of at least 600,000 TEU and will be capable of handling Panamax-class vessels.

The marine works are being carried out by the Belgian company Jan De Nul. However, the port operator has yet to be selected, and the project’s final financing model has not yet been determined.

The issue of Anaklia was discussed separately during meetings with the Kazakh and Uzbek delegations. Experts suggest that companies from Central Asia could eventually be considered as operators of the port’s terminals. The Georgian government has not announced any such agreement.

Anaklia’s commercial success will depend on securing guaranteed cargo volumes. For Georgia, therefore, agreements with Central Asian countries are not merely a matter of diplomacy. They also form part of the port’s economic rationale.

Western interest in Central Asia

Central Asia is not only a priority for the Georgian government. The United States, the European Union, China and Russia are all deepening their engagement with the region.

In April 2025, the EU and the five Central Asian states upgraded their relations to a strategic partnership. The bloc also announced a €12 billion Global Gateway investment package covering transport, critical raw materials, energy, water and digital connectivity.

In June 2026, the European Commission launched a new platform to develop transport infrastructure linking Europe with Central Asia via the Black Sea and the South Caucasus. Agreements signed with international financial institutions are expected to mobilise up to €2 billion in investment.

The United States’ primary interest lies in critical minerals. Central Asia is rich in uranium, copper, tungsten, gold and rare earth elements.

The countries of the region are using this growing interest to balance their foreign policies. They continue to cooperate with Russia and China while also seeking access to Western capital and markets.

What does closer cooperation with Central Asia mean for Georgia?

Experts agree that cooperation with Central Asia is important for Georgia. At the same time, the government is presenting these ties as a possible alternative to the country’s traditional Western orientation.

According to economist Rati Tsiklauri, the economic relationship between Georgia and Central Asia appears more substantial in official statements than it does in the actual trade statistics.

“Ultimately, all cooperation with Central Asia comes down to our role as a transit country. Unfortunately, our economy is not large enough to sustain a fully fledged two-way exchange of goods with these countries,” Tsiklauri said.

In Tsiklauri’s view, closer cooperation with Central Asia is a positive development. However, it should not become compensation for Georgia’s deteriorating relationship with the West.

“We should not try to build ties with East and Central Asia only to present them as proof that we no longer need the West because we have China, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. That simply won’t work,” Tsiklauri said.

Nika Alavidze, Georgia’s former deputy economy minister and co-founder of the public movement Georgia First, focuses on the quality of trade. In his view, vehicle re-exports generate revenue, but they cannot serve as a sustainable model for economic development.

“Re-exports do not create industry. Growing oil exports do not mean energy independence. Higher trade turnover does not amount to a technological breakthrough,” Alavidze wrote on his blog.

He argues that “portraying Asia as an alternative to the West is a dangerous political illusion.”

“The circumstances created by the Russia-Ukraine war have opened a temporary trade window for Georgia, but that is not a strategy—especially when it comes with serious reputational risks,” Alavidze said.

In his view, Georgia’s greatest asset is its integration with the Western system. The country can become a reliable legal, financial and transit platform for Central Asia, but only if it remains connected to European rules and standards.

“What matters to Central Asian markets is Georgia’s geopolitical role, not simply its geographical location. They fully understand that geography alone offers them nothing. By contrast, Georgia’s geopolitical weight allows them to integrate their economic model, culture, legal framework and institutions more smoothly with major Western markets. Asia needs a connection to Europe, just as Europe needs a connection to Asia. If we limit ourselves to serving only as a geographical corridor, we will gain nothing, remain merely a transit route and ultimately be left with little more than environmental or infrastructure-related costs alongside short-term benefits,” Alavidze said.

Economist Elguja Khokrishvili also sees Georgia’s geographical advantage as only a temporary opportunity. In his view, cargo owners will continue to use the Georgian corridor only as long as it remains competitive.

Khokrishvili also notes that the Central Asian countries possess other sources of leverage. Kazakhstan offers partners oil, uranium and a large market. Uzbekistan has gold, copper, uranium and a growing economy. Georgia’s main advantage, by contrast, is its geographical location.

“But geographical advantages quickly lose their value once alternative routes are developed,” Khokrishvili wrote.

Zaza Shengelia, a researcher at EPRC, highlights the financial and institutional support associated with Georgia’s EU candidate status. In his view, partnership with Central Asian countries cannot replace that resource.

“It would be a mistake to suggest that this partnership is an alternative or a substitute for the enormous institutional support that was practically within our grasp thanks to EU candidate status,” Shengelia said.

Taken together, the experts reach a similar conclusion: Central Asia is an important market and transit partner for Georgia. However, the economic value of these relationships depends to a large extent on Georgia’s connection with Europe.

Georgia can serve as Central Asia’s gateway to the West. But to do so, it must itself remain integrated into the West’s economic and legal space.

Otherwise, the country will be left with little more than a favourable geographical location. And a good place on the map is not an economic policy.

Georgia’s Asian pivot

World.title: ‘The whole village knew’: Harrowing story of Nata Vibliani, who survived childhood sexual abuse
World.content:
Nata Vibliani’s story

Forty-three-year-old Nata Vibliani says she was just nine years old when she was repeatedly sexually abused by four men from her village of Sgurishi in the mountainous region of Svaneti.

Nearly 35 years have passed since then. Nata now lives in Germany, far from Georgia. She has cut all ties with her family, relatives and her home village, but says she has never been able to leave the past behind. Three months ago, she posted a video on social media in which she recounted her story, identified the alleged perpetrators by name and accused the entire village of turning a blind eye.

Nata Vibliani’s harrowing account shocked Georgian society.

But the reaction did not stop on social media. About a month ago, police contacted Vibliani and opened an investigation into allegations of rape. The authorities must now establish not only what happened to a child 35 years ago, but also why her family, fellow villagers and law enforcement authorities failed to protect her.

Videos that prompted investigation

The 1990s, Svaneti. At the time, Georgia was being torn apart by several armed conflicts. Chaos and lawlessness prevailed, with armed men controlling the streets. The state existed largely on paper and was unable to protect its citizens.

Nata Vibliani. Photo: Formula

In a mountain village in Svaneṭi, Georgia, the story of a nine-year-old girl was unfolding.

The first video appeals by Nata Vibliani appeared on social media three months ago, but the broader public learned of her story after she appeared as a guest on a popular podcast hosted by journalist Tamuna Museridze.

Speaking from exile in a video recording, Vibliani recounted a childhood she says was destroyed by systematic sexual and physical abuse.

Vibliani publicly named four men, stating they were her relatives and fellow villagers. According to her, one of them—the brother of her godfather—raped her for several years. The other three, the woman says, are relatives of the first alleged abuser.

The videos have sparked mixed reactions. The majority of the public is demanding an investigation and the punishment of those responsible. However, some accuse her of damaging the reputation of Svaneti and the Svan people.

The case is being investigated by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti Police Department under the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Police have already questioned several individuals who may possess vital information.

On 21 July, Nata Vibliani herself was also questioned via video link.

According to publicly available information, no charges have been brought against anyone at this stage. Consequently, the individuals named by Vibliani are legally presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law, which is why we are not disclosing their names in this article.

Nata Vibliani’s childhood after her father’s death

Nata Vibliani struggles to recall the exact years the events took place, but she vividly remembers individual episodes of violence.

In Svaneti, she lived with her father, mother, and three siblings. Nata was the eldest of the children.

She was seven years old when her father died under mysterious circumstances, leaving four children with their mother. According to Vibliani, the abuse began shortly thereafter.

“I have a fourth-grade education. I remember the facts well, but I struggle to pinpoint the exact years. This nightmare began a year after my father’s death, just a few days after the anniversary of his passing. My father died in my arms when I was seven years old, leaving four of us children behind.”

According to Nata, a man close to the family—the brother of her godfather—raped her for the first time in a cowshed. The young girl was milking a cow when the man entered.

“He put his hand on my head and told me not to be afraid… I passed out from the pain, and I don’t know how long I lay in that cowshed in that state. When I regained consciousness, the man was no longer there. He had left me and run off.”

Vibliani says that after this incident, the abuse became systematic. While the location changed, the perpetrator’s control over her never wavered.

“He raped me in the bushes, at home, in the field,” Nata Vibliani told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

According to Vibliani, the man also threatened her at gunpoint. He directed the firearm at her younger siblings as well, using terror to keep her silent: if she spoke about the abuse, he would kill her brothers and sister.

“I fought back until he took out a gun and pressed the barrel to my mouth. He raped me like that. He also aimed the gun at my younger brothers and told me that if I made a single sound, he would kill them.”

Vibliani recalls another ordeal. According to her, the abuser tied her to a horse and dragged her to a pasture. The woman says this was done as punishment and a warning never to tell anyone about what had happened.

Pregnancy and unknown fate of her child

One of the most painful aspects of Vibliani’s story involves her pregnancy. She says she became pregnant by her abuser around the age of 14 and went into premature labor.

According to Vibliani, she was taken to give birth in the neighboring Samegrelo region. The child was born alive at a maternity hospital in Zugdidi. She says she saw the newborn’s dark hair and heard his voice, yet to this day she does not know what became of him.

“I know he was born alive—I saw him and I heard his voice. Based on my information, the doctor who delivered the baby is no longer alive. I remember a dialogue where a doctor or nurse asked what should be done with the child, and he [the man Vibliani accuses of sexual abuse] replied, ‘Kill him.’ I don’t know what happened after that.”

Nata Vibliani named fellow villagers who accompanied the abuser to Zugdidi and witnessed this conversation.

Corroborating this account will be one of the investigation’s most challenging tasks. It will require locating medical records, potential witnesses, and archival investigative files. It remains unknown whether these documents have survived after three decades.

“I Want to rid Svaneti of paedophiles”

Vibliani states that her pregnancy was no secret and that everyone was aware of it. For this reason, she directs her most painful questions not only at her alleged abusers, but at her fellow villagers as well:

“The whole village knew I was pregnant. Why didn’t they stand up for me when they heard what was happening in my grandfather’s house? Where were those Svan men who are now accusing me everywhere of wanting to tarnish Svaneti’s name? I want to rid Svaneti of paedophiles. They have no right to build a house on my land, mock my father’s memory, throw stones at me like a criminal, or drive me out of Svaneti in disgrace. They killed my child.”

According to Vibliani, the man who fathered the child spread rumors throughout the village claiming the baby was not his. She says he threatened a local boy and forced him to confess to having had sexual relations with Nata and claiming paternity of the child.

However, Vibliani believes everyone in the village knew the truth full well, but remained silent out of fear, as the man and his brothers were local criminal figures.

When entire village blames the victim

According to Vibliani, family members, relatives, and fellow villagers were aware of the abuse. Yet instead of support, she faced humiliation.

She recalls attending a fellow villager’s christening while pregnant. She was driven out of the event, called a “whore,” and children threw stones at her in the yard.

For Vibliani, this episode clearly demonstrates how the entire village shifted the blame for the abuse from the perpetrator to the child.

Vibliani also stresses that she was abused by multiple men. She alleges that subsequent assaults were carried out with the involvement of the first abuser in an effort to intimidate her and ultimately silence her forever.

“All three are relatives of this man. They raped me with his involvement to cover up his atrocity, so that I could never speak out as a woman, so that I could never say I had been raped by so many men.”

According to Vibliani, one of the three additional abusers was the primary perpetrator’s brother—a criminal figure who had just been released from prison.

First investigation closed in a week

Vibliani says that in the mid-1990s, her grandfather filed a police report regarding the sexual abuse. A case was opened by the regional police department in Zugdidi, and the child underwent a forensic medical examination.

“They even sent me the results of the examination. But this man [the abuser] had connections in the police and was able to cover up a lot. About a week later, my family withdrew the complaint, and that’s how the case ended.”

This detail could prove crucial for the ongoing investigation. If the original case files have survived, they may contain expert medical findings, witness statements, and other official records.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs has not yet publicly confirmed whether the 1990s case file has been located, nor has it commented on why the investigation was halted at the time.

Sale of family home and departure from Svaneti

According to Vibliani, as a result of the abuse and public condemnation, her family lost their ancestral home. In the late 1990s, under pressure from the community, they left the village.

In exchange for their house and land, the family was paid 22,000 GEL, a sum Vibliani considers symbolic. The children then moved with their mother to Zugdidi, where they were forced to live in hardship.

“I was still a minor at the time, and I even attempted suicide, but I survived. As soon as I recovered and regained my strength, I left home for Kutaisi. After that, I never spoke to my family members again—not to my brothers and sisters, not to my mother, not to anyone. When I needed help, nobody supported me, not even my mother.

It is true that I later re-established contact with my relatives, but they treated me like a criminal, so I no longer wanted to communicate with anyone,” Vibliani recalls.

In the interview, Nata Vibliani speaks of her mother with bitterness. In the victim’s view, her mother failed to protect her properly. At the same time, Vibliani notes that following her father’s death, her mother herself became a victim of sexual violence at the hands of fellow villagers.

Father factor

Nata remembers her father with tears in her eyes, saying that her life turned into a living hell after he died.

Vibliani says she began her fight for justice largely to honor her father’s memory.

Her father died in seven-year-old Nata’s arms from a gunshot wound to the heart; the origin of the shooting remains unknown, as no autopsy was ever performed.

Vibliani does not rule out suicide, as her father was in conflict with the community. The dispute stemmed from the fact that her father was adopted, rather than a biological descendant of the Vibliani lineage.

Her grandfather’s family did not want the extensive Vibliani lands to pass to an adopted son, and they persecuted the young girl’s father as a result. After his death, his wife and children were subjected to abuse, and the family was ultimately driven from the village.

What does Nata Vibliani demand?

Vibliani maintains that she began speaking out publicly about the abuse not out of revenge, but to seek justice.

She is represented by lawyer Mariam Barsonidze. On 15 July, Vibliani officially petitioned the Ministry of Internal Affairs for the assignment of legal counsel to the case.

The defence team’s primary demand was a timely and thorough interview of Vibliani. Her lawyer is now requesting that she be granted official victim status, which would allow Vibliani and her counsel full access to the case files.

“The horrific facts recounted by Nata Vibliani must be detailed comprehensively. Following this, she must be granted victim status, and as the victim and her legal counsel, we will have the full right to examine the investigative materials.”

According to the lawyer, this is not an isolated case. Its outcome is equally vital for other women who remain silent about the abuse they suffered during childhood.

Today, Nata lives in Germany and is a mother to an adult son and a grandmother. She has partially reconciled with her relatives; however, according to Vibliani, her family continues to treat her as though she herself were to blame for what happened.

Is justice possible 35 years later?

In interviews, Nata says that over these 35 years, not a single day has passed without her thinking about what happened to her.

Time poses the primary challenge for the investigation. Potential crime scenes have altered, some witnesses may have died, and memories face rigorous scrutiny in court.

At the same time, the statute of limitations does not automatically preclude prosecution.

In 2020, the law was amended so that the statute of limitations no longer applies to certain sexual offences committed against minors. However, in Vibliani’s case, investigators must first determine the exact timeframe of the last alleged act of abuse.

The legal classification of the offences must also be clarified in light of current legislation and recent amendments. The final assessment will depend on specific dates and circumstances.

Mari Varamashvili, a lawyer with the human rights organization Sapari, explains that the 2020 amendment will apply to the case provided the 30-year statute of limitations had not expired by that time.

“If it turns out that the 30-year statute of limitations had not lapsed by 2020, it means that no statute of limitations will apply to Nata Vibliani’s case.”

Under current law, rape is defined under Article 137 of the Criminal Code as sexual intercourse involving physical force, threats of violence, or taking advantage of a victim’s helpless state.

However, when evaluating actions allegedly committed in the 1990s, investigators will also need to examine the legislation in force at that time.

According to Varamashvili, investigators must also interview all potential witnesses and locate historical case records. Psychological evaluations could also prove highly significant.

Georgian courts have previously heard cases involving historical sexual abuse. In 2022, a court found a man guilty of raping a minor 25 years prior.

In 2024, another man was sentenced to 20 years in prison for raping his sister’s underage children.

While these precedents offer no guarantee of a favorable outcome in Vibliani’s case, they demonstrate that while passage of time complicates evidence gathering, it does not render an investigation impossible.

Danger even in exile

Vibliani fears persecution despite residing in Germany.

On 14 July, she told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that she had not left her house for four days.

“I have exposed five families in Svaneti. Five families hate me and are coming after me, and I don’t know which of them might decide to take revenge. Even though I am not in Georgia, I do not feel safe.”

For this reason, the investigation must extend beyond uncovering historical evidence; authorities must also assess the risk of potential intimidation and retaliation.

The Women’s Movement has called on law enforcement agencies to conduct an independent and effective investigation. The organization demands a trauma-informed approach, measures to guarantee Vibliani’s safety, and that she be kept fully informed of developments.

Vibliani’s public account highlights a critical issue: the true scale of child sexual abuse in Georgia remains unknown, as the country still lacks a comprehensive system for prevention, detection, and victim support.

World.title: Transparency International Georgia: ‘Georgia now has 90 political prisoners under PACE criteria’
World.content:
List of political prisoners in Georgia

According to Transparency International Georgia, there are currently 90 political prisoners in Georgia. The organisation has published a list of their names.

The list was compiled using the criteria set out in Resolution 1900 (2012) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

How were the cases assessed?

Transparency International Georgia said each case was assessed individually, based on the circumstances of the case, court decisions and international human rights standards.

The organisation said the list is based on legal criteria established by the Council of Europe rather than politically motivated assessments.

Under those criteria, a person may be considered a political prisoner if their detention is linked to:

violations of fundamental rights;

detention for political reasons where the alleged act does not constitute a criminal offence;

a punishment that is clearly disproportionate;

discriminatory treatment; or

judicial proceedings that fail to meet the requirements of a fair trial.

The list specifies which of these criteria are considered to apply in each individual case.

“The large number of political prisoners once again demonstrates the existence of politically motivated justice in Georgia and the deterioration of the human rights situation,” Transparency International Georgia said in a statement.

Who is on the list?

The list published by Transparency International includes several high-profile figures, among them journalist Mzia Amaghlobeli, the founder of the media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

Amaghlobeli was arrested overnight on 11-12 January 2025 in Batumi after being accused of slapping the city’s police chief. The incident followed what her supporters say was an insult by the police officer. She was sentenced to two years in prison.

Another person on the list is opposition politician Elene Khoshtaria, the leader of the Droa party. She was sentenced to 18 months in prison for painting graffiti on an election poster of Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze.

Opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, was also sentenced to prison. He received a sentence of two years and six months on charges of “promising a bribe to a public official” and “calling for the overthrow of the government”.

Opposition politician Nika Melia, one of the leaders of the Ahali party, is facing several criminal cases. Among them is the so-called government sabotage case, which is still pending and carries the possibility of a lengthy prison sentence.

Singer and activist Paata Burchuladze was arrested over the alleged “failed coup” of 4 October and sentenced to seven years in prison. He was convicted of attempting to seize a strategic facility, organising and leading group violence, and publicly calling for the overthrow of the government.

Poet Zviad Ratiani was sentenced to two years in prison for insulting a police officer.

The full list of political prisoners is available at the link below.

List of political prisoners in Georgia

World.title: Prince George turns 13 as he heads to Eton
World.content:
The UK's Prince George, second in line to the throne, has turned 13 as he readies to follow in his father Prince William's footsteps and start at the prestigious Eton College.

Kensington Palace shared a picture of the prince, as his grandfather King Charles III and his wife Queen Camilla wished him "happy birthday".

As the eldest child of the heir to the British throne, Prince William, and Princess Catherine, George is set to succeed his father as king one day.

Prince William and Prince George in the Royal Box watching the the Wimbledon men's singles final earlier this month. (AP: Dave Shopland/Invision)

But first, he will face another daunting challenge: the terrible teens and starting at Eton boarding school in September.

According to royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams, the young prince is being "inducted into things very gradually" and as he grows older, he will increase his public appearances.

Prince George heading to Eton College Prince George will attend Eton College this September, following in the footsteps of his father, Prince William.

The prince was born on July 22, 2013, at St Mary's Hospital in London to a global media frenzy and public celebrations. His full name is George Alexander Louis.

He was quickly whisked away on his first royal tour in April 2014, when his parents visited New Zealand and Australia, where the eight-month-old was seen excitedly interacting with the wildlife.

William, Kate and George initially lived in a rented farmhouse in rural Anglesey off the coast of north-west Wales.

Shielded from cameras from an early age, the prince's rare public appearances as a toddler were exhaustively reported in the British media, calling him "Gorgeous George".

Prince William with baby George during an official visit to Australia in 2014. (Reuters: Chris Jackson)

Since then, his birthday celebrations have been kept private as well, with the family occasionally sharing official photographs.

"William and Catherine have done extremely well in trying to bring him up in, in a simple way, sort of, as normally as possible," Mr Fitzwilliams told AFP.

In 2017, the family moved to an apartment in London's Kensington Palace, and George had his first day of school at a private school in south London.

They later moved to their long-term home on the Windsor estate, south-west of London, where George has attended the private Lambrook School since 2022, alongside his siblings, Charlotte, 11, and Louis, the youngest at eight.

Football and helicopters

He has already been part of high-profile events, appearing alongside his family on the balcony of Buckingham Palace for the Trooping of the Colour ceremony, and helping carry the train of his grandfather's robes during Charles's coronation in 2023.

Prince George alongside his sister Princess Charlotte at Trooping The Colour, the King's annual birthday parade, last month. (AP: Kirsty Wigglesworth)

Unlike Louis, who has been pictured comically pulling faces at events, George has appeared to be more serious and composed in public engagements.

"He was a bit shy in early years", said Mr Fitzwilliams, pointing out he has been seen being "helpful to Charlotte and Louis on occasions".

" If you look at him in the formal occasions, I think you can see him assuming a role reasonably easily. "

Beyond the royal title, Prince William has also passed onto George his love for football and his team Aston Villa.

The prince often accompanies William to Villa games, and his mother to the Wimbledon tennis tournament.

Prince George with his family at a carol service at Westminster Abbey in December. (Reuters: Aaron Chown)

He is also said to have an interest in helicopters and could follow in the steps of his father, who has worked as an air ambulance pilot.

In September, George will begin boarding at Eton, but his family will be close by in Windsor.

"This is where he'll be, as it were, inducted into statecraft, history," Mr Fitzwilliams said.

Like his father and uncle Harry, George will have security at the famous secondary school, which charges more than £63,000 ($120,000) in annual fees.

"Now he's a teenager, Eton beckons," Mr Fitzwilliams said.

"Eton is the big step towards maturity."

AFP

World.title: Rusted tin transformed into prize-winning portraits
World.content:
From daily work in mining to tens of thousands of years of history and culture, the red dirt and rocky hills of Western Australia's Pilbara represent many things to many people.

But for 26-year-old artist Jenna Pickering, it represents an endless canvas.

"Pop a bit of gesso on, and you can paint on anything," she said.

She often uses rusted tin or pieces of wood as the base for her meticulous oil paintings, often chosen to match her subject.

Jenna paints current Cossack caretaker Paddy on a found piece of tin. (ABC Pilbara: Mietta Adams)

"It absolutely makes it 10 times harder not having a flat object … sometimes I'm doing it, and I'm like 'why?'" she said.

Her goal is to paint as many local faces as she can during her month-long stay as the artist-in-residence at Cossack, a historic ghost town 1,600 kilometres north of Perth.

Jenna Pickering says found objects have more character and are more sustainable than regular canvasses. (ABC Pilbara: Mietta Adams)

Full-time career

Her unique blend of precise artistry paired with her quirky personality has picked up momentum on social media, garnering more than 100,000 followers.

Jenna Pickering's studio at Cossack is open to the public during her residency. (ABC Pilbara: Mietta Adams)

Pickering also gained national prominence as a finalist in ABC's Portrait Artist of the Year, and has won numerous prestigious art prizes.

That momentum pushed her to leave her job as a community events coordinator and become a full-time artist three months ago.

Loading

"I came to a point where I was like: an artist is a real job if I want it to be a real job," she said.

"People froth for some reason at me doing exactly what I'm doing.

"I'm only getting older, why not just throw myself in the deep end, hey?"

The self-taught artist paints faces on objects that "match". (ABC Pilbara: Mietta Adams)

Historic town transforms into arts hub

The artist-in-residence program is a key part of the Cossack Art Awards.

The awards, now featuring more than 300 paintings inside century-old stone buildings, started in 1993 as an idea from former caretaker Brian Hoey.

The Cossack Art Awards are one of the most secluded and distinctive art prizes in regional Australia. (ABC Pilbara: Mietta Adams)

It has since grown to be the richest acquisitive art award in regional Australia with a total prize pool of $97,000.

Pickering, who was the Cossack award winner in 2023, said it offered important recognition for regional artists and helped them stand out.

Cossack has a permanent population of just one resident. (ABC Pilbara: Mietta Adams)

"How amazing is it as an artist out here to have our stuff in front of all these people from all over Australia and the world?" she said.

" You get so many opportunities being a big fish in a small pond. "

The City of Karratha said more than 80 works had been sold in the three days since opening.

"Our region has become a renowned artistic hub and the calibre of artworks entered this year reflects the rich culture and creativity we have to offer," Mayor Daniel Scott said.

Cossack was the birthplace of Western Australia's pearling industry. (ABC Pilbara: Mietta Adams)

While Pickering said being a remote artist could make it challenging to travel to exhibitions or network with other artists, it was not enough of a deterrent to leave her Tom Price home.

"I think I'm so bush-ified, I would look like a weirdo in the city," she said.

"Once you live in the Pilbara, you stay in the Pilbara."

This year's overall Cossack Art Awards winner was Jenny Butt's Nyurnma (Burnt Country).

The three-week exhibition remains open until August 9.

World.title: Victorian teachers begin second major strike as pay talks stall
World.content:
Victoria can expect major statewide disruptions today as teachers and education support staff walk off the job in their second major strike action of the year.

State schools will effectively be closed during today's major strike action, with thousands expected to take part once again.

Roughly 35,000 educators and supporters marched through Melbourne's CBD in March as part of the 24-hour strike.

What you need to know about Victoria's second teacher strike Victorian state school teachers and educators are going ahead with their second 24-hour strike this year after union members rejected the government's latest pay offer.

The strike comes after Australian Education Union (AEU) members voted to reject the state government's latest pay offer on the weekend.

The union said just over half of its members opposed the government's new offer, which this time included support staff in a 28 per cent pay increase over four years and halving the number of compulsory meetings educators must attend.

Instead, the union is calling for the state government to agree to a three-year deal and for more action to alleviate educators' workloads.

AEU Victoria President Justin Mullaly said workloads were a key issue for teachers.

"They work in the lowest-funded schools in the country, and that means that they carry a significant burden when it comes to workload," he told ABC Radio Melbourne.

"They're working on average 12 hours unpaid per week. They need some relief from that.

"That's one of the key things that we need to see further addressed in negotiations."

AEU Victorian president Justin Mullaly. (ABC News)

Mr Mullaly said the union's concerns were more about staff shortages and workloads than the government's pay offer.

"When it comes to pay, there's no doubt that a 28 per cent pay increase is significant. We've always acknowledged that," he said.

"But when you've got a situation where people are working in schools where shortages of teachers continue, you've got to do more to attract and, in particular, retain the workforce."

Teachers gathered outside Victoria's Trades Hall in March. (ABC News: Stephanie Ferrier)

A Victorian government spokesperson said discussions with the union were continuing.

"Families are already juggling a lot, and today's disruption is disappointing," the spokesperson said.

"This deal would have made Victorian teachers and education support staff the best paid in the country together with the best conditions.

"This was a close vote, and we will continue to work with the AEU to resolve this matter."

In June, Victorian teachers went against AEU advice and voted down a pay rise of between 28 and 32 per cent.

In March, teachers and supporters took statewide strike action, marching to parliament in central Melbourne, with police estimating 35,000 people were in attendance.

The March strike was the first of its kind since AEU members took statewide industrial action in 2013 when negotiations with the Baillieu Coalition government broke down.

World.title: Star footballer's protest over transfer leads to training cancellation
World.content:
Wolverhampton striker Tolu Arokodare allegedly forced the cancellation of a training session after he refused to leave the pitch.

Sources said the 25-year-old Nigerian sat down and demanded the club let him move to Italian club Fiorentina.

Wolves have rejected a bid from the Serie A side, having accepted an offer from Turkish club Trabzonspor.

Arokodare's actions led to new boss Cesar Peixoto terminating the session.

Arokodare will not be involved in Wolverhampton's friendly at Maidenhead United as Wolves continue their pre-season plans.

Arokodare denied the reports on social media.

"I was very surprised and disappointed to see the media reports today, many of which are inaccurate. Throughout my career, I have always taken great pride in conducting myself professionally and maintaining the highest training standards," he wrote on X.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I remain under contract with Wolves, and my only intention is to fulfil my responsibilities professionally by training, doing my job, and contributing to the team in accordance with that contract."

The latest incident is another flashpoint in the forward's career at Wolves after he was disciplined in April following a confrontation with young forward Mateus Mane.

Arokodare signed a massive deal after leaving Genk before last season's EPL, but scored just three league goals as Wolves finished bottom of the Premier League and were relegated.

The incident presents an early challenge for Peixoto just weeks into his reign after he replaced Rob Edwards in a surprise move last month.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: OpenAI model goes rogue during testing and hacks startup
World.content:
OpenAI says an autonomous agent powered by its advanced artificial intelligence models went rogue during a security test and triggered a hack that compromised the infrastructure of AI startup Hugging Face last week.

The ChatGPT creator was testing capabilities of some of its most advanced models in a controlled environment, but the agent escaped containment, reached the internet and broke into Hugging Face to satisfy its testing goal.

The incident signals that AI's expanding capabilities are already fuelling the security threat experts long feared and even top developers can be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit.

The breakout was "an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities" and OpenAI is reinforcing its safeguards, the company said in a blog post.

It also drew attention as New York-based Hugging Face said it had used an open-source Chinese model to contain the attack because leading US models, unable to tell a defender from an attacker, refused to process the data needed for analysis.

Loading...

The company said in a blog post last week that it used Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2 for the analysis, which also allowed it to keep attacker data and any credentials within its systems.

GLM-5.2 and Beijing-based Moonshot's Kimi K3 have stirred Silicon Valley recently with capabilities nearing those of top U.S. models at lower costs and without the guardrails that block their American rivals from use in tasks such as cybersecurity.

"When a frontier model is attacking you and moving laterally inside your infrastructure, defenders need wide access to near-frontier tools within hours or even minutes, rather than being pointed towards a closed-door, vetted application programme for model access," Hugging Face Co-founder Thomas Wolf said on X.

Sign of things to come

The hack at Hugging Face, which hosts open-source large language models and datasets, rattled the cybersecurity community after the company said last week the breach "was different from anything we had handled before" and "was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system".

OpenAI's disclosure that its advanced models were responsible for the breach, despite having placed them in what it described as "a highly isolated environment," will likely intensify disquiet over the power and risk of frontier models.

Representative Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat, said the incident was alarming.

"AI is developing extremely fast with no real regulations to keep us safe," he said in a statement, calling for mandatory independent safety testing, mandatory disclosure of security incidents, and international cooperation "to keep people safe from absolute disaster".

The Office of the National Cyber Director, the US cyber defence agency CISA, and the US National Security Agency did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

Katie Moussouris, chief executive of Luta Security, said that the incident was a harbinger of breaches to come, saying that today's models were "like the world's cleverest octopus escape artists, with unlimited prehensile arms and the ability to squeeze through anywhere".

She said that "labs and government evaluators need to work on the ability to contain, monitor, and disclose to affected parties when an AI pulls another Houdini, ideally before it harms a third party. None exist today".

Matt Suiche, an engineer at agentic AI cybersecurity company Tolmo, said the incident showed that the frontier models were "closing the gap with state-of-the-art attackers".

News bosses call for AI deals Media leaders say AI developers should pay to license Australian journalism and culture used to train their models.

But he said that the sorts of breaches outlined in OpenAI's blog post were possible to carry out with technology that was available well beyond the walls of frontier research labs.

"This is what we've already seen internally, with our agents we already have results like this," Suiche said.

"We don't even have to use the latest models."

Reuters

World.title: Weightlifter puts 'best foot forward' for Comm Games
World.content:
Kiana Elliott always knew she wanted to compete in the Olympics.

When she was aged just three, the Sydney 2000 Games captured her attention.

"There was a little seed planted in my head," she said.

She thought gymnastics would be her pathway to the podium, but injury meant she had to retire from the sport at 14.

She discovered weightlifting while looking for another way to keep fit.

"I didn't even know it [weightlifting] existed, and I found it fun," Elliott said.

"I pursued it, and I've kept going and I'm still going."

Kiana Elliott finds weightlifting fun. (ABC News: Sophie Holder)

Elliott has now represented Australia in weightlifting at multiple events, including several Junior World Championships, three Pacific Games and the pandemic-delayed Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games.

She competed at the Birmingham 2022 Games, having suffered an injury just two months earlier.

"There was a big question mark on whether I'd be able to go," she said.

"I lifted about 90-to-94 per cent of my best and that was good enough for fourth.

" That left a little bit of a fire in me. "

According to the Australian Commonwealth Games website, Elliott is among 27 South Australians expected to compete at Glasgow.

'Anything can happen'

Elliott said she was focused on being in a good headspace ahead of the Games.

"I personally don't push too hard in terms of maximal weight and maximal attempts in the gym because I need to keep myself physically intact for competition," she said.

"Sport is like a little microcosm of life, it's the stories of the underdog, the triumph, the adversities, it puts you in a situation where it counts right now, so anything can happen on the day."

Weightlifter Kiana Elliott will compete in the 63kg competition at Glasgow. (ABC News: Sophie Holder)

Elliott said she would compete in the 63kg class against some "really great" athletes and people she respected at Glasgow.

" I just hope that I can put my best foot forward and compete as best as I can. "

Progressing past setbacks

Elliott's physical preparation coach at the South Australian Sports Institute (SASI), Michael Nash, said a lot of work had been put into Elliott's training program.

"That works with, not only what she's previously had with her injuries [but] then building that into the Comm Games as well," he said.

"[We] feel good about [how] she's progressing. She's had a few setbacks with injuries as well, so my main priority with her is to look at what she's been doing and adjusting her sessions to make sure she's getting the most out of [them] so she can perform as well as she can."

He said Elliott was one of the most "technically good" weightlifters he had seen in Australia.

Michael Nash says Kiana Elliott is one of the most "technically good" weightlifters he has seen in Australia. (ABC News: Sophie Holder)

'Geez, what's happening here?'

Elliott said more women and girls had taken up weightlifting since she first started in the sport 13 years ago.

"That's super exciting," she said.

"Maybe I've played a little bit of a part of making that visible, locally I know some other athletes that made [it] visible for me.

"There's nothing better than pursuing your own strength and pursuing your own capability.

"It's in a gym environment, gym environments are very masculine, very ego-based and there's something … amusing, fun, cool … to be in the gym as a female, and the guys are like 'geez, what's happening here?'"

Elliott described weightlifting as fun and simple.

"It's a numbers game so it's really, really easy to measure your progress and its addicting for that," she said.

Kiana Elliott fits her weightlifting training around her work commitments. (ABC News)

Elliott said she fitted training around her job at SA Pathology, where she worked part-time.

"I don't know about balance, it's a bit off-kilter," she said.

"I'm really lucky to have built a really good relationship with my employer. The people that work close to me, they understand what I'm trying to do."

She said the general public tended to believe athletes who represent their country had everything handed to them.

"And you're set up and you're ready to go, and it's really not the case," Elliott said.

"I feel really lucky, proud and happy to have a good bunch of people around me and that include the guys here at SASI.

"I train here at South Australia Sports Institute, just outside of the CBD in Adelaide.

"I live down by the airport, I work in the CBD, if things weren't so close together, I couldn't make it work."

World.title: Could cropping transform Queensland's cattle country?
World.content:
As floodwaters moved across North West Queensland earlier this year, Lucas Findley was already preparing to plant crops.

His outback property, north of Julia Creek, sits in country better known for cattle than cotton.

In January, about 850 millimetres of rain fell there in a single week as widespread flooding devastated cattle properties across the region.

Yet within seven days of the last rain falling, machinery was back in paddocks, protected by levee banks, while floodwaters continued to move across the landscape.

Tony Perrett (right) visited Etta Plains Station earlier this year to hear about the region's push to diversify agriculture. (Supplied: Office of Minister Tony Perrett)

Etta Plains Station emerged with soaked soil, full water storages and water available for irrigation through the dry season.

Before the end of the month, Mr Findley had finished planting almost 5,000 hectares of cotton.

Mr Findley, who heads Gulf Cotton, said the experience backed an argument he has been making for years.

Producers needed different options for their land, and not just because it was good for the bank balance.

Lucas Findley says cropping in North West Queensland is ready to expand. (Supplied: Minister Ann Leahy's Office)

"It's my belief it is the only way to flood mitigate this region: to diversify your cattle business into cropping," he said.

Now, a $5.3 million investment could transform an emerging cropping sector into a much larger industry for the north west.

Ambitious targets for cattle country

Tony Perrett's visit to the North West earlier this year helped prompt the new research investment. (Supplied: Minister Tony Perrett's Office)

The Queensland government and cotton and grains industries said this week they would jointly fund research through the Unlocking Farming Systems for North Queensland project.

It aims to kickstart production of 100,000 bales of cotton and grow grain and pulse production to $100 million annually by 2035.

The project will initially focus on the Flinders catchment around Hughenden, Richmond and Julia Creek, before expanding into the Gilbert catchment further north.

Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett said there would be more investment if cropping was proven to be viable over the longer term.

Putting the economics to the test

Richmond Shire Council expects its grain sorghum crop at Maxwelton to bring in about $500,000 this year. (ABC: Cam Lang)

About 200 kilometres east of Etta Plains, Richmond Shire Council has been testing whether broadacre cropping would work commercially in cattle country.

A Maxwelton chickpea crop harvested by the council in 2025 returned about $300,000 after costs, a return 10 times higher than running cattle over the same area.

Richmond Shire Mayor John Wharton said buyers had already been found for this year's crop, grain sorghum, and it would likely bring in about $500,000.

John Wharton with the council's grain sorghum crop at Maxwelton. (ABC Landline: Cam Lang)

"We're very pleased with the results," he said.

He believed the government's $100 million grain and pulse target was achievable.

"That could happen easily," he said.

" The land is there. The water's there. "

Cr Wharton said developing crop varieties suited to the area could mean more certainty for producers facing unpredictable wet seasons.

From crops to an industry

Mr Findley said the next step would be the ability to process crops locally, particularly cotton.

The scale of that investment can be significant.

A cotton gin that opened in Katherine in 2023 cost $70 million and can process up to 200,000 bales a year.

"A cotton gin is the main enabler for this region," he said.

" It's a chicken before the egg thing … but we need to somehow fund it, get it up and running and then move forward. "

Mr Perrett stopped short of committing government funding to a gin, but said local processing would bring broader economic benefits.

Water key to growth

Lucas Findley (left) with Minister Ann Leahy and Assistant Minister Sean Dillon at Etta Plains Station, north of Julia Creek. (Supplied: Minister Ann Leahy's Office )

While dryland cropping, which relies on rainfall and moisture in the soil rather than irrigation, is proving successful around Richmond, access to secure water remains a challenge for expanding irrigated agriculture.

Richmond Shire Council has since shifted its focus to dryland cropping, although Cr Wharton said irrigated farming remained important for the wider industry.

The state government is reviewing the Gulf Water Plan and undertaking the Gulf Regional Water Assessment, examining future water demand and supply options.

Draft findings are out for consultation.

Where cropping meets cattle country

Inspecting the Maxwelton crop and looking to the future of farming in the North West. (ABC Landline: Cam Lang)

For Mr Findley, expanding cropping was not about replacing the North West's generational cattle sector, but building a new sector alongside it.

Around Richmond, forage sorghum is already being grown to feed and finish cattle, while grain from the council's latest crop is destined for feedlots.

The change is visible on the Flinders Highway too.

Cr Wharton said 20 years ago grain trucks were rarely seen travelling the route.

"Now you see them every day," he said.

He said advances in farm machinery had also made large-scale cropping increasingly possible, allowing producers to plant large areas during short windows between monsoonal rain.

"The soils haven't changed, the weather hasn't changed, but the gear has."

World.title: Hobart council snack-saga motion to be heard behind closed doors
World.content:
Calls for an independent investigation into Hobart's deputy lord mayor will be debated behind closed doors, as a stoush over town hall snacks continues.

It comes after an email sent by one of the councillors spearheading the campaign against Deputy Lord Mayor Zelinda Sherlock was likened to blackmail and referred to Tasmania's Police Commissioner.

Cr Sherlock has been lambasted by a group of her fellow councillors this year, after it was revealed she previously brought home food and drinks from a council lounge.

Tasmania's Integrity Commission chose not to investigate the matter, finding it did not constitute misconduct, but furious councillors have refused to let the matter die.

A motion seeking an independent investigation into the dispute was tabled by councillors Louise Elliott, Will Coats, John Kelly and Marti Zucco ahead of next Monday's ordinary meeting.

Set to be debated during the closed section of the meeting, the motion calls for the Director of Local Government to investigate the incidents and the council's handling of them.

Email referred to police commissioner

The tabling of the motion comes after Cr Elliott sent an email to Cr Sherlock, in which she said footage of the incident was "considerably more concerning than I had anticipated".

In the email, Cr Elliott offered to withdraw her motion if Cr Sherlock publicly announced her resignation as an elected member by 4pm on Tuesday, 21 July.

Councillor Louise Elliot during a Hobart City Council meeting. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"If you do so, the proposed motions would be withdrawn from the council agenda, and the matter could then move forward without further public escalation," Cr Elliott wrote.

Fabiano Cangelosi, a lawyer representing Cr Sherlock, has alleged the email is akin to blackmail and referred it to Tasmania's Police Commissioner Donna Adams.

"I submit that the communication, considered objectively and in light of the relevant authorities, warrants formal investigation," Mr Cangelosi wrote.
