"In our submission, the communication plainly contains threats constituting an attack [on] our client's will to remain as an elected member of council."

Cr Elliot said the suggestion her email constituted blackmail was "laughable" and "absolutely absurd".

"She's clearly looking to deflect attention away from her own conduct because this is only a few days after myself and four others have seen the CCTV footage," she said.

"I was giving her a heads-up that this issue can't just slide and that I personally would encourage her to resign so the whole issue can be put behind everyone."

Hobart Deputy Mayor Zelinda Sherlock with a person whose identity has been obscured, exiting council chambers in January. (Supplied)

The dispute stems from revelations earlier this year that Cr Sherlock had taken food and drinks from the elected members' lounge in the Hobart Town Hall in early 2024.

Cr Sherlock acknowledged taking the items over several years and said she believed it was a workplace entitlement, describing it as a misunderstanding of council policy.

Hobart deputy lord mayor under fire over taking office snacks Despite her apology and the integrity commission dismissing the case, Hobart's deputy mayor is still facing backlash after she took snacks from council premises for her home office.

CCTV footage obtained by Cr Elliott under Right to Information provisions showed Cr Sherlock and a companion leaving the lounge on two occasions.

In the footage, the pair can be seen leaving the town hall with a fully-stocked shopping bag after visiting the elected member's lounge.

The released documents also showed correspondence between council staff trying to get to the bottom of the dwindling stock.

Cr Sherlock referred herself to Tasmania's Integrity Commission over the matter this March, which chose not to investigate the case on the grounds it did not constitute misconduct.

Saga described as 'political assassination'

Cr Sherlock described the saga as a "political assassination attempt" and said she "will not cower".

She wrote to her fellow elected members on Wednesday night, following the release of the agenda for the upcoming council meeting.

In her email, she said the matter had already been addressed by multiple parties, including the council's chief executive, and described it as a "misunderstanding I have unreservedly apologised for".

She provided them with a copy of Cr Elliot's email and her lawyer's submission to the police commissioner regarding the alleged blackmail.

"I ask only that elected members take those matters into account in deciding whether it is appropriate for council's processes to be invoked in the present circumstances," Cr Sherlock wrote.

Cr Sherlock, a member of the Tasmanian Greens, is due to become acting Hobart's Lord Mayor following the resignation of Anna Reynolds in August, before local government elections are held in October.

Seinfeld star Jason Alexander has apologised to model and media personality Courtney Stodden for a lewd comedy sketch the pair performed in 2012, when Stodden was just 17. The apology comes after Stodden publicly called out the sketch, which was performed for the US comedy website Funny Or Die, in a long Instagram post earlier this week. Jason Alexander has apologised to Courtney Stodden over a 2012 sketch. “ Jason Alexander repeatedly rubbed his phone across my breasts while saying there was ‘no signal’ in my head but ‘plenty of signal’ in my chest,” Stodden, now 31, alleged in the post, which included a photograph from the sketch in which Stodden is dressed in a red bikini top and Alexander appears to be touching her chest with a mobile phone. “Later in the sketch, he joked that when I turned 18 he’d like to take me behind the couch and ‘have his way’ with me,” she alleged.



“I was a minor. I didn’t have the legal power to decide whether I wanted to participate. The contracts were signed by adults. “Looking back now, I don’t see comedy. I see a 17-year-old girl whose body became part of an adult joke,” she said. She alleged that Alexander had written the sketch, which was titled The Donny Clay Show with Courtney Stodden and Alexander’s IMDB page does include a credit for it. On Thursday morning (AEST) Alexander – who came to fame as George Costanza, the best friend of Jerry Seinfeld’s titular character in the 1990s sitcom Seinfeld – gave a statement to Hollywood gossip site TMZ apologising for the incident. The cast of Seinfeld: Michael Richards as Kramer, Jerry Seinfeld as Jerry, Julia Louis-Dreyfus as Elaine and Jason Alexander as George. AFP



“Looking back at the comedy sketch in which Ms Stodden and I participated in 2012, I completely agree that it was inappropriate and I truly regret it,” he told the outlet. “But more importantly, I am deeply sorry for any harm or distress it has caused Ms Stodden. I offer her my sincerest apologies.” Following media coverage of the apology, Stodden told The Hollywood Reporter she had not heard from the 66-year-old star personally. “I appreciate Jason Alexander’s public apology. People keep asking if he’s apologised privately, and he hasn’t. A private apology would be meaningful, but meaningful action would be even more powerful,” she said. “If he truly regrets what happened, I’d invite him to support Unchained At Last and the fight to end child marriage through AB 1267,” she continued. “That’s how we turn accountability into lasting change.”



Courtney Stodden and Doug Hutchinson in 2013. WireImage Stodden is involved with the charity Unchained At Last, which seeks to end forced marriage and child marriage; AB 1267 is a proposed law in California that would set a strict minimum age of 18 for marriage or entry into a domestic partnership. Stodden was a child model who first came to widespread fame when she married The Green Mile actor Doug Hutchinson when she was 16 and he was 51. In an Instagram post on Tuesday (US time) Stodden made reference to the proposed law and her own experience. “I don’t want to spend the rest of my life proving why what happened to me was wrong. I want to spend it making sure the next child never has to explain why they deserved protection in the first place,” she said. Be the first to know when major news happens.

Macquarie Group chief executive Shemara Wikramanayake is retiring as boss of the investment giant after eight years in the job, to be replaced by the head of its banking arm, Greg Ward.

The investment bank on Thursday said Wikramanayake, who is 64 and has been chief executive since late 2018, will retire from November this year.

Shemara Wikramanayake has been in charge of Macquarie since 2018. Leigh Vogel

Chair Glenn Stevens said: “The Board extends its heartfelt thanks to Shemara, who leaves Macquarie in a strong position, with sustained growth across each of our diverse businesses and a highly capable senior team.”

World.title: Higher planning hurdles needed for coal mines and data centres: watchdog
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeClimate policy Higher planning hurdles needed for coal mines and data centres: watchdog Caitlin Fitzsimmons July 23, 2026 — 8:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW has fallen further behind its legislated emissions targets and will not catch up unless approvals of coal mines and data centres are curbed while the renewables rollout is accelerated, the independent watchdog has warned. Every major decision, especially in the planning system, should take account of the state’s legal commitment to reduce greenhouse emissions by 50 per cent of 2005 levels by 2030, and 70 per cent by 2035, the NSW Net Zero Commission said in its annual report released on Thursday. The NSW Independent Planning Commission is considering a proposal to extend the life of the giant HVO coal mine in the Hunter Valley. Dominic Lorrimer Current policies will see only a 44 per cent reduction by 2030 and 56 per cent by 2035, according to the Net Zero Emissions Dashboard updated on Wednesday. The gap has widened from the 46 per cent by 2030 and 62 per cent by 2035 expected a year ago, which was in turn worse than when the NSW government first revealed it was on track to miss the targets in 2024. The Net Zero Commission, an independent statutory body set up by the Minns government in 2023, warned there was no chance of meeting the targets without accelerated action, despite progress on renewable electricity, household energy efficiency measures and cleaner transport.



Climate Change Minister Penny Sharpe said the government had taken serious action to cut climate pollution, reducing emissions by 25 per cent since 2005 baseline levels, but there was more work to be done. The government remained committed to the legislated targets and would carefully consider the commission’s advice, she said. “While NSW is building the jobs and industries of the clean energy future, the Coalition is turning its back on Net Zero and renewable energy, risking critical investment and emissions reduction,” Sharpe said. The government scrapped the Coalition-era Net Zero Plan last year. A new plan with initiatives to get the state back on track for its emissions targets is expected by the end of this year. The commission’s annual report called out planning decisions in particular to “take account of the legislated targets, support renewable energy and low‐emissions industry, and carefully assess the impacts of proposed coal mine extensions, expansions and new data centres”. A concept image of a giant data centre, logistics and commercial hub planned on the former Kogarah Golf Club site. Sydney Morning Herald



The NSW Independent Planning Commission is currently considering whether to approve the extension of Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) North and South in the Hunter Valley, which the Environment Protection Authority has described as “the largest coal mining proposal in NSW history”. Activist group Lock the Gate says there are a total of 19 coal mining extensions or expansions in the pipeline, counting HVO as one project, which are collectively seeking approval to mine an additional 994 million tonnes of coal. Eleven coal projects have already been approved since the last election. Planning Minister Paul Scully said the government had added climate resilience to the objectives of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act, and ruled out new greenfield coal mines in NSW. Net Zero Commission chair Nick Rowley said the government should increase the use of technologies and policies proven to drive down emissions, and ensure planning assessments supported rather than hindered progress to the state’s targets. Livestock are a major source of Australia’s methane emissions. Alex Ellinghausen



“NSW has made important progress, and there is a clear path to build on,” Rowley said in a statement. The commission called for a greater focus on reducing methane emissions, since the potent greenhouse gas currently makes up 30 per cent of the state’s emissions. Implementing existing avoidance and abatement options to reduce emissions from livestock, landfills and coal mines should be a priority, the report said. Related Article Updated

Biodiversity Land clearing rampant as ‘recalcitrant’ NSW lags on reforms The electricity sector must deliver a large chunk of the emissions reductions through the closure of coal power stations, the report said. This was “currently not on track”, with Eraring power station’s closure having been delayed twice already, from 2025 to 2027 and then 2029. “It is vital its closure is not postponed further,” the report said. Despite considerable policy effort, the rollout of renewable generation, storage and transmission was behind schedule. This was of particular concern given forecast increased electricity demand from data centres, the report said.



Scully said the government would use planning controls to ensure data centres deliver the water and power infrastructure they need to operate. “Data centres are an important part of modern life, the digital infrastructure, modern economies and present a unique opportunity to drive investment in new renewable energy and recycled water projects,” Scully said. The Net Zero Commission also urged the NSW government to move from planning to delivery on adapting to a warmer, more variable and harsher climate. World.title: Crashes around the city as fog veils Brisbane, flights diverted
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWeather Crashes around the city as fog veils Brisbane, flights diverted Julius Dennis July 23, 2026 — 7:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Multiple crashes backed up traffic around Brisbane after the city was shrouded in fog on Thursday morning, as flights circled the airport awaiting instructions and some incoming arrivals were diverted from the city. A multi-vehicle crash on the Pacific Motorway at Klumpp Road in Mount Gravatt caused heavy traffic for city-bound commuters. The fog made for gloomy scenes in the city on Thursday morning. Julius Dennis One car rolled, and two elderly patients were taken to the Princess Alexandra Hospital. In the city’s north, a crash near the Wyampa Road overpass created significant delays in North Lakes.



Meanwhile, a small truck rollover on the Warrego Highway, west of the city, clogged the commute for drivers heading in from Ipswich, despite the fact the truck was headed west. The fog blankets the city along the Brisbane River. Brisbane Times/Felicity Caldwell Other small crashes around the city were also impacting traffic. Flights were diverted from the city, but an airport spokesperson said no departures had been affected. Qantas flights from Los Angeles and Singapore were diverted to the Gold Coast, as were a Virgin flight from Darwin and a Jetstar flight from Perth.



Another Jetstar flight from Manila was sent to Sydney, with flights circling the airport awaiting instructions. Fog descends on the Go Between Bridge. Brisbane Times/Felicity Caldwell The Bureau of Meteorology issued a warning about the dangerous driving conditions, with the fog stretching to the Sunshine and Gold coasts north and south of Brisbane, and as far west of the Sunshine Coast as Kingaroy. Meteorologist Jonathan How said visibility was incredibly low through the early morning, but the fog was expected to lift. Looking east in Mount Gravatt East, the neighbourhood is enveloped in fog. Brisbane Times/Marissa Calligeros



“Now the sun’s come up we are seeing some breaks in the fog,” he said. Temperatures were expected to reach 25 degrees in the city on Thursday afternoon. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Albanese to address Labor conference; Trump says US will ‘destroy’ Iranian civilian targets
World.content:
The Shadow Minister for Home Affairs and Immigration, Jonathan Duniam, was on ABC’s RN Breakfast earlier and was asked about Pauline Hanson’s comments on domestic violence.

He said her comments, where she referred to domestic violence as a “two-way street”, were a “garbled response.”

“I think it was a garbled response. I did note from her answer that she did describe domestic violence as a scourge.”

“I think, community and political leaders need to be very careful about how they speak about these issues, and if we’re serious about resolving matters of domestic violence, elder abuse, child sexual abuse, and exploitation. Then let’s not just have throwaway lines in interviews.”

Asked if he believed the Liberal party needs to “rebuild” in light of their polling numbers this year, Duniam said it was a “waste of time” discussing deals with other partys.

“My one pitch to Australians is work with us. My one pitch to my colleagues is let’s do our job, which is to get back to basics on policy, explain to Australians why our policies are better, and we’ll help them out in the in the pursuit of resolving the issues they face, and then convince people to vote for us.”

“Let’s not talk about other parties. Let’s not talk about deals, preference deals, or carve-ups of seats, or mergers, or coalitions. That is a waste of time.”

Every major decision, especially in the planning system, should take account of the state’s legal commitment to reduce greenhouse emissions by 50 per cent of 2005 levels by 2030, and 70 per cent by 2035, the NSW Net Zero Commission said in its annual report released on Thursday. The NSW Independent Planning Commission is considering a proposal to extend the life of the giant HVO coal mine in the Hunter Valley. Dominic Lorrimer Current policies will see only a 44 per cent reduction by 2030 and 56 per cent by 2035, according to the Net Zero Emissions Dashboard updated on Wednesday. The gap has widened from the 46 per cent by 2030 and 62 per cent by 2035 expected a year ago, which was in turn worse than when the NSW government first revealed it was on track to miss the targets in 2024. The Net Zero Commission, an independent statutory body set up by the Minns government in 2023, warned there was no chance of meeting the targets without accelerated action, despite progress on renewable electricity, household energy efficiency measures and cleaner transport.



Climate Change Minister Penny Sharpe said the government had taken serious action to cut climate pollution, reducing emissions by 25 per cent since 2005 baseline levels, but there was more work to be done. The government remained committed to the legislated targets and would carefully consider the commission’s advice, she said. “While NSW is building the jobs and industries of the clean energy future, the Coalition is turning its back on Net Zero and renewable energy, risking critical investment and emissions reduction,” Sharpe said. The government scrapped the Coalition-era Net Zero Plan last year. A new plan with initiatives to get the state back on track for its emissions targets is expected by the end of this year. The commission’s annual report called out planning decisions in particular to “take account of the legislated targets, support renewable energy and low‐emissions industry, and carefully assess the impacts of proposed coal mine extensions, expansions and new data centres”. A concept image of a giant data centre, logistics and commercial hub planned on the former Kogarah Golf Club site. Sydney Morning Herald



The NSW Independent Planning Commission is currently considering whether to approve the extension of Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) North and South in the Hunter Valley, which the Environment Protection Authority has described as “the largest coal mining proposal in NSW history”. Activist group Lock the Gate says there are a total of 19 coal mining extensions or expansions in the pipeline, counting HVO as one project, which are collectively seeking approval to mine an additional 994 million tonnes of coal. Eleven coal projects have already been approved since the last election. Planning Minister Paul Scully said the government had added climate resilience to the objectives of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act, and ruled out new greenfield coal mines in NSW. Net Zero Commission chair Nick Rowley said the government should increase the use of technologies and policies proven to drive down emissions, and ensure planning assessments supported rather than hindered progress to the state’s targets. Livestock are a major source of Australia’s methane emissions. Alex Ellinghausen



“NSW has made important progress, and there is a clear path to build on,” Rowley said in a statement. The commission called for a greater focus on reducing methane emissions, since the potent greenhouse gas currently makes up 30 per cent of the state’s emissions. Implementing existing avoidance and abatement options to reduce emissions from livestock, landfills and coal mines should be a priority, the report said. Related Article Updated

Biodiversity Land clearing rampant as ‘recalcitrant’ NSW lags on reforms The electricity sector must deliver a large chunk of the emissions reductions through the closure of coal power stations, the report said. This was “currently not on track”, with Eraring power station’s closure having been delayed twice already, from 2025 to 2027 and then 2029. “It is vital its closure is not postponed further,” the report said. Despite considerable policy effort, the rollout of renewable generation, storage and transmission was behind schedule. This was of particular concern given forecast increased electricity demand from data centres, the report said.



Scully said the government would use planning controls to ensure data centres deliver the water and power infrastructure they need to operate. “Data centres are an important part of modern life, the digital infrastructure, modern economies and present a unique opportunity to drive investment in new renewable energy and recycled water projects,” Scully said. The Net Zero Commission also urged the NSW government to move from planning to delivery on adapting to a warmer, more variable and harsher climate. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Crashes around the city as fog veils Brisbane, flights diverted
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWeather Crashes around the city as fog veils Brisbane, flights diverted Julius Dennis July 23, 2026 — 7:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Multiple crashes backed up traffic around Brisbane after the city was shrouded in fog on Thursday morning, as flights circled the airport awaiting instructions and some incoming arrivals were diverted from the city. A multi-vehicle crash on the Pacific Motorway at Klumpp Road in Mount Gravatt caused heavy traffic for city-bound commuters. The fog made for gloomy scenes in the city on Thursday morning. Julius Dennis One car rolled, and two elderly patients were taken to the Princess Alexandra Hospital. In the city’s north, a crash near the Wyampa Road overpass created significant delays in North Lakes.



Meanwhile, a small truck rollover on the Warrego Highway, west of the city, clogged the commute for drivers heading in from Ipswich, despite the fact the truck was headed west. The fog blankets the city along the Brisbane River. Brisbane Times/Felicity Caldwell Other small crashes around the city were also impacting traffic. Flights were diverted from the city, but an airport spokesperson said no departures had been affected. Qantas flights from Los Angeles and Singapore were diverted to the Gold Coast, as were a Virgin flight from Darwin and a Jetstar flight from Perth.



Another Jetstar flight from Manila was sent to Sydney, with flights circling the airport awaiting instructions. Fog descends on the Go Between Bridge. Brisbane Times/Felicity Caldwell The Bureau of Meteorology issued a warning about the dangerous driving conditions, with the fog stretching to the Sunshine and Gold coasts north and south of Brisbane, and as far west of the Sunshine Coast as Kingaroy. Meteorologist Jonathan How said visibility was incredibly low through the early morning, but the fog was expected to lift. Looking east in Mount Gravatt East, the neighbourhood is enveloped in fog. Brisbane Times/Marissa Calligeros



“Now the sun’s come up we are seeing some breaks in the fog,” he said. Temperatures were expected to reach 25 degrees in the city on Thursday afternoon. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

“I think it was a garbled response. I did note from her answer that she did describe domestic violence as a scourge.”

My one pitch to my colleagues is let’s do our job, which is to get back to basics on policy, explain to Australians why our policies are better, and we’ll help them out in the in the pursuit of resolving the issues they face, and then convince people to vote for us.”

World.title: Mercury spends $53m on stake in Datagrid NZ
World.content:
Mercury to take a 12.7 percent stake in Datagrid NZ

Datagrid is planning to build a large data centre in North Makarewa, Southland

Datagrid NZ remains majority owned by its Singapore-based parent

One of the country's biggest electricity companies has thrown its weight behind a firm planning to build a large data centre in Southland.

Mercury has invested US$30 million (NZ$53m) for a 12.7 percent minority equity stake in Datagrid NZ.

Announcing the investment, Mercury said Datagrid NZ was developing "what is expected to be New Zealand's most advanced large-scale data centre project".

The 360 megawatt project has been slated for North Makarewa, Southland, and won resource consent from the region's councils earlier this year.

It has support from the region's mayors, but has drawn concerns about the impact from water use.

The 78,000 square metre data centre is expected to open in 2028, fuelled by the explosion in global demand for artificial intelligence.

Datagrid NZ remains majority owned by its Singapore-based parent company.

Mercury's investment came after it signed a 140 megawatt power purchase option agreement with Datagrid in March.

Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton, who was also appointed as a director for Datagrid NZ, said it was a disciplined investment by the company.

"Investing in Datagrid NZ is aligned with our core strategy, bolsters our position alongside an important emerging source of long-term electricity demand, and is structured to preserve balance sheet strength and flexibility for our wider capital programme," Hamilton said.

Mercury, which has a large pipeline of new renewable energy projects, including a wind farm in Southland, said the investment would support long-term renewable electricity demand growth.

"We have a deep renewable development pipeline, and long-duration demand from large electricity users like Datagrid NZ provides us with the revenue certainty that underpins our investments in new renewable generation developments," Hamilton said.

Datagrid NZ founder and chair Rémi Galasso said speed of delivery was "crucial".

"Time to market is driving our strategy, and closing this round of investment funding allows us to move decisively," Galasso said.

World.title: Aotearoa's criminalisation of stalking: why the workplace is the next focus
World.content:
For many victims of harassment and stalking, the impacts do not stop at the front door.

The behaviour can follow them into the workplace, where perpetrators may use colleagues, systems or physical spaces as another way to intimidate and monitor them.

That was the reality for Cassie Roma, whose own experience with harassment and stalking stretched across almost a decade.

"It lasted years and started in the context of me doing some public speaking for work," she said.

"And turned into almost a decade of online and in real life [harassment], showing up at the workplace, my home, my child's school - just really horrific stalking by somebody not known to me," Roma said.

During that time, New Zealand had introduced the Harmful Digital Communications Act, and Roma said the person eventually left the country.

But Roma said the harm signalled a gap in support for people experiencing harassment and stalking, particularly when it followed them into their work lives.

"What I realised at the time was that there wasn't a lot of help for women and people, especially at work, going through these kinds of things," she said.

Cassie Roma. Supplied

One of the most difficult parts was the tricky feeling that she was placing a hefty responsibility on those around her.

"One thing I didn't realise at the time, but what I was feeling, was a lot of guilt for putting my colleagues and other people in situations where I felt like they needed to protect me," she said.

As she grappled with two individual harassment and stalking experiences that stretched across two different workplaces, she saw firsthand the difference a workplace response could make.

"I was very lucky in the first instance because management and leadership really helped keep me safe emotionally, physically, and in other ways.

"So I know what it looks like when this is done well, when you share something really vulnerable and scary in your personal life, and somebody in a position of power or a colleague actually sees you and offers you the support and I guess emotional safety that you need."

However, after Roma became more publicly recognised through her work as a leadership speaker and former senior executive, she experienced further instances of stalking.

With that came varied responses from organisations she worked with.

Those contrasting experiences, she said, reinforced a need for workplaces to understand how to recognise and respond to stalking.

"Having two really differentiated experiences really hit home to me the importance of, you know, being able to recognise, respond, and support people through different forms of stalking," Roma said.

She said stalking is often misunderstood, because it is not always one glaringly obvious or dramatic incident.

"It's this accumulation of behaviours that create that fear and control. It's not one frightening moment. It's hundreds of moments that kind of steal someone's sense of security," she said.

Stalking can include unwanted contact, monitoring movements, tracking social media activity, spreading rumours or using technology to intimidate and cause fear.

While anyone can experience stalking, women are disproportionately affected.

Victim-survivors may be targeted by former partners, acquaintances, colleagues or strangers, and technology is becoming an increasingly sly tool for surveillance and control.

What will the workplace guide do - and why is it important?

Now, just months after stalking became a standalone criminal offence in New Zealand, the government has launched a new workplace guide aimed at helping employers recognise stalking and respond safely.

It also aims to help support staff experiencing it.

The Workplace Guide to Addressing the Impact of Stalking has been developed by the Ministry for Women, alongside Shine and Human Resources New Zealand.

"I think this is such a really cool, amazing thing, this practical workplace response, because it enables businesses and empowers managers to be human in the face of something really vulnerable and scary, a very human experience," Roma said.

National Party MP Nicola Grigg sits in the House during Question Time. VNP/Phil Smith

Minister for Women Nicola Grigg said the guide builds on the recent law change, which made stalking a standalone criminal offence carrying a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment.

"We've been really specific in our thinking around first, you know, make it a crime, and because we know that this is occurring… quite often out in the public and with women, most particularly, being the victims of it," Grigg said.

"So now that we have enacted the law, I think it is the time to educate employers and, indeed, employees, about what stalking is, what it looks like, and how best to respond to it."

The guide provides practical advice for employers on how to recognise stalking behaviours, respond safely to disclosures, and mainly reduce risks in the workplace.

This will see measures such as developing workplace safety plans with employees, limiting perpetrators' access to workplaces, offering escorted walks to vehicles, protecting employees' personal information, having supportive conversations, and connecting victim-survivors with legal and specialist support.

Grigg said workplaces are an important part of the response, because they can provide support networks.

At the same time, they are often a place where harassment and stalking manifests.

"For most of us, the workplace is where we spend the majority of our day, and we develop close relationships, and we develop friends, but indeed, trusted relationships with our colleagues," Grigg explained.

"We often think of stalking outside of the home, and I suppose we probably think stalking as being followed home on the footpath at night. But actually, it can extend to, you know, obsessive texting or emailing or reading private documents or invading people's privacy.

"So again, this toolkit is about helping employees and employers recognise what it is, and most importantly, be able to respond to it."

Chief victims advisor to the Government, Ruth Money, said workplaces are often involved in stalking situations, whether the perpetrator is a colleague or someone using the workplace as a point of access.

"I have certainly worked with many victims of stalking who have been stalked at work by colleagues and/or at work by people who weren't work colleagues, with offenders showing up at work - for example, parking outside in car parks, waiting for you to finish at work, following you, delivering gifts - unwanted gifts," Money said.

"So a workplace can be a place of access to many offenders who wish to stalk people."

Money said education will be critical to ensuring the new law translates into purposeful support for victim-survivors.

"You can't support people unless you understand what stalking and harassment is, what it looks like, how it can affect people while they're at work, and how you can support people to be safe in your workplace," Money said.

"Many victims of stalking don't have a safe or trusted person to be able to disclose to, and if you don't know that it's a criminal offence, and you don't know how to react, then we will end up with our victims not being supported and not disclosing a crime."

Cassie Roma said the most impactful response is simple - listen and believe people when they come forward.

"I think the most impactful point, in the way that people can help the most, is to remember that we're all human," she said.

World.title: Nauru's government announces plans for embassy in Israel
World.content:
Nauru's government has announced plans to set up an embassy in Israel.

The government said Cabinet had endorsed the deployment of a scoping mission to Israel, to assess the diplomatic, operational, and logistical requirements to establish the embassy.

"A diplomatic presence in Israel will serve as an essential platform for advancing [Nauru's] foreign policy priorities, promoting sustainable development, and deepening bilateral engagement with one of the region's key partners," the government said in a statement on Wednesday.

"The creation of an embassy in Israel represents a significant milestone in [Nauru's] diplomatic outreach and underscores the nation's dedication to expanding its global partnerships in support of national development and strategic cooperation."

The statement did not specify which city the embassy would be established in, but Israel's foreign minister Gideon Saar said it would be in Jerusalem.

In a translated social media post shared by Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Saar said the Nauruan embassy is expected to be the tenth embassy in Jerusalem, and the fifth since he took office, coming after he also reached an agreement with Colombia's incoming foreign minister on a similar move.

Fiji and Papua New Guinea are among several countries which have diplomatic missions in Jerusalem rather than Tel Aviv, which is controversial due to the sensitive nature of a territorial dispute between Israelis and Palestinians, who both claim Jerusalem as their capital.



Fiji opened its embassy in Jerusalem in September 2025.

Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said earlier last year that establishing an embassy "is not a blanket endorsement of another country's policies; it is a bridge that allows Fiji to work directly with partners".

Fiji also reaffirmed its support for a peaceful two-state solution "where both Israelis and Palestinians can live in dignity and security".

In March this year, Fiji's human rights watchdog warned that the country's pro-Israel foreign policy and diplomatic engagement works against its international obligations and could be enabling "genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity" in Gaza.

Israel has also opened its permanent diplomatic base in Suva.

In January, Saar said that Samoa will open an embassy in Jerusalem this year.

Samoan Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa (La'auli) Leuatea Schmidt said he instructed Samoa's foreign ministry to begin preparations for the embassy's opening by the end of the year, according to a recording of the speech posted on the Samoan government's Facebook page.

When PNG opened its Israeli embassy in Jerusalem in 2023, the Palestinian Authority called it an "aggression" and a "violation" of international law.

PNG Prime Minister James Marape said at the time the move had deep religious significance.

"Many nations choose not to open their embassies in Jerusalem, but we made the conscious choice," he said.

"This has been the universal capital of the nation and people of Israel.

"For us to call ourselves Christian, paying respect to God will not be possible without recognising that Jerusalem is the universal capital of the people and nation of Israel."

The United States, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo and Paraguay also have embassies in Jerusalem.

World.title: What's behind the surge in financial complaints?
World.content:
Financial complaints surge Nine To Noon Download MP3 8m

It's been a record-breaking year for financial complaints, with a near 50 percent increase in the number lodged with the Financial Ombudsman.

These mainly included complaints about KiwiSaver providers when seeking hardship withdrawals, as well as being declined, along with electronic transaction services when people tried to recover funds through account number mistakes or scams.

Financial Ombudsman Susan Taylor told Nine to Noon there were 1596 complaints in the 2025/26 financial year, with 532 disputes investigated by the office - a 49 percent increase on the previous year.

Taylor said it was the sharpest increase in complaints in 15 years.

The surge was driven by ongoing economic stress, debt challenges and the use of AI to submit complaints, she said.

"For some New Zealanders, economic conditions remain very challenging."

She said using AI to submit complaints had it advantages and disadvantages.

"It makes our service more accessible to people who may have felt reluctant, but the disadvantages are in that sometimes the complaints can be very lengthy. Sometimes it gives them the wrong information."

Most of the complaints regarding KiwiSaver had to do with people feeling as though a KiwiSaver supervisor should have accepted their application for hardship withdrawal or they weren't able to get out the amount of money they wanted.

Susan Taylor, the Financial Ombudsman and CEO at Financial Services Complaints Ltd (FSCL). (File photo) FSCL

She said there were also quite a few complaints about service this year, including delays with a large amount of people wanting to withdraw KiwiSaver.

"When people apply for hardship withdrawals they are usually in a very vulnerable situation and any delays in the process only makes it harder for them," Taylor said.

"We've seen some concerns around timeliness, where we've felt the person is having to wait too long for it to get in front of a supervisor."

The other main sort of complaint Taylor had been seeing related to money transfer services for people who were sending money overseas.

"We've had a few service complaints where a person feels the process has been far too slow and it has taken too long to get overseas and caused issues. Also seen where people are the victims of scams and fraud."

In the case of scams, Taylor said often when someone found out they had been scammed the money was already long gone and they were seeking help to try and get that money back and felt their provider should've done more to help them.

World.title: Connectivity failure behind Waikato Hospital IT outage
World.content:
Waikato Hospital hit by major IT outage Morning Report Download MP3 6m

A connectivity failure at Waikato Hospital meant staff had to revert to pen and paper after a widespread IT outage.

Health NZ said late on Wednesday evening that the problem - which began at 10.44am - had been fixed, but it was continuing to monitor the situation.

Te Whatu Ora/Health NZ chief information technology officer Darren Douglas said there had been an issue with its main data centre which meant users weren't able to connect.

Thames, Te Kūiti, Tokoroa and Taumarunui hospitals were also affected, which resulted in longer wait times in the emergency department, some delayed surgeries, and forced staff to revert to paper systems.

Douglas told Morning Report the outage was down to a network connectivity issue.

"The connectivity between our network that our users use to access systems in our main data centre failed, so effectively the systems in our data centre - though they were running ok - none of the users could access them."

Both the equipment providing connectivity as well as secondary equipment in place as a "fail over" had not worked, he said.

Urgent care and emergency services were prioritised, but some non-urgent appointments were diverted.

Douglas was unable to clarify whether ambulances needed to be diverted significant distances away.

Staff had told RNZ patient history was limited to paper reports and any recent AI transcribed reports could not be accessed.

Health New Zealand group director of operations for Waikato Stephanie Doe said on Thursday that Waikato hospitals were operating as usual following the outage.

She said during the Wednesday outrage urgent care, including the Emergency Department, was prioritised with additional resource in place.

Doe also added there had been no widespread ambulance diversions from hospitals.

"One ambulance in North Waikato was sent directly to Middlemore Hospital rather than being brought to Waikato Hospital. The diversion had no impact on patient care."

A St John spokesperson also confirmed the IT outage had very little impact on the ambulance service.

The Public Service Association has been warning hospital IT outages would keep happening due to cuts to Health NZ's digital team.

Douglas did not believe that the outage was an example of resulting impacts of these cuts.

"When we went through our restructure process one of the things we were very clear about is that we were prioritising operational support for these critical systems."

He did say that they were dealing with a complicated system that had been underinvested for decades.

"We are running a really complex environment with a lot of ageing technology and a lot of district variation as well, so it's very difficult."

World.title: PM Christopher Luxon tight-lipped on 'grey-zone' advice
World.content:
The Prime Minister has said "grey-zone" operations are being deployed by states but he won't release the advice he has had about that.

Grey-zone attacks are usually state-sponsored but designed to evade culpability, such as in Europe when drones were spotted hovering ominously over oil rigs and military bases but no one knew whose they were, or when small consumer items exploded in postal depots and a Russian test-run was suspected.

Christopher Luxon said in a pre-Budget speech, "International relations are moving from an economic focus to one dominated by security concerns.

"Competition now means cyber-attacks, disinformation, supply chain coercion, and grey-zone operations are primary tools of statecraft."

RNZ asked under the Official Information Act for the advice Luxon has received on grey-zones and a summary of any initiatives or research done.

A newly received OIA response says there are several documents in scope but his office will not release any of them, or even their titles, on various grounds, including national security.

"No public interest has been identified that would be sufficient to outweigh the reasons for withholding that information," it said.

The problem analysts say is how to deter such acts without sparking a broader conflict.

In a separate statement a spokesperson for Luxon said New Zealand was seeing states deploying grey-zone operations as an instrument of statecraft.

"Grey-zone operations are typically defined as hostile actions that fall short of warfare and include things like the sabotage of sub-sea infrastructure, such as cables and pipelines, that has occurred in the Baltic Sea or coercive on-water maritime tactics that disrupt shipping, as we have seen in the Strait of Hormuz," the spokesperson said.

"These types of activities undermine the global security order."

The country was focused on preventing cyber-attacks, as well as upping defence capabilities to respond to grey-zone operations, they added.

In June the government announced the rollout of a 24/7 monitoring system for undersea telecommunications cables. A vessel getting too close to a cable will trigger an alert and warning.

World.title: Explainer: Why fog is worse in winter and why it keeps causing flight delays
World.content:
Explainer - Have you had a flight delayed by fog recently? You're not alone. What is fog, and will there ever be a way to beat it?

As the country settles into midwinter, foggy weather is a common morning sight - and while it may be pretty in pictures, it can cause havoc for commuters and air travellers with delayed and cancelled flights.

What causes fog, and how do airports know when it's too dangerous to fly? Here's what you need to know.

A foggy start to the day by the waterfront in Auckland's CBD. EDWARD GAY / RNZ

What is fog, anyway?

"It's basically having a cloud on the ground," said MetService communications meteorologist Alywn Bakker.

"Fog is what happens, essentially, when the air gets so much moisture in it that it can't hang on to it anymore, and it starts to sort of condense out."

The most common kind of fog in New Zealand is what's known as "radiation fog."

Don't worry, despite the name, radiation fog won't turn you into the Incredible Hulk. It gets its name from changes in radiative heat during the course of a day, and typically forms overnight or in the early morning during the coldest hours of the day, then disperses once the sun comes up.

It's "where everything's really still and cold," Bakker said.

"There's not a lot of wind. It's very moist and everything starts to cool down at ground level."

Clear skies are better conditions for radiation fog, as cloudy nights tend to absorb heat emitted by the Earth's surface and bounce it back down, keeping the land from cooling quite as much.

This handy MetService graphic shows how that works:

Supplied / MetService

Fog forms when the air temperature and the dewpoint temperature get close together. The dewpoint is the point at which condensation occurs - when air becomes saturated with water vapour.

"If those two temperatures are very close together, that's when you're going to be getting fog," Bakker said.

There are several other kinds of fog - such as advection fog, which forms when warm moist air moves over a cool surface, and often leads to sea fog.

There's also freezing fog, which is seen in places like Central Otago and can cause hoarfrosts and black ice.

You can even sometimes see the rare fogbow, created from fog droplets instead of rain droplets like rainbows are - one was photographed in Australia just recently.

Multiple flights have been delayed by fog at Auckland Airport in recent weeks. Supplied

Why does fog keep causing flight delays and cancellations?

Low visibility is the obvious answer, and while technology can help navigate the haze, nature is still in the driver's seat.

"We understand fog-related delays can be disruptive for travellers, particularly when plans are time-sensitive," an Auckland Airport spokesperson told RNZ.

"Safety comes first in low-visibility conditions, and we appreciate people's patience while the airport, airlines and Airways work through the impacts."

Airways New Zealand is a state-owned enterprise that manages air traffic, including air traffic towers across the country.

An Airways spokesperson said tools such as meteorological observations, forecasts and visibility measuring equipment are used to monitor fog. Some runways use Runway Visual Range equipment, which measures visibility along the runway.

"Low Visibility Procedures are typically triggered when runway visual range falls below 1200 metres, or when fog prevents air traffic control from maintaining visibility of key operational areas of the airfield," the Auckland Airport spokesperson said.

"What this means is aircraft movements are managed more cautiously, with greater spacing and more controlled movement around the airfield. This can reduce the number of flights able to arrive and depart in a short period."

Airways doesn't make the call on whether airlines delay or cancel flights, and said its role is to "provide air traffic management services and ensure aircraft can operate safely within the prevailing conditions."

"When visibility is reduced, Airways may implement low visibility procedures and manage air traffic accordingly. Airlines then make decisions about delays, cancellations or diversions based on a range of factors, including weather conditions, aircraft capabilities, crew requirements and their own operational considerations."

Fog doesn't affect all flights equally. Aircraft and airlines have varying levels of certification and capability to operate in low visibility.

"Different aircraft are approved to operate in different weather conditions depending on their onboard navigation systems and whether they are operating under visual flight rules or instrument flight rules," the Airways spokesperson said.

"Some aircraft are approved to operate in lower visibility than others, which can influence whether flights continue operating as planned or experience delays," the Auckland Airport spokesperson said.

An aircraft's ability to operate in low visibility also depends on the equipment available at the airport, the Airways spokesperson said.

Auckland Airport has New Zealand's most advanced low-visibility landing capability, a Category III Instrument Landing System.

"This is one of the most advanced landing systems available," the Airways spokesperson said.

"The system combines radio guidance, specialised runway lighting and ground infrastructure to help suitably equipped aircraft land safely in very low visibility conditions. While it doesn't eliminate the impact of fog, it can help reduce disruption by allowing some aircraft to continue operating safely when visibility is significantly reduced."

Auckland Airport also recently completed a major upgrade of its airfield lighting control system and said it "is continuing to work with Airways on opportunities to further improve efficiency during low-visibility operations."

Fog watches can also affect ferry travel if visibility becomes too hazardous for boats.

Drivers should be cautious in the fog. RNZ

What should I do if I'm driving?

For drivers, the NZ Transport Agency recommends extreme caution in foggy conditions. And watch how you use your headlights.

"If you drive with your headlights on full beam in fog, the light will just reflect back on you. Dip your lights - it'll be much easier to see," NZTA's website advises.

If your car has fog lights, use them - but only use them in fog or other reduced visibility conditions such as snow.

"You can't use your fog lights when the weather is clear, even at night. The law is very clear on this," NZTA has cautioned.

That's because front fog lights produce very intense lights that can dazzle other drivers. The Automobile Association (AA) notes that "They give off a short, wide beam of light that is designed to shine through the fog, lighting up the area directly in front of the vehicle and helping the driver see the sides of the road better."

"They are aimed as low as possible because fog itself often hangs no higher than a couple of feet above the road, and if a fog light is aimed high, it will produce glare in the fog and will blind oncoming drivers."

Rear fog lamps have a low beam of red light to help vehicles behind you see better in snow or fog.

Fog in Auckland city. RNZ

Are some parts of the country worse for fog than others?

Auckland may seem very foggy some mornings, but Hamilton has it beat.

"Hot spots" for fog include Hamilton and Dunedin, Bakker said.

"You'd be expecting between 10 to 12 fog events a month at Hamilton compared to Auckland" which would normally have about three, he said.

Rivers are actually big generators for fog.

"Anywhere that is near a river that really ups your fog risk," Bakker said.

"Rivers, they're a good moisture source, but they don't really contribute to keeping the place warm. Whereas the sea really does help contribute to keeping the place warm. It's why Auckland is pretty mild."

OK, but will we ever find a way to beat our nemesis, fog?

Many companies have investigated ways to combat fog - a few years ago, the Christchurch start-up company Pyper Vision was reportedly looking at developing a spray that could absorb moisture. The company continues to work on fog forecasting technology advances according to its website.

Humans have been looking at ways to beat fog for a long time - during World War II, Britain developed the FIDO system - Fog, Intensive, Dispersal Of - a network of pipes and petrol burners capable of clearing fog from runways to help fighter planes take to the sky.

"That would drive the fog off," Bakker said. "You know, you're heating the place up, but it also creates a bunch of updrafts, which makes it really difficult to land."

Despite all the technological advances of the modern world, fog is still a bit of a mystery.

"Fog is really quite difficult to predict," Bakker said.

"The thing about fog is, it's a really finely balanced set of circumstances. So you need the right temperature, you need the right wind speed, you need the right moisture. And if any of those is off, you won't get it."

Auckland Airport's spokesperson said safety remains the top priority when dealing with the unpredictable nature of fog.

"Fog itself can't be prevented, so the focus is on forecasting, preparation and having the right infrastructure in place when visibility drops. While weather conditions can still cause delays and cancellations, these investments help support safe flight operations during low visibility conditions."

But while having your flight delayed is no fun, on the relative scale of weather disaster possibilities fog remains fairly chill.

"Fog is irritating but low impact," Bakker said.

World.title: Philipsen claims Tour de France stage as UCI defends late-night drug tests
World.content:
Jasper Philipsen has capped a fine team performance to win stage 17 of the Tour de France, with defending champion Tadej Pogačar protecting his overall lead.

Mathieu van der Poel led his Alpecin-Premier Tech teammate Philipsen to his first stage victory of this Tour overnight by controlling the pace and containing counterattacks through the last kilometres.

Philipsen finished just ahead of Mauro Schmid and Olav Kooij.

The Belgian rider described a "a roller-coaster of emotions" after what had been a disappointing Tour for him personally.

"I prepared very, very well. I was in the shape of my life, I think, and the first stages, the first 12 days, were just horrible. I couldn't find myself, couldn't find the feeling I was hoping for," said Philipsen, who thanked his team colleagues.

"I was like an angry bird at the table. I was just disappointed in myself, angry that I couldn't take [a] stage win, that I didn't find my feeling. And the team, they had to deal with it, not only the riders, the staff. This one is for them to keep on believing."

Pogačar, who is chasing a third straight Tour title and fifth overall, maintained his lead of just over four and a half minutes over Remco Evenepoel, the winner of the previous two stages.

But it was a bad day for Pogačar's UAE Emirates XRG teammate Adam Yates, who struggled and only made it back within the time limit. The British rider slumped over his handlebars, clearly exhausted.

The race ends on Sunday in Paris.

The relatively flat 174.7km route from Chambery to Voiron was the last favourable stage for sprinters before the Tour takes to the Alps, and it led to a day of attempted breakaways, with many riders vying to put themselves in contention.

Van der Poel was among the leaders after Côte de Saint-Jean d'Arvey, the last significant climb, and they were joined by others before Yates's problems began in the peloton.

Mads Pedersen was the next to attack the leaders with 65km remaining, and the green jersey-holder invigorated the group when he joined them.

More sprinters broke away, swelling the group to 30 riders, before Pedersen, Ben Healy, Michal Kwiatkowski, Felix Engelhardt, Ed Planckaert and Jasper Stuyven struck out 57km from the finish.

Stuyven attacked on his own 26km from the line, leaving his five former co-leaders to chase or wait for the main bunch. They were caught. The only question was whether the 34-year-old Stuyven had the stamina to claim his first Tour stage win.

The Belgian rider was caught with less than 4km remaining, and Van der Poel did the rest for Philipsen.

Support for Tour night doping tests A former cyclist who took performance-enhancing drugs, now a team boss at the Tour de France, supports doping tests in the middle of the night at cycling's biggest race.

Philipsen's stage win moved him just behind Pedersen in the contest for the green jersey awarded to the rider with the most points.

With four stages remaining, Pedersen of Lidl-Trek had 452 points, followed by Philipsen on 445. Biniam Girmay of Eritrea was next with 361 points.

Cycling's governing body, the UCI, responded to criticism of unannounced anti-doping controls after Pogačar and his main rival Jonas Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday for tests by the Swiss-based International Testing Agency.

Vingegaard subsequently crashed during Sunday's stage and had to abandon the race.

The UCI said it acknowledged the night-time testing "can disrupt riders' rest and recovery" and said it remained an exceptional measure.

"While fully aware of how onerous such a measure is for riders, the UCI nevertheless underscores that these controls serve an overriding interest: the fight against doping," the body said in a statement.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
