World.title: When Gordon Bray and his Homebush schoolmates ruled their rugby world
World.content:
It's not easy for Gordon Bray to name his favourite memory from a lifetime involved with rugby union.

Regarded as one of international rugby's greatest broadcasters, Bray called almost 400 Test matches, including a host of significant moments in the Wallabies' storied history.

World Cup victories, the 1984 Grand Slam, series wins over the All Blacks, and British and Irish Lions … Bray was behind the microphone for so many of Australian rugby's milestone achievements.

His service to the game and sport broadcasting was recognised in 2005 when he was made a Member of the Order of Australia in the Queen's Birthday Honours list.

Gordon Bray called rugby during his broadcast career with the ABC, and the Seven and 10 networks. (ABC)

But aside from Bray's commentary work, there's one event from his rugby journey he considers to be among his most treasured memories.

Bray was scrum half in the 1965 Homebush Boys High first XV when they won the prestigious NSW-wide knockout competition, the Waratah Shield.

"I think that Waratah Shield victory is right up there with any rugby experience I've been involved with," Bray tells ABC Sport.

Bray isn't the only member of Homebush's 1965 first XV who proudly remembers the tense 8-3 win over Oakhill College in the Waratah Shield final.

Packing down in the second row that day was John Symond, later to become one of Australia's best-known businessmen when he founded Aussie Home Loans.

"The Waratah Shield was definitely the highlight of my whole school experience, that's for sure," Symond recalls.

"It just stands out as the pinnacle of my schooling."

The official team photo of the 1965 Homebush Boys High first XV. (Gordon Bray)

Partnering Bray in the halves was another of the first XV's stars, Greg Bell.

A first-grade player for the respective Western Suburbs rugby and cricket clubs in Sydney after leaving school, Bell enjoyed several highlights in his sporting career.

But the Waratah Shield win is among the most cherished.

"It meant a hell of a lot," says Bell, casting his mind back 61 years.

Bell scored the winning try in the final, a moment he's often recounted to his children.

"That win is a story we heard many times over the years," Bell's daughter Mel says with fondness.

Capturing the first XV's performances as the team's photographer was John Coates, who would become International Olympic Committee (IOC) vice-president and Australia's most influential sporting administrator.

Bray considers Coates as much a part of the Waratah Shield triumph as any of the players who took the field.

For Coates, being around the first XV was an experience he reflects upon with affection.

"They were my heroes," says Coates, who was Australian Olympic Committee (AOC) president from 1990-2022.

The 1965 Homebush Boys High first XV returned to the school last year. (Facebook: Homebush Boys High)

To mark the 60th anniversary of the Waratah Shield win, Coates, Bray, Symond, Bell and other members of the first XV returned to their old school in Sydney's west as guests of honour last year.

They're now in their late 70s, but the bonds of friendship have survived the test of time, and the emotion of the victory remains as strong as ever.

"I can still feel it today," Bray says with pride.

'Our own little dynasty'

Jack 'Pug' Mason was brief and to the point.

Speaking to a select group of year-nine rugby players in 1964, the Homebush Boys High first XV coach let them know they were on his radar.

"He (Mason) picked out five of us and said, 'You're going to be playing in the firsts next year,'" remembers Bray, who was a supremely talented scrum half.

"There were five boys from year 10 in the 1965 team, and the rest were doing their leaving certificate."

Mason's decision to mix rookies with experienced campaigners was the perfect recipe for winning the Waratah Shield, which was the high-water mark in Homebush's rugby history.

But the school was already a dominant force in the sport before its crowning achievement.

Ex-students Arthur Summons (a dual international) and Geoffrey Vaughan represented the Wallabies and played three Tests together in 1958, which was a rare achievement for a public school.

Geoffrey Vaughan (fourth from right in back row) and Arthur Summons (right in front row) before the Wallabies' 1958 Test against England at Twickenham. (Getty Images)

As the NSW Combined High Schools Sports Association (CHS) reorganised sport into fixed zones at the beginning of the 1960s, Homebush continued to make its presence felt in rugby.

The school had a stranglehold on the North-West Metropolitan CHS zone, winning eight straight first-grade premierships between 1961-68.

Bray's elder brother John was 1963 first XV captain, guiding his team through an undefeated run in the zone, which was arguably the CHS's strongest.

Gordon Bray remembers Homebush's zone matches with fondness. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"It was a very fierce rugby zone," Bray says.

"Our main rivals were Epping Boys High and Normanhurst Boys High.

"They were laden with talented players, and we always had ding-dong battles but managed to still win our zone premiership.

"We were forging our own little dynasty out there at Homebush in the western suburbs."

CHS rugby enjoyed a golden era in the 1960s, with almost 70 public schools involved in the game by the end of the decade, and Homebush was one of the powerhouses.

Homebush players regularly appeared in the CHS first XV, which proved more than competitive against their rivals from NSW's hallowed private school competitions in the annual representative matches.

Highlights of these fixtures for the CHS first XV included a convincing 42-0 defeat of Combined Associated Schools in 1966 and a 28-3 triumph over the Athletic Association of the Great Public Schools in 1968.

The CHS and CAS first XVs pictured playing each other in the 1960s. (Mitchell Library/State Library of NSW/Tourism Australia)

It wasn't uncommon for CHS schools to offer both rugby union and league, and Homebush was no different.

But there's no doubt about which code was the school's top priority.

"The school had a fantastic rugby culture," Bray says.

"We did have rugby league at the school, but rugby union was very much the number one football code."

Homebush's fearsome record in rugby didn't go unnoticed.

It helped convince a talented forward at St Patrick's College Strathfield to ask his parents if he could switch schools.

All roads lead to Homebush

It's fair to say John Symond didn't take the direct route to Homebush Boys High.

"My parents had fruit shops," Symond explains.

"They used to build up a little fruit shop, sell it and get a few bob.

"My older brother, sister and me would hop on the back of an old fruit truck and go to another suburb and so on.

"That is why I went to 11 schools."

John Symond played in the second row for the 1965 Homebush Boys High first XV. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Before starting at Homebush, which was the 11th school, Symond attended St Patrick's for two terms after his family made a mid-year move from Queensland to Sydney.

They had a business in Strathfield, so it made sense for Symond to be enrolled at St Patrick's, which was a Christian Brothers school.

Symond, however, had other ideas.

"The reason I switched to Homebush for my last two years of high school was I was playing sub-district rugby and half of the team all went to Homebush," he says.

"I got my parents to agree for me to switch to this great school I told them about."

Homebush Boys High has paid tribute to John Symond's first XV career. (Facebook: Homebush Boys High)

There was one detail, though, Symond chose to leave out when he spoke with his parents.

"I didn't mention anything about playing rugby, but that was the reason I went," Symond says with a chuckle.

Symond played third grade after arriving at Homebush, before graduating to the first XV in his final year of school.

Like Bray, he would be one of several fresh faces in 1965, while the first XV would also welcome a recruit to their off-field staff.

'Such a good organiser'

When John Coates was drafted into service as the first XV's photographer, Bray gave his close friend a firm instruction.

"The condition was I had to capture his dive pass," Coates says.

His work behind the lens was ultimately given the seal of approval.

"He managed to get a couple of good shots," Bray cheekily says.

Gordon Bray performing the perfect dive pass for Homebush. (Supplied)

Coates was in the same school year as Bray and excelled at rowing as a coxswain.

He would captain Homebush Boys High's rowing squad and earn a school blue.

Coates didn't play rugby but relished being involved with the first XV.

"I was not a footballer," Coates says.

"I had a congenital hip issue, and I had to stop playing as it was too dangerous.

"Because I couldn't play, they were the people I liked to mix with."

Sport meant everything to Coates, and Homebush was the ideal setting to cultivate his passion.

"We had a lot of fun with sport," Coates says.

"It's what you went to school for."

Bray shared Coates's love of sport, but occasionally the pair got up to some old-fashioned mischief.

"My only problem with Gordon was he was one of those who led me on the punt at a young age," Coates says with a laugh.

"We'd nick off from school and get out to Canterbury or Randwick (racecourses). We had a lot of fun."

John Coates has been involved with the Olympic movement for much of his professional life. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

Both knew when it was time to be serious, however, with Coates ultimately given added responsibilities as the first XV's "de facto manager".

But Bray still had an influence on some of Coates's tasks when he began his expanded role.

"Gordon proposed that I select the best-and-fairest award," Coates says.

"Of course, Gordon would win that every week.

"Somehow, Gordon had me consulting or being a team selector as well, which was just as crazy."

The managerial experience held Coates in good stead when he continued his involvement with rowing after school.

His professionalism and attention to detail were among the reasons he quickly rose to become Australia's rowing section manager at the 1976 Montreal Olympics, aged just 26.

It was the start of Coates's remarkable career with the Olympic movement.

John Coates was Australia's chef de mission at six consecutive Olympics. (Reuters)

Among a multitude of appointments, he served as IOC vice-president (2013-17 and 2020-2024) and a member of its executive board (2009-12), and was Australia's chef de mission at six Olympics (1988-2008).

During his tenure as AOC president, Coates played a significant role in Australia's revival on the Olympic medal tally.

"In the final two years at Homebush, he (Coates) was involved in managing the first XV as he was such a good organiser," Bray says.

"You could see Coatesy was one step ahead. He has been our pre-eminent sporting administrator.

"It all began at Homebush."

Authority and charisma

Jack Mason's players didn't feel they needed to ask their coach how he got the nickname 'Pug'.

"He looked as though he had been in the boxing ring with his flattened nose," Bray says with the utmost respect.

Homebush's first XV coach Jack Mason (centre of back row). (Supplied)

Mason began at Homebush as a physical education teacher in 1951 following postings in Dubbo, Mudgee, Parkes, North Strathfield and Ashfield.

He eventually became first XV coach and sports master, the latter being a fitting appointment given his family's athletic pursuits.

Their proudest sporting achievement came when daughter Michele won silver in the women's high jump at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.

Mason wasn't afraid to enforce discipline at Homebush, although first XV players conveniently escaped punishment.

"I remember with PE classes, he would lock up the change rooms and be the last into the gymnasium," Bray says.

"All hell would be breaking loose before he got there.

"He'd arrive, and suddenly everyone would be like, 'Oh God, he's here,' and he would start reprimanding students.

"To anyone in the first XV he would say, 'You're OK.'"

Jack Mason's daughter Michele won an Olympic silver medal as a high jumper. (Getty Images)

As a rugby coach, tactics weren't Mason's strong suit.

"He wasn't a real strategist, but he really believed in us," Bray says.

"He had authority as a coach, but it was more his charisma that had an effect."

Greg Bell also noted Mason wasn't a master tactician, although he couldn't fault his effort.

"He put everything he had into it," says Bell, who first played under Mason in 1964.

"He was as conscientious as anyone could be."

Symond still speaks glowingly of Mason, who he felt had genuine care for his players.

"He was terrific," Symond says.

"He was quite dedicated to our team. He took a real strong interest in us. He was so involved."

Mason may have lacked tactical acumen, but he had an ace up his sleeve.

Late in the 1965 season, 'Pug' called upon a friend who lived near the school.

That friend's name?

George Thomas Bryan Palmer.

Homebush's 'secret weapon'

Bryan Palmer, as he was more commonly known, served as a Wallabies coach during the 1960s.

He also happened to be one of Australian rugby's most enigmatic characters.

"A phenomenon of nature," respected Sydney Morning Herald rugby journalist Phil Wilkins wrote of Palmer in 1967.

"Rugby crusader, psychologist by instinct, bombastic, dogmatic … interesting," Wilkins continued.

"A legend in his lifetime."

Bryan Palmer was one of Australian rugby's more colourful characters. (Classic Wallabies)

Born in 1899, Palmer made his mark on Australian rugby as a player and coach.

He was selected for the famous 1927/28 Waratahs tour of Great Britain, Ireland, France and North America but withdrew because his wife was expecting their first child.

When their son was born, he was named Bryan Rugby Palmer.

In 1931, Palmer was included in Australia's squad for its New Zealand tour but didn't play a Test after suffering blood poisoning.

Bryan Palmer (with the ball) pictured coaching a rugby team in the 1950s. (UNSW Archives)

Fortuitously, he gained his first experience in supervising players after replacing tour manager Tom Davis, who had to return to Australia.

There were numerous coaching appointments in the following decades, including more than one stint in charge of the Wallabies.

Palmer coached NSW with success, recording a stunning 12-11 win over the All Blacks in 1962 and a 21-9 defeat of Ireland in 1967.

The Sydney Morning Herald's headline describing NSW's win over the All Blacks in 1962. (Supplied)

His coaching philosophy was built around demanding commitment from players, both on and off the field.

Hyperbole was frequently used to illustrate his point.

"Nobody's going to get my permission to miss training unless he is dying in his bed," Palmer bluntly told Wilkins when profiled in the Herald.

In 1965, Palmer wasn't called upon by Mason to help at Homebush until the Waratah Shield semifinals.

"He was the one who sat us down and worked out what we were to do and where," Greg Bell says.

Bray describes Palmer as the first XV's "secret weapon".

"He would get us in a huddle and start talking with that gravelly voice, but he wouldn't look at us," Bray says.

"He sort of looked at the horizon. He'd look beyond us. We were just spellbound, just riding every word.

"When he actually made eye contact with you, you felt a really strong personal connection.

"We all bought into it. It was a little bit eerie but very inspiring.

"We couldn't believe just how lucky we were."

Preseason preparations

Before Palmer came on board, the first XV gathered at their home ground, Airey Park, to prepare for the 1965 season.

They knew there were massive shoes to fill.

Bill Laing (left), Greg Bell, Peter Countouris and Nigel Morgan (right) at the first XV's 2025 reunion. (Facebook: Homebush Boys High)

Homebush had won four straight North-West Metropolitan zone premierships in the top grade by this stage, losing only two matches in the competition during the previous three seasons.

Jack Mason also had a hole to plug in terms of team personnel.

The star of the 1964 first XV was captain Tony Ford, rated by revered CHS coach Bill Toft at the time as the best schoolboy fullback he had seen in more than a decade.

On the CHS tour of New Zealand that same year, Ford was given the nickname 'Boots' by none other than the legendary All Blacks fullback at the time, Don Clarke, due to his prodigious talent as a goal kicker.

Clarke was known as 'The Boot' for the same reason.

Ford, who would later play first grade for the Western Suburbs rugby league club, was going to be hard to replace.

An excerpt about Tony Ford from a 1969 edition of The Rugby League News. (Rugby League News)

But Mason believed he'd found a worthy candidate: Dave Hassall.

"Dave was a big, sturdy fullback," Bray says of Hassall, who was also adept at rugby league and cricket.

"He was a goal kicker with a massive boot. A brilliant sportsman."

Along with Bray, Hassall was one of the year-nine students Mason had identified in 1964 as first XV prospects for the following season.

Bruce Shipton (winger), Frank Gardner (centre) and Warren Piggott (utility forward) were the other three.

The squad could still rely on experience, with third-year veteran and loose forward Peter Countouris named captain, and fly half Bell appointed his deputy.

Among other players returning was mobile "line-out specialist" Warwick Hincksman, who towered over the opposition at 6'3" tall.

Homebush Boys High first XV squad Peter Countouris (captain), Greg Bell (vice-captain), Warwick Hincksman, Dave Hassall, David Morgan, Richard Morgan, Nigel Morgan, Wal Krooglik, John Symond, Bill Laing, Gordon Bray, Dave Sayers, Frank Gardner, Victor Amasoff, Bruce Shipton, Trevor Blundell, Warren Piggott

"There was no (preseason) camp or anything like that," Bray says.

"We just rolled up at training. After school, you'd go down to Airey Park, and Jack would do a lot of talking and stand on the sideline and yell at us."

Premiership defence

If Homebush's preseason matches were anything to go by, Mason's bombastic approach to training was having little impact.

Homebush snuck home 3-0 against St Patrick's College Strathfield, before falling 19-8 to North Sydney Boys High, who were the giants of the CHS North Shore zone.

But once the North-West Metropolitan competition began, Homebush hit its straps.

"We had to find some centres because we were short in the back line," Bell says.

"So we got a couple of those (Gardner and Dave Sayers), and we improved as we went along."

Zone matches Opponent Result Epping Boys High 14-11(W) Meadowbank Boys High 16-8 (W) Drummoyne Boys High 19-8 (W) Normanhurst Boys High 13-9 (W) Asquith Boys High 23-3 (W) Epping Boys High 14-9 (L) Meadowbank Boys High 37-9 (W) Drummoyne Boys High 28-6 (W) Normanhurst Boys High 14-8 (L) Asquith Boys High 28-11 (W)

Homebush clinched the zone premiership courtesy of an 8-2 win-loss record, with first-round victories over Epping (14-11), Normanhurst (13-9) and Asquith Boys High (23-3) the highlights.

"The Waratah Shield at the start of the season wasn't a major focus," Bray says.

"Our zone rivals were our main target."

With rugby consuming Bray's life, his studies sometimes took a back seat on Wednesdays when zone matches were played.

As he sat in class ahead of the afternoon kick-off, Bray's mind easily wandered.

"On match day, school lessons were a really big distraction," says Bray, laughing at the memory.

"I remember we always had a double economics period before a match.

"The economics teacher would be shaking his head and saying, 'You're not listening to a bloody word I'm saying, are you?'.

"Of course, I was thinking about the game and psyching up."

'Pretty serious business'

At its participation peak in the late 1990s, the Waratah Shield was contested by more than 150 schools across NSW and the ACT.

The Commonwealth Bank was a naming-rights sponsor for several years, such was the Shield's prestige.

Open to public and private schools, the Waratah Shield featured an array of talent during its heyday.

The Ella brothers (Matraville High), Michael O'Connor (Phillip College), Brett Papworth (Epping Boys High), Ricky Stuart (St Edmund's College), George Smith (Cromer High) … the list can easily go on.

Gary Ella (left), Glen Ella, Eddie Jones and Mark Ella (right) won the Waratah Shield twice with Matraville High. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Named in honour of the 1927/28 Waratahs, the competition was first won by Randwick Boys High in 1963, with Hurlstone Agricultural High School triumphing in its second year.

An "also-ran" in its first two Waratah Shield tilts, Homebush started the 1965 campaign with an 11-6 win over Fairfield Boys High.

Punchbowl Boys High was the next opponent in the quarterfinals, with Homebush claiming a 14-9 victory.

"We didn't know much about Punchbowl," Bray says.

"We played them at Airey Park, and they were mainly rugby league players.

"Once we won that quarterfinal, we suddenly realised this is pretty serious business."

With Homebush safely through to the semifinals, it was time for Jack Mason to bring in the cavalry.

Palmer's words of wisdom

Having orchestrated a win over the All Blacks as NSW coach, Bryan Palmer was over-qualified to be Mason's assistant.

So the first XV weren't surprised when Palmer took control of training ahead of the Waratah Shield semifinal against the highly respected Balgowlah Boys High.

"Poor old 'Pug' Mason, he got left in the wings with Bryan around," Bell says.

"He [Palmer] had so much more acumen and knew what he was doing."

But not all of Palmer's instructions were based around on-field strategy.

"He told the backs we had to be show ponies and entertainers," Bray says.

Gordon Bray worked for ABC Sport from 1969 to 1994. (ABC)

"He said, 'You guys do all the fancy stuff. You have to be immaculately groomed.'

"'I want Brylcreem in your hair. I want your collar up and starched. I want your shorts white and starched.'

"'I want white tape on your boots, and you've got to be able to see your own reflection in the toes.'"

Palmer also gave the forward pack a series of directives.

"They had to rub dirt on their face, Vaseline around their eyebrows," Bray says.

"They had to have dishevelled hair.

"They had to look angry, ugly and mean, and scare the living daylights out of the opposition when they lined up against them before the kick-off."

Palmer's words of wisdom had the desired effect, as Homebush defeated Balgowlah 11-3 at Airey Park to earn a spot in the final.

John Symond's second-row partner Wal Krooglik crossed for a try, which was worth three points at the time.

Prop Nigel Morgan and winger Victor Amasoff also scored tries, while Dave Hassall added a conversion.

By now, excitement about Homebush's chance of winning the Waratah Shield was building at the school.

A year-eight student was even inspired to write the following poem describing the semifinal victory, dedicating the piece to Mason.

Our second rower with pure nerve

Beat the defender with a body swerve.

Passing defenders by and by,

Went near the posts to score a try.

The kick was taken with good flight

And soared inside the left upright.

The opposition soon kicked high

And our prop crashed in to score a try.

The conversion kick this time was missed

But still eight points were on the list.

Their outside centre had some kicks,

But only one between the sticks.

Next our winger went in to score,

To increase the points three further more.

With now the score eleven to three,

We'd won the match quite comfortably.

Next up was the final, with Oakhill College eagerly awaiting Homebush.

A worthy opponent

Based in the north-west Sydney suburb of Castle Hill, Oakhill College was established by the De La Salle Brothers in 1936, the same year Homebush Boys High first opened its doors.

Oakhill's march to the 1965 final included a 13-11 win against Homebush's zone adversary Epping and a 14-6 semifinal victory over Fort Street Boys High.

"Oakhill has always been a good rugby school," Symond says.

"I still see their name pop up every now and then."

The final was played at Chatswood Oval, which hosted a NSW vs Queensland interstate fixture earlier that year.

More than 1,000 spectators made the trip to Sydney's Lower North Shore on a late August afternoon, with Homebush principal Kevin Myers and much of the school's student body coming out to cheer on the first XV.

Contributing to the sense of occasion, Australia's top referee Roger Vanderfield was appointed to officiate the final.

Roger Vanderfield was a prominent figure in Australian rugby for decades. (Getty Images)

Despite the demands of his role as medical superintendent of Royal North Shore Hospital, Vanderfield regularly found time in his busy day to partake in what he described as his "relaxation".

Even family holidays were not off limits.

"Dr Roger Vanderfield, regarded as Australia's leading rugby union referee, will have charge of a non-competition match between Ainslie and Lyneham at Griffith Park at 12:30pm today," The Canberra Times reported in 1965.

"Dr Vanderfield, who is holidaying with his family at Thredbo, requested a game in Canberra as he wanted to keep in condition."

Vanderfield refereed more than 1,200 rugby matches, including 13 Tests.

He served as International Rugby Football Board (now World Rugby) chair, among a series of administrative roles.

When Vanderfield died in 2008 at the age of 80, several obituaries and tributes mentioned he was meticulous about his appearance.

He paid particular attention to his hair, which was noted by the Homebush backs ahead of the Waratah Shield final.

"All the backs were lining up to get to the mirror before the game to make sure there was not a hair out of place," Bray says.

"We were held up for about 10 minutes because of Dr Roger Vanderfield, who had beautifully slickered hair. He was always immaculately groomed.

"He was in front of the mirror for 10 minutes, so it was very frustrating for the backs who could have been stretching and warming up.

"We were all queued up behind him."

Once their grooming duties were completed, the Homebush players — resplendent in the school colours of maroon, blue and white — joined Vanderfield and Oakhill on the field and the final got underway.

'War of attrition'

It may be more than 60 years ago, but Bray's recollection of the final hasn't diminished.

"It was a very dour match, I remember," he says.

"It was a real war of attrition."

On a more light-hearted note, Bray can recall Homebush receiving a helping hand from Symond's parents, courtesy of their fruit shop.

"They used to supply us with the oranges at half-time and full-time," Bray says.

"We had plenty of oranges that day."

Dave Hassall provided Homebush with its early points. (Supplied)

The score was deadlocked at 3-3 during the second half of a titanic affair, with Homebush's points coming via a Dave Hassall penalty goal.

"Defence just dominated. It was a war," Bray reflects.

"Our forwards really got stuck in, but Oakhill was a very good side. It was very hard to make breaks.

"We had excellent backs, and we tried all our fancy stuff, even a little bit of kicking in behind the defensive line with little grubber kicks."

As the final wore on and tension filled the air at Chatswood Oval, it was clear Oakhill wasn't willing to concede.

If Homebush was to get on top, a moment of inspiration would be needed.

Greg Bell knew what he had to do.

Bell's brilliance

Athletic ability came naturally to Bell.

"He was an outstanding sportsman, one of the best schoolboy rugby players I saw," Bray says of his teammate.

"He was quite a nuggety hard-running type. Very aggressive, built like a mini hooker but he was very fast and very skilful, and had a great rugby brain."

Greg Bell's sporting exploits as a teenager attracted local newspaper attention. (Supplied)

Aside from rugby, Bell skippered Homebush Boys High's first XI cricket team to an undefeated zone premiership in 1965, topping the batting statistics with 277 runs at an average of 70.

In baseball, he had played centre field for the NSW under-16 representative team at the national championships.

With the Waratah Shield final on a knife's edge, Bell seized his moment on the halfway line when he found a gap in Oakhill's defence.

"There were a couple of times I cut through between the [Oakhill] five-eighth and the inside centre and one of those was the try in the second half," Bell says.

"I did it in the first half, and they had enough cover defence to tackle me just short of the line."

According to Bray, Bell's try was poetry in motion.

"He burst through on halfway and ran around the fullback," Bray says.

"It was a piece of individual, game-breaking brilliance."

Greg Bell (right) pictured with first XV teammate Bill Laing (left) and principal Kevin Myers. (Supplied)

Hassall's conversion made the score 8-3 in Homebush's favour, but Oakhill refused to give up.

With Bryan Palmer and Jack Mason's match-day addresses ringing in their ears, Homebush's players gritted their teeth and fought through exhaustion to seal victory.

"Their speeches at half-time and before the game were so inspiring," Bray says.

"They said, 'This is going to go right down to the wire, and you guys have got to roll your sleeves up all the way.'

"'If you backs have to get down and dirty in the closing stages, do it.'

"We all just defended, tackled everything in sight and just wouldn't give an inch, so we were able to squeeze home.

Waratah Shield matches Opponent Result Fairfield Boys High 11-6 (W) Punchbowl Boys High 14-9 (W) Balgowlah Boys High 11-3 (W) Oakhill College 8-3 (W)

"There was a sense of euphoria about what we had achieved."

As his teammates celebrated, Bell enjoyed a moment to himself inside Homebush's dressing room.

But he was soon joined by referee Vanderfield.

"Dr Roger Vanderfield walked into the rooms and sat down next to me and said, 'Do you know how you scored that try?'" Bell recalls.

"I said, 'Nah. All I remember is putting the ball down.'

"He said, 'Well, I'll tell you. You cut through here, and then you stayed outside, and you didn't try and cut back in as you had done in the first half.'

"He told me all about it."

After the Waratah win

Homebush Boys High won the Metropolitan North-West premiership in 1966, but its Waratah Shield defence ended in the early rounds following an 11-8 defeat to Hurlstone Agricultural School.

Hurlstone lost the final 20-3 to a Manly Boys High line-up featuring Stephen Knight, who made his Wallabies Test debut against the Springboks three years later.

Gordon Bray is listed among the first XV captains on Homebush's honour board. (Supplied)

Bray captained Homebush's 1967 first XV in his final year, leading the team to another zone premiership.

The Waratah Shield proved elusive, however, with Epping defeating Normanhurst 9-6 in the final to claim the first of three straight titles.

Epping's 1967 captain, Jack Newton, would achieve international sporting fame eight years later when he finished runner-up to Tom Watson at the British Open following a thrilling 18-hole play-off.

Jack Newton (left), pictured with Tom Watson at the 1975 British Open, was a talented junior rugby player. (Getty Images)

A friendly counterpart to Newton on the rugby field, Bray left Homebush amid much praise, with Jack Mason saying he was "close to being the complete halfback."

His 1965 teammates couldn't agree more.

"He (Bray) was one of the best players in the team," Symond says.

"He was a fantastic halfback."

Mason departed Homebush at the end of 1968, retiring from the service of the NSW Department of Education.

He would exit a winner after guiding the school to its eighth consecutive zone premiership.

Homebush continued producing rugby talent and added two more Wallabies to its honour board, Fili Finau and Rodney Blake.

Rodney Blake played seven Tests for the Wallabies in 2006. (Getty Images: Chris McGrath)

Blake was a member of Homebush's 2001 first XV, which won the Metropolitan North-West zone premiership and reached the Waratah Shield quarterfinals.

Incidentally, their quarterfinal loss came at the hands of Oakhill College, who triumphed 26-19.

Homebush no longer enters the Waratah Shield, which is staged in a significantly condensed format (compared to its glory days) and was not contested between 2018-21.

But the school has enjoyed success in other sports, while ex-students Mitchell Starc and the late Phillip Hughes made Homebush proud by playing Test cricket for Australia.

CHS rugby — in the 15-a-side format — isn't as strong as it once was, although the teachers, coaches and players involved aren't at fault.

Rugby programs need funding and resourcing, and the public schools can't compete with the financial war chests enjoyed by those in the private system.

An increase in existing support from governing bodies and clubs is crucial.

"It's got to be a priority going forward," Bray says.

"It takes money, good coaching and equipment."

Return to Homebush

In Bray's words, "10 survivors" from the 1965 first XV returned to Homebush Boys High last November to present the school with a framed photo of the team and speak with students.

Skipper Peter Countouris flew to Australia from his Greek base for the occasion, illustrating how much the Waratah Shield victory meant to the players.

The Homebush old boys regaled current students with stories about the win, as well as their other experiences at the school.

The 1965 Homebush first XV had the chance to catch up 60 years after their triumph. (Supplied.)

For Greg Bell, who was school vice-captain in his final year, there was a touching moment with one of his successors.

"The school vice-captain walked up to me and said, 'I believe you were the school vice-captain, so I was wondering if I could get a photo with you as this means a lot to us,'" Bell says.

"It really showed the school has a great background."

John Coates attended the get-together, much to Bray's pleasure.

"Having John Coates there was very special," Bray says.

"He was a fantastic support for the team. It was so good to have him there for the reunion."

Coates says it was a "wonderful experience", allowing him to reflect on the profound impact Homebush Boys High had on his life.

When IOC officials toured Sydney during the bidding process for the right to host the 2000 Olympics, he made sure to let them know where he did his schooling.

"The Sydney Olympics were basically at Homebush," Coates says.

"When we were first selling the bid, I used to make a point: 'This is where I went to school, just up on the hill there.'"

As the Sydney bid team prepared for the final IOC vote, Coates met with Nelson Mandela during a trip to Africa.

Coates proudly spoke of how Homebush was a beacon of multiculturalism.

"I had an hour with Mr Mandela, along with Gough and Margaret Whitlam, in August 1993 before the vote on Sydney [the following month]," he says.

"In Africa, I was able to talk about the diversity of the students at Homebush Boys High. It was a source of great pride to me."

The reunion gave the ex-players a chance to reminisce about their victory. (Supplied)

John Symond takes delight in recalling his time at the school.

Selected as the 1965 first XV's most improved player, Symond still thinks back to the lessons he took from rugby into the business world.

"The memory I have of that is just outstanding," he says.

"I learned the value of being involved in teams and friendship."

Injury meant Symond could not continue playing rugby after school, while Bray also hung up the boots when his broadcast career intervened.

He joined the ABC as a specialist trainee in 1969, beginning a 25-year career with the organisation.

"It meant my rugby career was over," says Bray, who also worked for the Seven and 10 networks.

After Bray's playing days were cut short, calling international rugby provided decades of highlights.

But there's a moment that will always hold a special place in his heart.

"That Waratah Shield win is one of my most cherished memories," Bray says.

World.title: AFL's first publicly gay player calls for respect in Crows-Pies match
World.content:
Leigh Ryswyk has never taken his partner to a footy presentation night.

He said players in heterosexual relationships might not give the action a second thought, but for athletes from the LGBTQIA+ community it could be a source of anxiety.

Ryswyk made history four months ago, when he became the first current or former AFL player to publicly come out as gay.

"It was really emotional, it really was … when I heard myself say 'I'm gay' on radio, I actually cried," Ryswyk said.

"It's been a whirlwind … a lot of fun, it's been great."

The former Brisbane Lions player said he had not been treated any differently since coming out and has called on fans to show respect during tonight's match between Adelaide and Collingwood.

Leigh Ryswyk is calling on fans to act respectfully during the Crows clash with Collingwood. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The clash will be the first time Crows midfielder Izak Rankine faces the Pies since directing a homophobic slur at Isaac Quaynor in round 23 last year.

Rankine received a four-game ban and expressed remorse for his actions.

The last time Adelaide hosted Collingwood, sections of the crowd booed Quaynor, which the Crows later described as "disappointing and not appropriate".

Ryswyk said the booing was unfair because Quaynor had not done anything wrong.

"We want people to be calling things out because in the community we don't want these things here … we want the world to be a better place for everyone in it," he said.

Izak Rankine was suspended for four matches. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Ryswyk said it was also important to move on when lessons had been learnt.

"I think Izak's done the work and his actions will show that," he said.

Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks also urged fans to refrain from inappropriate conduct.

"We'll do what we can to entertain and put on a show that's what it's about, we ask our supporters to just enjoy that and then be respectful like we ask of all our players," Nicks said.

Step in the right direction

In 2024, the Free to Exist report found more than half of queer people have witnessed discrimination in sport.

Ryswyk, who now plays in SA for the Barossa Districts Football Club, said although there had been some incidents of homophobia in the VFL this year, he believed progress had been made across leagues.

Leigh Ryswyk speaks with North Melbourne players at Arden Street (Supplied: North Melbourne FC)

The North Melbourne Football Club on Wednesday became the first AFL club to invite Ryswyk to host an education session about LGBTQIA+ inclusion in the game.

He said he would be more than happy to present at other clubs, should they reach out.

Ryswyk said his teammates had been "so supportive" and he had received messages and notes from people around the world who had since worked up the courage to come out.

"If there's a queer kid out there who goes 'I don't know if I can be in that footy world', because they don't see anyone like them … if I can help one kid, that's why I did it," he said.

"If [I] can help someone else be who they are, then it puts a smile on my face."

Leigh Ryswyk designed this pride jumper for his current club, Barossa Districts. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Ryswyk also designed pride jumpers for his local club's women's side, while the men's team wore rainbow arm bands to celebrate pride round for the first time this year.

"We're not trying to change football, we're just talking about inclusion and diversity and how that makes others feel," he said.

He said his partner attended the pride game and the club made him feel comfortable.

He plans to bring his partner to his end of year football presentations for the first time this year.

World.title: Your guide to every day of the Commonwealth Games in Australian time
World.content:
With 10 sports crammed into 10 full days of action in Glasgow, it may be hard to keep track of what's on and when at the Commonwealth Games.

So, here's the full schedule of every day of the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games with all times and days in AEST.

You can find the full official schedule here. Organisers say all schedule details are subject to change, depending on a number of criteria.

Day 0 (July 23-24)

Aussie watch:

There was not supposed to be any competition on Thursday before the opening ceremony, but an extra session of bowls and para bowls was added because of what organisers described as "unprecedented demand".

Bowls (6:30pm to 1:25am)

Sectional play — Men's singles, Women's pairs, Para mixed pairs B2-B3.

Opening ceremony (5am, July 24)

Held at The Hydro at the Scottish Event Campus, which will also host the netball.

KT Tunstall is headlining and is joined by Tom Walker, Nina Nesbitt, Valtos, Callum Beattie, and Nathan Evans and Saint Phnx.

More than 600 volunteers are also performing.

Day 1 (July 24-25)

Aussie watch:

The first full day of competition and the first medals will be awarded early in the para powerlifting.

The swimmers hit the water with Lani Pallister a major favourite in the 400m freestyle at 4am, Australia's youngest athlete in 14-year-old Mia Hogan swims in the S13 100m freestyle, and the night wraps up with the 4x100m freestyle relays (Australian women have won gold at every Commonwealth Games since 1998, the men have won the past four).

This is the only day of para powerlifting, featuring 2022 women's bronze medallist Hani Watson in the women's heavyweight category.

3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball (7pm-6:30am)

The first day of group matches across men's, women's, women's wheelchair and men's wheelchair competition split across three sessions.

The Australian able-bodied men play New Zealand, Nigeria and hosts Scotland; the abled-bodied women play Kenya, Jamaica and Fiji; while both Australian wheelchair teams take on England.

Artistic gymnastics (7pm-6:15am)

Men's team final and individual qualification.

Bowls (5:30pm-7:15am)

Sectional play — Men's singles, Women's pairs, Para mixed pairs B2-B3.

Boxing (8pm-6:45am)

Women's — 54kg Round of 16, 57kg Round of 32, 60kg Round of 16.

Men's — 55kg Round of 32, 65kg Round of 64, 70kg Round of 32.

Para powerlifting (10pm-6:30am)

Men's and women's lightweight medals will be decided in the early session (10pm to 1:30am).

Both heavyweight divisions will be decided from 3am to 6:30am.

Swimming

Early heats (7:30pm-10pm): Women's 400m Freestyle heats, Men's 200m IM Heats, Women's S13 100m Freestyle Heats, Men's S13 100m Freestyle — Heats, Women's 200m Backstroke — Heats, Men's 50m Backstroke — Heats, Women's 50m Butterfly — Heats, Men's 100m Breaststroke — Heats, Women's SM10 200m Individual Medley — Heats, Men's S10 100m Butterfly — Heats, Women's 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay — Heats, Men's 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay — Heats

Late finals and semis (4am-7am): Women's 400m Freestyle — Final, Men's 200m Individual Medley — Final, Women's S13 100m Freestyle — Final, Men's S13 100m Freestyle — Final, Women's 200m Backstroke — Final, Men's 50m Backstroke — semifinal, Women's 50m Butterfly — semifinal, Men's 100m Breaststroke — semifinal, Women's SM10 200m Individual Medley — Final, Men's S10 100m Butterfly — Final, Women's 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay — Final, Men's 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay — Final

Day 2 (July 25-26)

Aussie watch:

Australia starts its netball gold medal defence against Tonga, captained by Queenslander and former Firebirds mid-courter Hulita Veve.

Gymnast Georgia Godwin, a two-time gold medallist at Birmingham 2022, hits the Glasgow International Arena as she continues her comeback from a torn Achilles tendon. She will be joined by Emily Whitehead, Kate McDonald and Breanna Scott, who also won team silver four years ago, with 19-year-old Paris Olympian Ruby Pass the only new face in the squad.

Sam Short starts his packed schedule (200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m) with the 400m heats and final, and Mollie O'Callaghan and Lani Pallister go in the women's 200m freestyle.

3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball (7pm-6:30am)

The Australian teams have the day off.

Artistic gymnastics (7pm-5:45am)

Women's team final and individual qualification.

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

Bowls (5:30pm-7:15am)

Sectional play — Men's singles, Women's pairs, Para mixed pairs B2-B3.

Boxing (8pm-6:15am)

Women's — 65kg Round of 16, 70kg Round of 16, 75kg Round of 16

Men's — 60kg Round of 32, 65kg Round of 32, 80kg Round of 32

Netball (6pm-7:30am)

The Diamonds take on Tonga in the first of their group games in the early session, likely after 7:30pm.

Swimming

Early heats (7:30pm-10pm): Women's 200m Freestyle — Heats, Men's 50m Freestyle — Heats, Women's 100m Backstroke — Heats, Men's 100m Butterfly — Heats, Women's 100m Breaststroke — Heats, Men's 400m Freestyle — Heats, Women's S14 200m Freestyle — Heats, Men's S14 200m Freestyle — Heats, Mixed 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay — Heats

Late finals and semis (4am-7am): Men's 400m Freestyle — Final, Women's 100m Backstroke — semifinal, Men's 50m Freestyle — semifinal, Women's 200m Freestyle — Final, Men's 50m Backstroke — Final, Women's 50m Butterfly — Final, Men's 100m Butterfly — semifinal, Women's S14 200m Freestyle — Final, Men's S14 200m Freestyle — Final, Women's 100m Breaststroke — semifinal, Men's 100m Breaststroke — Final, Mixed 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay Final

Day 3 (July 26-27)

Aussie watch:

The Diamonds face an early test, taking on 2018 gold medallists England from about 7:30pm.

World record holder Cam McEvoy hits the water for the 50m freestyle final, distance queen Lani Pallister returns for the 1,500m, and rising 17-year-old Sienna Toohey shoots for the first of three potential medals in Glasgow, in the women's 100m breaststroke.

Georgia Godwin will be hoping to defend her 2022 individual all-around gold medal.

3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball (8:30pm-6:15am)

Australian able-bodied men face Guyana and Cayman Islands; able-bodied women face Cayman Islands and Uganda, men's wheelchair face Kenya; women's wheelchair face South Africa.

Artistic gymnastics (9pm-6am)

Competitors for the men's and women's individual all-around finals are selected based on rankings from the team finals, with a maximum of two gymnasts from each country allowed.

The men's individual all-around final runs from 9pm to midnight across floor, pommel horse, rings, vault, parallel bars and horizontal bar.

The women compete from 3am to 6am across floor, vault, uneven bars and beam.

Bowls (5:30pm-7am)

Sectional play — Men's singles, Women's pairs, Para mixed pairs B2-B3

Boxing (8pm-6:45am)

Women's — 57kg round of 16.

Men's — 55kg round of 16, 65kg round of 16, 90kg round of 16, 90kg+ round of 16.

Netball (6pm-7:30am)

The Diamonds face an injury-hit England in the second game of the first session, after Wales vs Scotland from 6pm.

Swimming

Early heats (7:30pm-9:45pm): Women's 100m Freestyle — Heats, Men's 50m Breaststroke — Heats, Women's 1,500m Freestyle (Slower Heats), Men's 200m Backstroke — Heats, Women's 100m Butterfly — Heats, Men's S9 100m Backstroke — Heats, Women's S9 100m Backstroke — Heats, Men's 4 x 200m Freestyle Relay — Heats

Late finals and semis (4am-7:15am): Women's S9 100m Backstroke — Final, Men's S9 100m Backstroke — Final, Women's 100m Breaststroke — Final, Men's 100m Butterfly — Final, Women's 100m Freestyle — semifinal, Men's 50m Breaststroke — semifinal, Women's 100m Backstroke — Final, Men's 200m Backstroke — Final, Women's 100m Butterfly — semifinal, Men's 50m Freestyle — Final, Women's 1500m Freestyle — Final, Men's 4 x 200m Freestyle Relay — Final

Weightlifting (6:30pm-6am)

Men's — 60kg and 65kg

Women's — 48kg

Day 4 (July 27-28)

Aussie watch:

The athletics program starts, marking the first of three days that feature swimming as well as track and field.

Australia's much-hyped sprint stars hit the track in the men's and women's 100m heats. And, after silver in 2018 and bronze in 2022, Rhiannon Clarke tries to complete her set of Commonwealth medals with a gold in the women's T37/38 100m final.

Mollie O'Callaghan, Shayna Jack and Meg Harris go for back-to-back podium sweeps for Australia in the women's 100m freestyle.

3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball (8:30pm-6:15am)

Australian men's and women's wheelchair teams take on Canada.

Artistic gymnastics (10pm-2:30am)

Individual finals for the men's floor exercise, pommel horse and rings; and women's vault and uneven bars finals.

Athletics

Early heats and qualifying (7pm-10:30pm): Women's high jump qualifying, hammer throw qualifying, 100m heats, 100m T37/38 heats; Men's 400m hurdles heats, long jump qualifying, 100m heats, T37/38 100m heats, 110m hurdles heats

Late finals session (3:30am-7am): Women's 100m T37/38 final, F55-57 shot put final, 800m heats, 10,000m final; Men's T37/38 100m final, 110m hurdles final, high jump final, hammer throw final, 3,000m steeplechase final, T20 1,500m final

Bowls (5:30pm-7am)

Sectional play and semifinals — Men's singles, Women's pairs, Para mixed pairs B2-B3

Boxing (8pm-6:30am)

Women's — 51kg round of 16

Men's — 60kg round of 16, 70kg round of 16, 80kg round of 16

Netball (11pm-7:30am)

No Diamonds today as group games continue.

Swimming

Early heats (7:30pm-9:15pm): Men's 200m Butterfly — Heats, Women's 400m Individual Medley — Heats, Women's 50m Backstroke — Heats, Men's 100m Freestyle — Heats, Women's 50m Breaststroke — Heats, Men's 800m Freestyle (Slower Heats), Women's SB8 100m Breaststroke — Heats, Men's SB9 100m Breaststroke — Heats, Women's 4 x 200m Freestyle Relay

Late finals and semis (4am-7am): Women's 400m Individual Medley — Final, Men's 100m Freestyle — semifinal, Women's 100m Freestyle — Final, Men's SB9 100m Breaststroke — Final, Women's SB8 100m Breaststroke — Final, Women's 100m Butterfly — Final, Men's 50m Breaststroke — Final, Women's 50m Backstroke — semifinal, Men's 800m Freestyle — Fastest 8, Women's 50m Breaststroke — semifinal, Men's 200m Butterfly — Final, Women's 4x200m Freestyle Relay — Final

Weightlifting (6pm-7:30am)

Men's — 71kg and 79kg

Women's — 53kg and 58kg

Day 5 (July 28-29)

Aussie watch:

The men's and women's 100m semifinals and finals will hopefully feature some Australians. And the women's high jump final gives Nicola Olyslagers (bronze in 2018) and Eleanor Patterson (gold in 2014 and silver in 2022) a chance to add to their hauls.

Kyle Chalmers aims for more gold in the men's 100m freestyle, with Lani Pallister (800m freestyle), Mollie O'Callaghan (50m backstroke) and defending 200m breaststroke champion Zac Stubblety-Cook also in action.

The Diamonds take on Malawi in their third group game on Wednesday morning.

3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball (2:30am-6:30am)

Two semifinal qualifiers for each of the four disciplines.

Artistic gymnastics (10pm-2:30am)

Individual finals for the men's vault, parallel bars and horizontal bar; and women's beam and floor exercise finals.

Athletics

Early heats and qualifying (7pm-9:30pm): Women's heptathlon day one, discus qualifying, 400m heats, shot put qualifying; Men's 800m heats, 400m heats

Late finals session (3:30am-7am): Women's heptathlon day one, high jump final, 100m semis and final, hammer throw final; Men's 100m semis and final, T20 long jump final, 10,000m final

Bowls (5:30pm-7am)

Medal matches — Men's singles, Women's pairs, Para mixed pairs B2-B3; Sectional play — Men's pairs, Women's singles, Para men's pairs B6-8, Para women's pairs B6-8

Boxing (9pm-6:15am)

Women's — 54kg quarterfinals, 60kg quarterfinals, 65kg quarterfinals, 75kg quarterfinals

Men's — 55kg quarterfinals, 65kg quarterfinals, 90kg quarterfinals

Netball (11pm-7:30am)

More group games, including Diamonds vs Malawi in the late session from 4am.

Swimming

Early heats (7:30pm-10:15pm): Men's 400m Individual Medley — Heats, Women's 200m Individual Medley — Heats, Men's 50m Butterfly — Heats, Women's 50m Freestyle — Heats, Men's 200m Breaststroke — Heats, Women's 800m Freestyle (Slower Heats), Men's 100m Backstroke — Heats, Women's S13 50m Freestyle — Heats, Men's S13 50m Freestyle — Heats, Mixed 4 x 100m Medley Relay — Heats

Late finals and semis (4am-7:15am): Men's S13 50m Freestyle — Final, Women's S13 50m Freestyle — Final, Men's 100m Freestyle — Final, Women's 200m Individual Medley — Final, Men's 400m Individual Medley — Final, Women's 50m Freestyle — semifinal, Men's 50m Butterfly — semifinal, Women's 50m Backstroke — Final, Men's 200m Breaststroke — Final, Women's 50m Breaststroke — Final, Men's 100m Backstroke — semifinal, Women's 800m Freestyle — Fastest 8, Mixed 4 x 100m Medley Relay — Final

Weightlifting (6:30pm-6am)

Men's — 88kg

Women's — 63kg and 69kg

Day 6 (July 29-30)

Aussie watch:

The Diamonds have perhaps their toughest match-up of the group stage against South Africa on Thursday morning.

Rising athletics star Cam Myers starts his campaign in the mile, while 44-year-old veteran Eliza Ault-Connell chases her fourth Commonwealth Games medal and is joined by Mikaela Dingley in the women's 1,500m T53/54.

The swimming program wraps up with Lakeisha Patterson trying to equal her haul of three Paralympic gold medals with a third Commonwealth title in the women's 100m S9 freestyle. And Sam Short completes his packed schedule with the men's 200m and 1,500m freestyle finals on the same night.

3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball (8:30pm-6:30am)

Semifinals from 8:30pm to 12:30am, and medal matches from 1:30am to 6:30am.

Athletics

World.title: How we got to Glasgow 2026 and what the Commonwealth Games will look like
World.content:
As we adjust our body clocks from the FIFA World Cup, you would do well to stay a little out of whack as the 2026 Commonwealth Games kicks off in Glasgow.

It's been an unusually rocky road for the sporting carnival, so here's what you need to know.

When are the Glasgow Commonwealth Games on?

The 2026 Commonwealth Games start on July 23 and run through until August 2 (the early hours of August 3 in Australia).

The first event of the Games takes place on Day Zero, with an extra session of bowls and para bowls added to the schedule (from 6:30pm AEST July 23 to 1:25am July 24) due to "unprecedented demand".

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

Later that day, the opening ceremony will be held from 5am AEST on July 24.

Track and field star Nina Kennedy will be Australia's flag-bearer and para swimmer Tim Hodge will carry the King's baton.

Most days, competition will start about 5:30pm AEST and wrap up the following morning after 7am, with swimming (July 24–30) and athletics (July 27 — August 2) finals in that morning slot.

ABC Sport will be live blogging every day of the Games.

Weren't they supposed to be in Victoria?

Oh boy, were they ever.

It was a rollercoaster year for then-Victorian premier Daniel Andrews. (AAP: James Ross)

There was an initial campaign from regional centres in Victoria — Greater Shepparton, Wodonga, Bendigo, Ballarat, Warrnambool and Traralgon — to host the 2030 Games.

Then, in April 2022, it was confirmed that the Commonwealth Games would head to Victoria four years early, in 2026, centred in Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo and Gippsland, with an opening ceremony in Melbourne.

Then-premier Daniel Andrews spruiked the jobs, infrastructure and income the Games would bring to the regions and promised "a Commonwealth Games like no other".

Daniel Andrews gleefully announced the success of the bid in Ballarat. (ABC Ballarat: Lexie Jeuniewic)

Turns out he was right, just not in the way he or we might have expected.

Over time, criticism of the decision mounted, adjustments were made to the plans, and costs blew out.

Then, in July 2023, just 15 months after winning the hosting rights, the Victorian government announced it was pulling out of hosting, much to the chagrin of Commonwealth Games Australia and the international organising body.

Andrews said the cost, initially slated to be $2.6 billion, was looking more like $6 billion and it was no longer tenable.

Loading...

Shortly after withdrawing, the then-government reached an agreement to pay $380 million in compensation to the Commonwealth Games Federation (now Commonwealth Sport), Commonwealth Games Federation Partnerships and Commonwealth Games Australia.

In September 2024, it was announced Glasgow would host again, 12 years after the 2014 Games in the Scottish capital, albeit with about $200 million from Victorian taxpayers.

As a result of the truncated planning time, a month later organisers announced the slate of sports would be cut way back.

So, what sports are being played at Glasgow 2026?

Glasgow hustled to put together these Games with just 10 sports, down from more than 20 (depending on how you count it) at the 2022 Games in Birmingham.

Hockey, diving, badminton, beach volleyball, cricket, road cycling, mountain biking, rhythmic gymnastics, rugby sevens, squash, table tennis, triathlon and wrestling were all ditched, leaving us with:

3x3 basketball and 3x3 wheelchair basketball

Artistic gymnastics

Athletics and para athletics

Bowls and para bowls

Boxing

Judo

Netball

Para powerlifting and weightlifting

Swimming and para swimming

Track cycling and para track cycling

Where will the events be held?

The Hydro will host the netball and opening ceremony at the 2026 Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The events selected meant the slimmed-down Games could be hosted in existing venues in a 13-kilometre corridor along the River Clyde.

Swimming will be held at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre and Scotstoun Stadium will host the athletics.

Glasgow International Arena will pull double duty as the venue for track cycling (at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome) and artistic gymnastics.

The Scottish Event Campus includes three venues: The Hydro, which will host the opening ceremony and the netball; the Armadillo, for weightlifting and para powerlifting; and the SEC Centre, a series of exhibition halls where the basketball, bowls, boxing and judo will play out.

Who is competing for Australia?

Australia is sending 255 athletes to Glasgow, competing in every sport on the program.

The athletics team has 86 competitors, while the Dolphins are bringing 59 swimmers.

World.title: Kennedy arrives early to lead Australia into Glasgow opening ceremony
World.content:
Nina Kennedy will carry the Australian flag in the Glasgow 2026 opening ceremony before she tries to defend her Commonwealth Games pole vault title.

Kennedy is the first of the Australian athletics team to touch down in Glasgow, with the track and field program not starting until Monday.

"I am so proud to follow in the footsteps of so many great Australians who have carried the flag before me. The Commonwealth Games have always meant so much to me; it's where I won my first medal back in 2018," Kennedy said.

"This is my third Games, and I'm lucky enough to be defending my title. My final isn't until later in the week, so I'll get a bit of a sleep-in the morning after.

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

"I've worked with our team to make sure I'm as prepared as I can be, and there's no version of the Games where I'd miss the chance to carry that flag."

Kennedy won gold in Birmingham after claiming silver four years earlier on the Gold Coast.

Since then she has broken the Australian record, become a world champion in 2023 and won Olympic gold in 2024.

A torn hamstring wiped out her 2025 season, including the chance to defend her world title last year, but she has returned to competition without missing a beat in 2026, breaking the national record for a 10th time just two weeks ago in Monaco.

"I've had a long road with injuries to get back to this point, so to be trusted with this now, on top of everything else so far this season, means more than I can really put into words," she said.

Kennedy will be joined by another reigning gold medallist, para swimmer Tim Hodge, who will carry the King's Baton at Friday morning's (AEST) ceremony at the Hydro.

Hodge is defending SB9 100m backstroke gold from Birmingham. (Reuters: Jeremy Lee)

Hodge's international journey began in Glasgow as a 14-year-old at the 2015 Para Swimming World Championships.

2026 marks his third Commonwealth Games, where he will try to defend the SB9 100m backstroke gold he won in Birmingham.

"I've been lucky enough to compete at two Commonwealth Games already, and I've watched the team come into the stadium both times and felt so much pride watching the green and gold walking in," Hodge said.

Australia's Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games baton. (Supplied: Commonwealth Games Australia)

"To now have that role myself, to have it happen in Glasgow of all places, the same city where I made my international debut, means the Games already feel special.

"It's the first time that I'll march too. I'm usually competing first day. I can't wait to feel the excitement."

The baton relay started at Buckingham Palace in March last year, when King Charles III put his full message into Scotland's baton.

Unlike previous years, every nation has their own, each containing one word of the message, which will be read in full by the King at the opening ceremony.

It is also the first time a King's baton has been carried for the Commonwealth Games, with the royal tradition starting at the 1958 Cardiff Games, five years after the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.

World.title: Eels defend Luai's 2027 signing ahead of Chiefs move
World.content:
Parramatta coach Jason Ryles says he is unapologetic about agreeing to Jarome Luai's one-season stopover at the Eels.

Luai, who is the PNG Chiefs' marquee recruit for 2028, last week signed with the Eels for next season.

A four-time premiership winner with the Panthers, Luai was released by Wests Tigers, which want to give their younger halves opportunities in first grade.

Ryles said he had no concerns Luai's arrival would discourage Parramatta's halves prospects.

Luai joins Parramatta, Marshall slams relationship breakdown rumours Benji Marshall has slammed "bull**** rumours" claiming a fractured relationship with Jarome Luai contributed to the star five-eighth's early exit from Wests Tigers.

He said signing Luai was a win for the 15th-placed Eels' stable of younger halves options, which includes Joash Papalii, Lincoln Fletcher and Lorenzo Talataina.

"We're sitting in a spot on the ladder that we don't want to be," Ryles said.

"It's no-one's fault directly but we need more experienced players. Jarome fits that bill at the moment.

"We have got younger players that are coming through our pathways and our system that may be ready in 12 months.

"But this gives them an extra bit of time to … learn off a true pro that's won a lot of premierships."

Amid a season of injury concerns for the Eels, centre Will Penisini could return from osteitis pubis via reserve grade this weekend.

Ryles said he was hopeful veteran prop Junior Paulo and outside back Bailey Simonsson would be back from their long-term injuries in "the next one or two weeks".

World.title: Lewis breaks Australian 100m record, beats five-time Olympic champ
World.content:
Torrie Lewis has set a new Australian women's 100 metres record after breaking her own national record at a meet in Slovakia.

Lewis ran a time of 11.04 seconds, beating her previous record time of 11.08 as she beat out Jamaica's five-time Olympic champion Elaine Thompson-Herah, who finished in second.

The 21-year-old Lewis also competed in and won the 200m event, where she ran a 22.66.

It is the third separate time Lewis has broken the Australian 100m record, having previously done so as a 19-year-old in 2024 by running an 11.10 before lowering that mark to 11.08 at last year's World Championships.

Lewis beat out Jamaican sprint icon Elaine-Thompson Herah (pictured). (Getty: Al Bello)

Lewis made her Olympic debut in the 200m event in Paris two years ago and finished in the semifinals after running a then-personal-best time of 22.89. She also competed in the 4x100m event in Paris.

The women's 100m record is owned by late American sprint legend Florence Griffith-Joyner, who ran a 10.49 at the US Olympic trials in 1988. Thompson-Herah holds the second-fastest 100m mark of all time at 10.54.

Griffith-Joyner also holds the world record for the 200m, 21.34, a mark she set at the 1988 Olympics in Seoul.

Both records are among the longest-standing across all women's athletics.

The career-best 100m time comes at the perfect time for Lewis, who is poised to compete in the 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Tech.title: Meta won’t have to face the next planned social media addiction trial
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Less than a week before Meta’s lawyers were set to return to a Los Angeles courtroom, the plaintiff accusing the platform of inflicting harm dropped the case. Brought by 15-year-old Florida plaintiff going by initials R.K.C., the case was set to be the second in a set of bellwether trials meant to test legal arguments that social media giants allegedly broke the law by creating features that hooked and harmed teens.

TikTok, Snap, and YouTube previously settled claims brought by R.K.C. for undisclosed amounts. “In light of the overall successful result of the litigation and his concerns about enduring a grueling weekslong trial, he has elected to withdraw his claims against Meta,” R.K.C.’s lawyers Emily Jeffcott and Rahul Ravipudi said in a statement. “He’s ready to close this chapter and focus on his recovery and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a normal life.” That means Meta got out of this case without having to pay a settlement. “The claims never held up, and this outcome makes clear that we will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said in a statement.

Meta got out of this case without having to pay a settlement

Multiple cases have already begun to test claims about social media companies allegedly misleading users about the safety of their products and inflicting harm. Meta and Google’s YouTube lost the first bellwether case tried at the courthouse, with a jury finding them to be negligent and ordering them to pay a total of $6 million in compensatory and punitive damages to the single plaintiff. Separately, a New Mexico jury ordered the company to pay a $375 million penalty, and the state is preparing for the next phase of trial seeking structural business changes.

There’s still seven more bellwether cases on deck in the California state courthouse in LA, and a separate set of cases pending in a federal court in Oakland. Meta, Tiktok, Snap, and YouTube settled with a school district that was set to be the first in that separate set of bellwether cases seeking money to cover mental health-related costs to students allegedly caused by their platforms. Meta is still set to face claims brought by state attorneys general in federal court next month, alleging that it illegally misled the public about harmful and allegedly addictive features.

Tech.title: Tesla’s revenues are bouncing back, but profits are still weak
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After a dismal two years of weakening demand, falling sales, and damage to its brand by Elon Musk’s political activities, Tesla’s road to recovery continues apace. On the heels of an impressive delivery report, the company released its earnings for the second quarter of 2026 — giving us the latest glimpse at the EV company that Musk has said he wants to transform into a leader of AI and robotics.

Despite that mission, Tesla remains a car company. And in the second quarter, it sold an impressive 480,126 vehicles, about a 25 percent increase compared to the second quarter of 2025. (For a direct-to-consumer company like Tesla, deliveries are a proxy for sales.)

Tesla certainly did a good job shrinking its inventory, which is good for the balance sheet. But what about those numbers?

Tesla certainly did a good job shrinking its inventory, which is good for the balance sheet. But what about those numbers?

Tesla said it earned $1.11 billion in net income on $28.2 billion in revenue in the quarter that ended June 30th. That’s a 26 percent increase in revenue but a 5 percent increase in profits over the second quarter of 2025, when the company earned $1.17 billion in net income on $22.5 billion in revenue. Tesla exceeded revenue expectations from Wall Street, which assumed approximately $26.4 billion in revenue.

But there were still signs of trouble. The company reported negative free cash flow of $1.1 billion, a sign that Tesla’s operating revenues are insufficient to cover its capital expenditures. Basically, Tesla is spending more — on AI infrastructure, robotics, and manufacturing — than its earning on car sales and energy installations. Last year, some analysts predicted that negative free cash flow could trigger a steep drop in share price. (Tesla’s share price is down 14 percent so far this year.) The company said it had $43.5 billion in cash on hand, but its capital expenditures were up year over year 142 percent to $5.7 billion this quarter.

In a shareholder deck, Tesla said it “generated over $100B in revenue on a trailing twelve-month basis for the first time.” It also touted Cybercab production at its Gigafactory in Texas, and said Tesla Semi production “remains on track” at its Nevada facility later this year. And it said it began construction for its Optimus humanoid robot production at the factory in Fremont after decommissioning the assembly line for the Model S and X.

“Tesla is in its largest and most exciting period of investment,” the company states. “From here, there remains much hard work as we aim to revolutionize transportation, energy and productivity through our leading real-world AI. Scaling will be non-linear, and we are focused on long-term value creation. We’ve never been more optimistic about the future.”

Automotive gross margins, which measures revenue minus the direct cost of manufacturing the vehicle, remains an important number for Tesla. They fund the company’s multi-billion dollar investments in AI, autonomous driving, and robotics, while also providing a buffer for Tesla to slash vehicle prices when demand slumps.

In the second quarter, Tesla said its automotive gross margins were 16.3 percent, minus revenue from the sale of regulatory credits (a revenue stream that will soon cease to exist, after the Trump administration’s elimination of penalties for automakers who exceed emission standards). That’s up over the 15 percent margins in Q2 2025, but down from 19.2 percent in Q1 of this year.

YANTAI, CHINA - JULY 03 2026: New IM5 electric cars wait for shipment to overseas market in a port in Yantai in eastern China’s Shandong province, Friday, July 3, 2026. (Photo credit should read stringer/ Feature China/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

Tesla’s energy business remained a bright spot for the company. It reported $3.1 billion in energy generation and storage revenue, a 13 percent increase over the same period in 2025.

The earnings report is the latest evidence that Tesla was starting to turn the corner on a dismal two years of declining sales and falling profits. It also comes as the company faces tough questions about its slow progress in expanding its robotaxi operations. Tesla’s autonomous vehicle project has fallen far short of Musk’s prediction of covering 50 percent of the US population by the end of 2025. The company recently launched robotaxi operations in two Florida cities, Orlando and Tampa, but a crowdsourced tracker shows only a handful of cars were available.

Tesla rolled out a new update to Full Self-Driving (v14 Lite) for its vehicle owners, bringing personalized driving preference learning to individual Teslas. But the number of crashes involving Tesla drivers using Autopilot and FSD continues to grow at an alarming rate, with Electrek reporting 207 crashes in May 2026 alone.
